REPORT

The main thrust of the programmes and activities of the Department of Scientific and
Industrial Research (DSIR) relatés to research by industry, technology transfer, National
Information System for Science and Technology (NISSAT) and management of two public
sector undertaking, NRDC and CEL. While the short term objectives of the programmes on
research by industry and technology transfer are promotion of R&D by industry and
enhanced efficiency of technology transfer both within the country and from outside. The
long term objective of these programmes is technological self-reliance. The broad objectives
of NISSAT are to provide scientific and technological information, promote information
sharing and support development of information systems. The Department also looks after
all matters concerning the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) which
functions autonomously as a registered society and as a network of 40 laboratories and 81
field stations/extension centres/regional centres spread all over the country.

2. The Committee was informed that CSIR laboratories have responded to the changes
introduced by the industrial, economic and trade policies which were initiated by
Government in recent years to integrate the Indian economy with the global economy.
Successful technology transfers have taken place in many areas. Some of the laboratories
have entered into collaborative agreements with multinationals and internationally renowned
business houses. The laboratories work in close collaboration with Indian industry and
provide complete solutions, technology packages, turnkey plants, consultancy, etc. The
Committee was told that CSIR is also contributing significantly to the accomplishment of the
various societal programmes requiring S&T inputs. It has increased significantly its income
from sources outside direct central Government grants to it. The Secretary, DSIR informed
the Committee that besides industrial research, CSIR has commitments to support futuristic
areas and basic research.

3. The Secretary, DSIR informed the Committee that CSIR has been doing well over
the years and to highlight his point he drew the attention of the committee to the fact that in
respect of CSIR laboratories, fram 1992-93, every year the total external cash flow is
increasing at a rate of over 20%. What is particularly encouraging is that the component
from industry, which is indicative of CSIR linkages with industry, is increasing at a faster
rate. He informed the Committee that the global business of CSIR is also increasing and it is
exporting technologies to concerns like DuPont and many other well known international
firms. If one takes another measures of successful accomplishments like the number of
international patents which CSIR laboratories are filing, the product value of the goods that
are coming out as a result of R&D carried out in CSIR laboratories and in terms of basic
science and good research publications, one finds that CSIR, inspite of a lot of constraints
has been making good progress. The Secretary elaborated on this by providing the following
information to the Committee. During 1993-94, 198 patents were filed nationally and 80
were granted, which is 14 of the total patents filed in the country. Internationally, the CSIR
laboratories filed 18 patents out of which they were granted 12. With regard to the
technology development and transfer, during 1993-94, the number of processes licensed (first
time) were 35. 180 agreements were signed and a sum of Rs. 1.06 crores was earned as
royalty and premium. During that year about 2100 publications were brought out. The
Committee was also informed that the industrial production based on the CSIR knowhow is
also increasing. In monetary terms the industrial production through: CSIR knowhow during
the year 1993-94 was Rs. 2250 crores. This amount is expected to increase to Rs. 2500 crores
in 1995-96.


4. In its Thirteenth Report the Committee had made certain recommendations regarding
the modernisation of the CSIR laboratories, removal of obsolescence and the upgradation of
facilities. In that Report the Committee had also expressed the opinion that economy
measures and budgetary cuts applied by the Government from time to time should not affect
scientific and technological research that have been approved after careful consideation.
There were other aspects like providing of enough funds to the Department for meeting its
committed liabilities under non-plan sector, etc. which needed clarifications from the
Planning Commission. The Committee had, therefore, decided that the representatives of
the Planning Commission should also be requested to give their views on the
recommendations of the Committee contained in its Thirteenth Report.

5. The Committee examined the budgetary allocations of the Department for the year
1995-96.” While considering the Demands for Grants-of the Department, the Committee also
got an opportunity to review the work relating to various projects and programmes which
fall within the mandate of the Department.

6. The Principal Adviser, Planning Commission informed the Committee that no
economy measures and budgetary cuts were applied on the Department during 1994-95. No
such cuts are envisaged during the Annual Plan 1995-96 either. Regarding the modernisation
programme, it was clarified that the Annual Plan (1995-96) proposals of DSIR, (including
CSIR), were jointly reviewed by the Planning Commission and DSIR/CSIR. The plan
allocation was decided on” the basis of commitments on the various programmes and
availability of resources. With regard to the modernisation programme of CSIR laboratories,
the requirement projected by CSIR was considered during the mid-term review. Taking into
consideration the resource position, a sum of Rs. 10 crores was additionally provided for
selective modernisation during the annual plan 1995-96; this was specifically based on the
follow-up of the recommendations of the Committee. The Committee was told that,
depending on the projectisation of modernisation programme and generation of internal
resources through sponsored research, etc. suitable allocation would be considered at an
appropriate stage.

7. The Secretary, DSIR underlined the need to modernise facilities at the national
laboratories in order to carry out research of international standard and to be globaily
competitive. He informed the Committee that an in-depth exercise was initiated by all the
forty constituent laboratories of CSIR and a modernisation programme was chalked out both
in respect of equipment and facilities. The proposal was submitted as part of the Mid-term
Appraisal Document to the Planning Commission. A requirement of Rs. 100 crores was
Projected for the year 1995-96. The Planning Commission appreciated the need for
modernisation of the CSIR laboratories and suggested that CSIR should indicate its
requirements project-wise along with the financial implications so that a comprehensive view
could be taken on the proposal by the Planning Commission. Subsequently, CSIR initiated
an exercise and six specific tasks/programmes were identified which were in the area of
Catalysts, CFC Substitutes, New Drugs, Food, Wood Substitute and Coal Beneficiation.
After detailed examination the Finance Minister was approached to provide an additional
support of Rs. 40 crores to CSIR for the year 1995-96 so as to accomplish the specific tasks
and build confidence, capability and credibility of the CSIR system.

7.1 The Committee appreciates the fact that the Planning Commission has recognised the

*For details of the Demands for Grants see schedule.


3

need for modernisation of the CSIR laboratories which have a great role to play in the
changed economic climate; and for the year 1995-96 it had recommended an additional outlay
of Rs. 10 crores for selective modernisation of CSIR laboratories in relation to specific
projects. The Committee, however, is of the view that selective modernisation of CSIR
laboratories based on specific project areas whilst of value, and providing a sharper focus for
accomplishing relevant research will not gear the system to deal with the new situation of
globalization and intense international competition. A carefully planned one-time grant to
remove obsolescense and to modernise the facilities is called for. At the same time the
Committee also realises the over-all resource constraints. The Committee has noted with
satisfaction that the external cash flow generated by CSIR is increasing. The Committee is,
therefore, of the view that the Planning Commission may consider providing matching grants
equivalent to the extra budgetary resources generated by CSIR in future and a part of it can
be utilised for modernisation of its laboratories on a continuing basis. However, convinced of
the need for immediate modernisation of some of the laboratories of CSIR, the Committee
strongly recommends that a one-time grant of Rs. 50 crores may be provided for the year
1996-97 which is the last year of the Eighth Five Year Plan.

8. Last year, in its Thirteenth Report, the Committee had noted that CSIR had been
diverting funds from plan allocation to meet the expenditure in the non-plan category. The
Committee had recommended that enough funds be allocated to CSIR to enable it to meet
its committed liability under non-plan so that the need for such diversion of plan allocation
did not arise; and the plan funds could be utilised for their primary purpose.

8.1 The Secretary, DSIR informed the Committee that utilisation of plan funds for
committed non-plan liabilities has been of concern to CSIR as also to both the Planning
Commission and the Ministry of Finance. During the mid-term appraisal of the Eighth Five
Year Plan, the Planning Commission had expressed the view that the most important
drawback in the CSIR system was that the plan funds were being utilised for non-plan
commitments. Due to the efforts of the Planning Commission and DSIR the Ministry of
Finance had allocated an additional non-plan outlay to CSIR for the year 1993-94. But this
had given only partial relief to CSIR. An additional allocation of Rs. 27.79 crores was
provided for 1993-94, and for 1994-95 a sum of Rs. 16.50 crores was allocated at the R.E.
stage to partially offset the increase in committed liabilities under non-plan.

8.2 In the budget estimates for the year 1995-96 the total budgetary allocation for CSIR
is Rs. 384.85 crores out of which Rs. 233.85 crores is the non-plan component and remaining
Rs. 161 crores is the plan component. According to the Secretary, the anticipated non-plan
committed expenditure during 1995-96 is Rs. 301.50 crores. There is thus a difference of Rs.
77.65 crores between the anticipated non-plan expenditure and actua! allocation. This deficit
would be met from the internal resources of CSIR to the extent of Rs. 25 crores, and the
balance of Rs. 52.65 crores would have to come from plan funds.

8.3 The Committee takes note of the fact that despite a clear recommendation to make
sufficient provision in the non-plan outlay of CSIR to meet its committed liability, adequate
non-plan allocation has not been made in the budget estimates for the year 1995-96. The
Department will have to still divert money from its plan funds to meet its committed liability
under non-plan. The Committee would like the Department to sort out this problem with the
Planning Commission and the Ministry of Finance so that plan funds are not diverted to non-
plan activities. Such a diversion adversely affects the R&D activities of the Department. DSIR
should also make an intensive study of the so-called committed non-plan expenditure to see
how this could be reduced progressively. A continuing increase under this Head is clearly
undesirable and cannot be supported in the long run.


8.4 The Committee also hopes that the Department would estimate its non-plan
commitments for the Ninth Five Year Plan well in advance following the guidelines issued by
the Planning Commission so that the unusual situation of meeting non-plan liabilities by
diverting plan funds does not arise in the subsequent years.

9. Last year this Committee had recommended that the Emeritus Scientist Scheme
should be examined from the viewpoint of funds available, effectiveness, desirability of
enlargement, etc. The Comimittee wanted to know the views of the Planning Commission on
providing additional plan budgetary support for human resource development activities,
including the Emeritus Scientist Scheme, a proposal which was sent to the Planning
Commission by the Department for being considered at the mid-term appraisal of the Eighth
Plan concerning the activities of the Department.

9.1 The representative of the Planning Commission pointed out to the Committee that
the outlay to DSIR for the human resource development programmes like Fellowships,
Scientists’ Pool, Emeritus Scientist Scheme, etc. are supported under the non-plan sector. In
addition, plan support is provided for extra-mural research. He assured the Committee that
though the Emeritus Scientist Scheme is covered presently under non-plan segment, if,
however, the Scheme is projected under plan, depending on the resource position, necessary
funds would be provided. The Secretary, DSIR, elaborating on the pointed raised by the
Committee said that there had been an increase of Rs. 5 crores in the non-plan budget
estimated for the year 1995-96 on the Scheme for Human Resource Development. On the
plan side the existing level of Rs. 4 crores had been maintained during 1995-96. The
Emeritus Scientist Scheme has been provided financial support to the extent of Rs. 60 lakhs
in 1995-96 as compared to Rs. 51 lakhs last year.

9.2 The Committee expresses its happiness over the fact that in this year’s budget of
DSIR there is an increase of Rs. 5 crores in the outlay earmarked for Human Resource
Development. The Committee hopes that with this increased allocation, the Department would
support more of such fellowships and associateships as have a definite bearing on scientific
and industrial development; there should be some emphasis in these schemes for the backward
regions and disadvantaged sections of society.

10. Answering a question on in-house R&D, the Secretary informed the Committee that
in-house R&D in industry is undertaken by the industrial units themselves with their own
finances. DSIR is the administrative department which grants recognition to in-house R&D
centres set up by industry, which on the basis of such recognition, are permitted certain
facilities and can avail of tax exemptions. He informed the Committee that about 1250
industrial units have set up R&D centres which have received recognition from DSIR. These
centres concentrate on R&D for improvement of product/process, quality improvement and
cost reduction. These centres also work on the absorption of imported technology. The
incentives and support measures presently available for encouraging R&D in industry
include: Income Tax Relief on R&D expenditure as per 1.T. Act; 125% Weighted Tax
Deduction for sponsored research programmes in approved national laboratoriesinsitutions;
Accelerated Depreciation Allowance on plant and machinery based on indigenous
technology; Price Control Exemption on production of bulk drugs based on indigenous R&D
efforts; Financial Support for R&D programmes taken up by industry either in-house or
jointly with national laboratories/institutions; and National Awards for outstanding K&D
achievements.

10.1 As regards the scheme of Weighted Tax Deduction, as per the notification of
September, 1993, approved research programmes sponsored by industry in any of the


National Laboratories functioning under CSIR, ICMR and ICAR were eligible for the
Weighted Tax Deduction under I.T. Act, 1961. By a notification issued in November, 1994
the scope of the scheme was widened to cover the laboratories of Defence Research
Development Organisation, Department of Electronics, Department of Biotechnology and
Department of Atomic Energy, Universities and Indian Institutes of Technology. The
Secretary informed the Committee that DSIR had given wide publicity to the scheme. As on
31st March 1995, four sponsored research programmes valued at Rs. 43.85 lakhs by industry
in the CSIR laboratories have been approved by DSIR and one more programme is under
consideration.

10.2 The Committee is happy that Government is providing incentives for encouraging in-
house R&D in industry; and the scheme of Weighted Tax Deduction, which originally existed,
and after being abandoned for sometime has been brought back is, no doubt, attractive to
bring about interaction between industry and the Government laboratories. Though DSIR has
given wide publicity to the Weighted Tax Deduction Scheme through newspaper advertisement
and in-house R&D Industry Update, as also through the workshopsconferences organised by
DSIR, the Committee feels that this scheme still requires more publicity and promotion. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that publicity for this scheme may also be organised
through electronic media, besides newspaper advertisements, etc. In addition DSIR will have
to organise get-togethers on specific areas/projects where industry and national R&D can
work together to mutual advantage. Major promotional efforts to bring about increasing
interaction is called for.

11. Last year the Committee had recommended that DSIR should strengthen its
linkages with socio-economic Ministrie/Departments with regard to society-related
programmes. The Committee was ihformed that dialogues have been initiated with socio-
economic Ministries/Departments, State Government agencies and NGOs with a view to
identifying societal needs which called for development of appropriate technologies and their
transfer to the beneficiary groups. The interaction has particularly been strengthened with
the socio-economic Ministries and scientific departments. These departments have provided
additional allocations, in the areas of leather, water oilseeds and pulses, bio-technology,
environment, ocean sciences, electronic materials, etc. S&T inputs to small scale sectors are
also being offered. :

11.1 The Committee notes that, with regard to society-related programmes, the
Department has set up linkages with several socio-economic MinistriesDepartments and
scientific departments: The Committee hopes that such linkages would generate various locale
specific approaches and appropriate technologies for the benefit of rural masses and society-
related programmes.

12. Programme Aimed at Technological Self-Reliance (PATSER) of DSIR aims at
promoting and accelerating the efforts of industry to undertake Research, Design,
Development, Engineering (RDDE) Projects for Technology Absorption and Technology
Development. The Committee was told that these projects have considerable commercial
potential and relate to new ‘or improved project/process technologies. Through this scheme,
strong R&D linkages have been established between industry, national laboratories and
institutions as well as user industry. While examining the allocation for this scheme the
Committee noticed an increase from Rs. 7.68 crores in the last year’s budget te Rs. 9.23
crores in the budget estimate for the year 1995-96. The Committee wanted to know the
reasons for this increase.

12.1 It was explained to the Committee that over 30 new projects have been supported


under the programme by DSIR during the year 1994-95. In addition, there are about 30 on-

" going projects of industry which have been approved by DSIR before 1994-95. Budgetary
estimates for these projects in 1994-95 under PATSER was Rs. 7.68 crores. In order to meet
further financial requirements of these on-going projects in 1995-96 amounting to Rs. 4
crores, as well as financial requirements of over Rs. 5 crores for about 30 new projects to be
supported by DSIR during 1995-96, a budget estimate of Rs. 9.23 crores was indicated under
PATSER. Financial commitment of industries for these projects has been on an average
about 70% of the Project costs.

12.2 The Committee hopes that, by supporting an increasing number of important RDDE
projects of industry having high techno-socio-commercial inputs, PATSER will be able to
enhance its thrust during 1995-96 in promoting and accelerating the efforts of industry in
technology development as also involving industry in developing and commercialising new and
improved products or processes in various sectors of economy which would strengthen
linkages between industry and national research organisations. The Committee would like
DSIR to make a study of the approach adopted by MITI of Japan for such purposes. The
Committee would also like DSIR to examine how funding from the to-be-established
Technology Development Fund (under DST) can be used meaningfully in this area.

13. The Committee wanted to know if any of the CSIR: laboratories is working in the
area of Developing Neem as contraceptive and for any other medical uses. To this, the
Secretary replied that the Central Food Technological Research Institute, Mysore; Indian
Institute of Chemical Technology, Hyderabad; and National Chemical Laboratory, Pune are
working on deyelopment of Neem-based derivatives for insect control. No CSIR laboratory
is developing Neem as a contraceptive. The National Institute of Immunology and Defence
Institute of Physiology and Allied Sciences, however, are working on its development as a
spermicidal agent. According to the Secretary, CSIR labs are developing soap nut as
spermicidal agent for use as a vaginal contraceptive and it is under Phase III clinical trials.

14. The Committee also expressed concern over the arsenic contamination in potable
water in some areas of West Bengal which is a problem of very serious magnitude. The
Committee wanted to know if CSIR could help in the matter. The Committee was told that
detection of arsenic in potable water will not be difficult and some of the CSIR laboratories
could help in detecting and assessing degree of contamination.

14.1 The Committee hopes that CSIR would ensure that its relevant laboratories provide
belp in solving the problem of arsenic contamination in potable water in some parts of West
Bengal and would provide whatever assistance would be required by the Public Health
Engineering Department of that State to chalk out a programme to tackle the problem.

15. The Committee referred to the shortage of residential accommodation for the
scientists working in the CSIR laboratories and wanted to know about the steps which are
envisaged by the Department to tackle the situation. The Secretary, DSIR explained that
residential accommodation is a major problem, particularly in the metropolitan cities. The
satisfaction level is around 26% on an average. For 1995-96 a budgetary provision of Rs.
13.5 crores has been made under the scheme on residential building.

15.1 The Committee expresses its concern over the shortage of residential accommodation
for scientists working in the CSIR laboratories. Lack of residential accommodation is a
éeterrent to attracting talented scientists to CSIR and it will even be difficult to retain
talented people if no proper accommodation is made available to them. The Committee,
therefore, feels that more funds be earmarked for this activity in the coming years. The
Department should also encourage staff members to build their own houses and Government
could consider enhancing the present limit of House Building Advance admissible to the
employees.


16. After making a detailed scrutiny of the Demands for Grants of the Department of
Scientific and Industrial Research and assessing the progress of various important
programmes and projects administered by it, the Committee recommends that the Demands
for Grants of Rs. 411.03 crores, as sought by the Department of Scientific and Industrial
Research for the year 1995-96, under demand No. 73 are in order and may be approved.

INTRODUCTION 
The Ministry of Science and Technology was established in 1971 to formulate 
and implement Science and Technology polic ies, identify, and promote "frontline" 
research in science and technology infrastr ucture. The Ministry ha s three Departments, 
namely Department of Science & Tec hnology, Department of Biotechnology and 
Department of Scientific and Industrial Re search. Through Department of Science and 
Technology, the Ministry coordinates intra- governmental and international cooperation 
and provides funding for domestic institutions and research programs. The Department of 
Scientific and Industrial Re search is a technology tran sfer organization, and the 
Department of Biotechnology, runs a number of developmental laboratories. 
2. The following constitute the mandate of DST:-  
 Formulation of policy statements a nd guidelines on Science and Technology 
(S&T). 
 Promotion of new areas of scientific research. 
 Co-ordination of inter-Departmental S&T efforts. 
 Support basic and applied research in universities and other institutions. 

 International S&T Co-operation. 
 Support high quality research in autonom ous bodies where specialization ranges 
from advanced medical research materials to astronomy. 
 Catalyzing S&T interaction in societal  programmes, and entrepreneurship 
development.  
 Science popularization, communicati on and S&T Management Information 
System. 
 Promotion of Commercialization of home grown technology. 
 Support to technology development prog rammes, technology information and 
assessment. 
 Providing services in the areas of: 
(i) Surveying & Mapping  
(ii) Technology Development and Application  
3. ORGANISATIONAL SETUP 
3.1 The Department of Science & Technology is the nodal Department of the 
Ministry of Science and Technology.  The Or ganizational Structure of the Department 
has evolved over the years to re spond quickly to the issues relating to the promotion and 
development of Science & Technology in the country. Broadly, the organisational set up 
of the Department has been divided into Autonomous Institutes, Scientific Groups, 
Technology Development Board, Scientific Services besides the Administration and 
Integrated Finance divisions. Ther e are 19 Autonomous Institutes and 5 
Science/Engineering Professional bodies wh ich are working in diverse areas for the 
promotion of Science and Technology. In addition, one new autonomous body viz. 
National Centre for Molecular Material  Rese arch, Thiruvanathapuram has been recently 
set up and National Innovation Foundation, Ahmedabad which was earlier a ‘Corpus 
Funded’ Financial Institute  has been taken over by the Department  as fully funded 
autonomous Research Institute. The Scientific Groups inter-alia consists of the Science 
& Engineering Research Council (SERC), Na tional Council for Science & Technology 
Communication (NSCTC), National Resources  Data Management System (NRDMS), 
International Division, Nati onal Entrepreneurship Board (NEB), National Science and 
Technology Management Information System (NSTMIS). The Scientific Services has 
two subordinate offices, viz., National Atlas and Thematic Mapping Organisation 
(NATMO) and Survey of India (SoI) under its administrative control. 
3.2 The detailed budget allocation of the De partment of  Science and Technology, for 
the year 2013-2014 was considered by the Department-related Committee on Science & 
Technology, Environment & Forests on the 16
th April, 2013.

7. Science, Technology and Innovation Policy 2013 
7.1 Department of Science and Technol ogy is primarily entrusted with the 
responsibility to formulate Policies, their implementation, identification and promotion of 
thrust areas of research in different sect ors of science and technology and assessment of 
science and technology activities in the country.   
7.2 The Department formulated Technology Policy Statement in 1983 and two 
decades later, Science and Technology Policy was introduced in 2003.  New Science 
Technology and Innovation Policy has been initia ted this year by the Department which 

was released by the Prime Minister at the 100 th Session of Indian Science Congress at 
Kolkata.  Some of the key elements of the policy include:- 
 Promoting the spread of scientific tempers amongst all sections of society. 
 Enhancing skill for applications of science among the young from all social strata. 
 Establishing would class infrastructure for R&D for gaining global leadership in 
some select frontier areas of science. 
 Positioning India among the top five global scientific powers by 2020 and 
 Fostering resource-optimized, cost-effective innovations across size and 
technology domains.  
7.3 When the Committee enquired about th e performance of Science & Technology 
Policy 2003, the Department stated that Science and Technology Policy 2003 stressed on 
raising the quality of life of the people of the country, particularly  of the disadvantaged 
sections of society, by creating wealth fo r all; making India globally competitive; 
utilising natural resources in a sustaina ble manner, protecting the environment and 
ensuring national security, etc.   
7.4 The Department further informed that  since the enunciation of the Science & 
Technology Policy 2003 several new programmes and schemes have been introduced to 
vigorously foster scientific research in universities and other academic, scientific and 
engineering institutions; to attract the brightest young persons to pursue careers in science 
and technology by conveying a sense of excite ment concerning the advancing frontiers, 
and by creating suitable employment opportunities for them.  
7.5 The Department also informed that th e industrial R&D investment grew by 250% 
and the sales by 200% between 2005 and 201 0.  The gross budgetary support for the 
science and technology sector has significantly  increased during the last decade.  The 
impact of such increase is becoming evident.    Another significant achievement of STI 
Policy, 2003 is now India ranks ninth globally in the number of scientific publications 
and 12th in the number of patents filed.  Th e Composite Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) of 
global share has increased from 1.8% in 2001 to 3.5% in 2011. 
7.6 Focus Areas of STI Policy, 2013 
 The main advantage of STI Policy,  2013 over Science & Technology Policy,2003 
is that the former seeks to integrate innova tion, as an instrument of Policy which was 
hitherto not  accorded due importance,  with Science & Technology.  Science, technology 
and innovation can though exist separately on their own in disconnected spaces, it is their 
integration that leads to new value cr eation.  Innovation thus implies Science & 
Technology 
Based solutions that are successfully deployed in the economy or society. 
7.7 The Department informed that with th e STI Policy, 2013, the Department’s focus 
would be on  preparing statement for aspi rational goals; to focus on innovation for 
application of knowledge for wealth and va lue creation; to adopt evidence-based 
approaches for policy development; to enrol stakeholders through wi de consultations; to 
focus on Public Private Partnership for attractin g private sector investment into R&D; to 
strike a balance in R&D priorities- excellence and relevance; to approach by integrating 
science, research and  innovation system for high technology  led path as a specific policy 
goal; and to include measurements and accountability as indicators for investments. 
7.8 Department further added that the Gove rnment has taken some other important 
measures to encourage Research and Devel opment in the country namely: induction of 
new and attractive fellowships; strengthe ning infrastructure for Research and 
Development (R&D); and encouraging public-private R&D partnerships, etc.  

7.9 The Committee understands that STI Policy, 2013 is a Policy document which 
draws a broad roadmap which inter-alia includes use of science & technology for the 
benefit of people and advancement of India as a global scientific power.  These are 
undoubtedly noble objectives but to make them laudable the Department needs to pursue 
them with all vigour and earnestness in order to ensure that they do not remain  only on 
paper but are translated into reality.  
7.10 The Committee, therefore, recommends that the key goals enshrined in the 
Policy document should be realised within the given timeframe particularly the goal 
of positioning India amongst the top five global scientific powers by 2020 and the 
Department must make all out efforts to achieve these goals.

resources with value addition for Income  generation - aiming towards providing 
affordable technology solutions for better livelihood opportunities and improved quality 
of life. For making wider technology impact, an integrated development programme on 
resource management and livelihoods generati on was implemented exclusively in 25 SC 
dominated villages in Madhya Pradesh, Ma harashtra, Gujarat,  Rajasthan, Andhra 
Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Kerala. Development of workable technology packages like 
energy-efficient rural jaggery-making system s; briquetting technology package using 
invasive biomass and fuel efficient stov es with reduced fuel wood consumption; 
development of energy efficient cooking devi ces; small scale unit for extraction of non-
edible oil at village level;  water manage ment in difficult areas.  Artificial glacier 
technology in Leh-Ladakh region;  setting up of small scal e extraction unit of virgin 
coconut oil in Nicobar island and development of value added products from fresh mahua 

(Madhuca indica ) flowers to generate employment in  the rural areas etc. are other 
tangible deliverables of the programme showing potential to benefit society at large and 
SC & ST population in particular.  
12.4 In this endeavour, a long term Core gran t extended to 21 science based  voluntary 
groups under societal programme of DST has enabled them to do innovative and adaptive 
R & D in rural and other disadv antaged areas thus providing  technological solutions at 
the village level  for livelihood generation & so cietal benefits including Scheduled Caste  
&  Scheduled Tribes  population in their geographical coverage area.  
12.5 The Committee feels that in a country such as ours, where a large section of 
the population lives in abject poverty, te chnological achievements made in the 
laboratories would be more  valuable it these also address the cause of the 
underprivileged masses and help in alleviat ing their poverty.  In this context, the 
Committee appreciates the programme undertaken by the Department for 
livelihood generation and improving the quality of life of people at large particularly 
the scheduled castes and scheduled tribes  by providing affordable technology 
solutions and other scientific interventions.   
12.6 The Committee, however, would like to see such benefits extended further to 
cover more and more scheduled castes  and scheduled tribes population and 
accordingly, recommends that the Depa rtment should further expand this 
programme.  
13. MODERNISATION OF MAPPING ORGANIZATIONS (SoI AND 
NATMO) 
13.1 The National Atlas and Thematic Mappi ng Organization set up in 1956 primarily 
aims at preparing National Atlas of India.  Subsequently, its scop e and activities were 
extended to new fields of geographical research, themat ic mapping covering all the 
academic and applied aspects of geography and allied subject.   
13.2 Survey of India, the National Survey  and Mapping Organisation of the country 
under the Department of Science & Tech nology, is the oldest organisation of 
Government of India, set up in 1767.  As the Nation’s principal mapping agency, SoI 
bears special responsibility to ensure that  the country’s domain is  explored and mapped 
suitably to provide base maps  for expeditious and integrated development and that all 
resources contribute their full  measure to the progress, pros perity and security of our 
country now and for generations to come.  Th e Department is undertaking infrastructure 
modernization and technical skill developmen t of Survey of India (SoI) and National 
Atlas and Thematic Mapping Organi zation (NATMO) under the programme 
“Modernization of Mapping Organizations”.  
13.3 So far as the Budgetary allocations are concerned, the Committee finds that 
programme for Modernisation of Mapping Or ganisations was allocated   350.86 Crores 
at B.E. 2012-13 which was reduced to Rs 333.0 7 crores at R.E. 2012- 13 i.e. a reduction 
of  17.79 crores. However, the Department could utilise an amount of  276.36 crores 
by 22
nd February,2013 thus showing underutilisa tion of 66.71crores.  At B.E. 2013-14, 
allocation has been incr eased to .348.62 crores i.e. an increase of about 15.55 crores 
over R.E. 2012-13, despite the fact that both SoI and NATMO failed to fully utilize the 
B.E. allocation. When asked about the reas ons for underutilisation of fund, the 
Department replied that the curtailment of funds at RE 2012-2013 stage was mainly 
attributable to 10% cut imposed on Non-Plan  expenditure by Ministry of Finance.  
Further, from the ‘Salaries’ head of SoI, .11.47 crores was curtailed due to non-
proportionate expenditure.   Hence the allocati ons of both organizations were reduced by 
.17.79 crores at R.E. 2012-13.   

13.4 The Committee desired to know as to  what measures were taken for 
modernization of SoI and NATMO.  Informin g about the schemes for modernization of 
NATMO & SoI, the Department informed th at during the financial year 2013-14, both 
SoI and NATMO proposed to initiate certain schemes and measures for modernization.  
Survey of India proposed to take up the following Plan Schemes : 
(i) Formation of Geospatial Data set fo r National Geospatial Information System 
(NGIS) 
(ii) Redefinition of India Vertical Datum 
(iii) Creation of National Topogra phical Database on 1:10,000 scale 
(iv) Modernization of Tidal Gauge Network 
13.5 Through these Schemes, efforts would be made to mode rnize/upgrade the 
equipments, hardware and software availa ble in SoI; Introduce new technological 
innovation in the field e.g. Advance methods  of Data Capturing, Digital Aerial 
Photography, Digital Photogramme tric Processing, Data storage and Dissemination, etc.  
Capacity building of the human resources by  upgradation of techni cal skills; and up 
gradation and modernisation of the office buildings and other estates. 
13.6 NATMO proposed to mould its activities towards the path forward into the Geo-
spatial space by way of using geo-spatial te chniques in preparation of Micro, macro and 
meso-level maps in NATMO.  Software, Ha rdware, Computer peripherals, Geospatial 
Information system (GIS), Global Positio ning System (GPS) gadgets were being 
procured by NATMO.  NATMO is using GIS,  GPS and Remote Sensing techniques and 
their utilities for catering to geo-spatial data  and other utilities which could be used for 
planning and development by the government bodies as well as the common people of 
the country. The Rashtriya Atlas Bhavan of NATMO is going to be completed very soon 
which will house a special Geo-spatial laboratory.   
13.7 The Committee notes that the Department  is undertaking modernisation and   
upgradation of infrastructure and techni cal capabilities of SoI and NATMO under 
the programme “Modernisation of Mappi ng Organisations”.  The Committee, 
however, notes that in the year 2012-13, Department failed to fully utilise funds 
made available to it under this programme .  Modernisation of infrastructural 
facilities and upgradation of data capturing and processing capabilities and 
technical skills of these organisations a re  essential for efficient exploration and 
mapping of the country's domain and to ensure that all resources  available in the 
country contribute their full measures to the progress, prosperity and security of 
our country.  The Committee, therefore, expresses its displeasure that the 
Department has not even been able to fu lly utilise funds meant for upgradation of 
infrastructure of its two important or ganisations and recommends that the 
Department should take all necessary measures to ensure early and successful 
implementation of this programme.   
14. DISHA PROGRAMME FOR WOMEN SCIENTISTS 
14.1 The Department informed the Committee that during the year 2012-13, under this 
programme 20 new projects to benefit women had been sanctioned. Apart from this, 176 
projects under Women Scient ists Programme (WOS)-A schol arship scheme; 29 projects 
under WOS-B scholarship scheme and 100 sc holarships for training in IPR under WOS-
C scheme were sanctioned by the Department during 2012-13.  
14.2 The Department further informed that ‘DISHA’ for women science and 
technology professionals have been re-looked and redesigned in a holistic manner. New 
initiatives have also been incorporated to address the mobility issue among the women 

scientists and to use the women scientific pool available to work and address societal 
issues through technological solutions and effective science communication.  
14.3 Coming to budgetary allocations to the programme the Committee finds that at 
BE 2012-13, the DISHA programme was allocated . 49 crores and have been enhanced 
by . 4 crores i.e. . 53 crores during the current fiscal 2013-14.   
14.4 The Committee notes that DISHA Programme has been launched by the 
Department to encourage women to pursue a career in science research as also for 
augmenting the pool of women scientists in the country and is a socially useful 
programme.  The Department has funded projects and provided scholarship to 
women scientists under this programme.  Th e Committee, further, notes that there 
has been a marginal increase in the funds allocated to the programme in the current 
fiscal year and hopes that Department will make efficient use of funds allocated in a 
transparent  and objective manner so th at objectives of the programme are 
achieved. 
15. SCHOLARSHIPS FOR RETAININ G RESEARCH TALENT AND 
PROMOTION OF SCIENCE IN THE COUNTRY 
15.1 The Committee desired to know the de tails of efforts being made by the 
Department for retaining research talent in  the Country and initia tives announced in the 
new Science, Technology and Innovation Policy, 2013  to check brain-drain. Replying to 
the query the Department informed that Ministry of Science and Technology is 
implementing several initiatives including the fellowship scheme to attract and retain 
Indian scientists who have se ttled in various part s of the world for pu rsuing research in 
India in their respective field of  expertise as well as in home country research programs.  
These initiatives include:-  
(i)  “Ramanujan Fellowships” seeks to attract brilliant scientists and engineers from all 
over the world to take up scientific research  in India. The Ramanujan Fellows can work 
in any of the scientific institutions and universities in the country and they are eligible for 
receiving regular research grants through the extramural funding schemes of various S&T 
agencies of the Government of India. Sin ce its inception, 184 Indian origin scientists 
working abroad have been offered this “Fellowship”  
(ii)    “ Innovation in Science Pursuit for Insp ired Research (INSPIRE)” Faculty 
Award under ‘Assured Opportunity for Research  Careers (AORC)’ scheme initiated in 
July, 2011 provides opportunity to the scie ntists under 32 years of age who have 
completed their doctoral research from any recognized university/ academic institution in 
the world. Each “INSPIRE Faculty Awardee”  receives a consolidated amount equivalent 
to the scale of the Assistant Professor of an IIT as Fello wship amount with .7 lakh per 
year as Research Grant for 5 years.   
(iii) Collaborative projects with Scientists  and Technologists of Indian Origin (CP-
STIO): The programme seeks to attract the Scientists and Technologists of Indian Origin 
for strengthening institutional and human capacity building.  
(iv)    Young Investigator Meet (YIM): It is organized every year in India and overseas 
to create awareness amongst scientists working in overseas laboratories.  
15.2 The Department has further informed  that with stagnation of R&D funding 
systems in developed economies and improveme nts in R&D funding pattern in India, 
there are indications of reversal  of flow of researchers at this time especially after the 
implementation of 6
th pay commission recommendations. There are also indications of 
attracting talent from manu facturing sector within th e national employment market. 
While international experience in research is  to be welcomed, bleeding-out of talent for 
research for want of opportunities in India needs to be avoided.  

15.3 Informing about the initiatives take n in the new Science, Technology and 
Innovation Policy 2013 the Department apprised that the Policy envisages making careers 
in science, research and innovation attractiv e enough for talented and bright minds. It 
also envisages, establishing world class infrastructures for R&D; creating an environment 
for enhanced private sector participat ion in R&D and creating a robust national 
innovation system that will be conducive to stop the brain drain.    
15.4 The Committee commends the measures taken by the Department to attract 
and retain Indian scientists who have se ttled in various parts of the world for 
pursuing research in India in their respectiv e field of expertise as well as in home 
country research programs and notes with satisfaction that measures taken have led 
to reversal of flow of researchers.  The Committee recommends that further 
measures be taken to make career in sc ience, research and innovation lucrative 
enough to attract best talent available in the country.   
16. NEW PROGRAMMES PLANNED DURING THE XII PLAN        
16.1 The Department of Science and Technology has started two major new 
programmes namely “Building National Capaci ty and Capability for High Performance 
Computing” and “National Geospatial Informat ion System” (NGIS) in the XII Five Year 
Plan. These are large nationally coordinate d projects with super-ordinate goals and 
expectations.  
16.2 These two programmes have been a llocated budgetary support amounting to 
.100.00 crores and .200.00 crores respec tively at B.E. 2013-14.  The Committee 
desired to know the aims and objectives of these new programmes and the roadmap 
drawn under National Geographic Informati on System (NGIS) to enable smooth 
transition of the country from e-governance to geo-spatial governance.  A brief account 
of aims and objectives of these two schemes provided by the Department is given below:-  
16.3 SUPER COMPUTING FACILITY AND CAPACITY BUILDING : 
The Planning Commission has drawn a Na tional Supercomputing Roadmap in the 
XII Plan which covers seve ral aspects of supercompu ting, namely, architecture, 
supercomputing grid resting on National Know ledge Network and the million core cloud 
supercomputer.  The aim of the scheme is  to undertake projected development of high 
capacity petascale (over 1,000,000,000,000,000 flops) supercomputers and technologies 
that may create an opening lead ing to building Exa-scale (over 
1,000,000,000,000,000,000 flops) supercomputing capability.  It also aims at capacity 
and capability development in the area of hardware and more in the area of application 
software to meet the demands of the scientif ic community from all disciplines. The DST, 
the Department of Electronics & Information Technology (Deity) in consultation with the 
Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru and Center for Development of Advance 
Computing (C-DAC), Pune, are preparin g the strategies for implementing the 
Programme. 
16.4  NATIONAL GEOGRAPHIC INFORMATION SYSTEM (NGIS) 
The NGIS has been set up with the objectives of establishing a “National GIS” as a 
Decision Support GIS-platform with a systematic nation-wide, seamless GIS Asset and to 
realise an organisational stru cture of Indian National GIS Organisation (INGO) that will 
be responsible for National GIS system, maintaining and operating the GIS Platform. 
16.5 The NGIS Mission will also organise the GSIS Asset-GIS database for the whole 
country for the first time.  The Mission woul d also develop National GIS Applications 
software suite required fo r different Ministries for governance. According to the 
Department, the Major elements of the Na tional GIS platform include creation of 

National GIS infrastructure, GIS portal development, National GIS standardization and 
process definition would be a key for success of National GIS.   
16.6 An innovative mission struct ure is planned for implem entation of National GIS, 
which would take care of overlaps and integration and alignment of all efforts to National 
GIS. The apex body of NGIS will be the National GIS Advisory Board (NAB) to provide 
overall policy-direction, advi ce/guide, and review to a ssess performance and suggest 
improvements and fine tuning of Mission and also function as the think tank for NGIS.  
16.7 DST has also constituted a High Power Governing Council (HPGC), with 
Secretaries of Department of Space, the Department of Electronics & Information 
Technology (Deity) and Ministry of Earth Scie nces as Co-Chairs.  A full time Mission 
Director would also be selected with a small and nimble NGIS Mission Directorate. 
16.8 The Committee feels that the above programmes are of great national 
importance and hence recommends that the Department should make every possible 
effort to successfu lly implement them in a time bound manner.  The Committee, 
further, recommends that the Department must ensure that the allocated outlays for 
these two schemes are fully utilized. 
17. The Committee hopes that Department of Science & Technology shall make 
prudent utilisation of funds allocated to it under Demand No. 85 for the year 2013-
14 having due regard to the recommendations made by the Committee and 
efficiently implement its various programmes and schemes in the year 2013-14.

REPORT 
INTRODUCTORY 
 Environment, over the years, has emerged as a key component a nd all pervading theme 
on the broader contours of economic growth w ithin sustainable development framework.  
Environmental concerns in the process of developmental philosophy have, however, 
sharpened further in the recent years with  the consequences of the environmental 
degradation manifesting in numerous ways su ch as global warming, scanty and scattered 
rainfall, changing weather pattern, depleting glaciers, receding water flow in major rivers, 
poor and pathetic state of e nvironmental resources – land, ai r & water and their adverse 
impact on human health, etc. also known as climate cha nge on the one hand and with 
blatant, brazen and reckless exploitation of natural reso urces resulting in massive 
deforestation and degeneration of green covers on the other.  As recently as on 18th April, 
2013, Supreme Court, in its landmark judgment,  decreed that environment & ecology are 
national assets, they are subject to interg enerational equity a nd the principle of 
sustainable development has been  rendered as part of Articl e 21 of the Constitution of 
India.  Yet, the national commitment to a clean and healthy environment as enshrined in 
Articles 48(a) and 51(a)(g) of the Indian Constitution and the aspiration that human 
beings should be able to enj oy a decent quality of  life remains a far cry.  The reasons are 
not far too difficult to find out.  The fact is that the reas ons are both obvious and opaque.  
An evolving and expanding society, such as  ours, in desperate pursuit of economic 
prosperity for poverty alleviation, livelihood secu rity and restoration of  greater justice to 
those deprived is bound to c onfront environmental challe nges.  Secondly, exponential 
population growth, inappropriate  technology, consumption choi ces, paradigm shift in 
amicable and harmonious relationship of co-existence between people and ecosystem, 
proliferation of polluting indus tries, unplanned urbanisation, etc. have prominently and 

routinely been attributed to be the chie f drivers of environmental degradation and 
ecological imbalances.  But there are certain ot her latent yet potent contributory factors 
which need attention and focus too.  These ar e institutional failures resulting in lack of 
enforcement of rights of access to and use of  environmental resources, failed and flawed 
regulatory regime, governance constrains in environmental management, policy lacunae, 
disincentivising  environmen tal conservation, to mention a few.  The widely 
acknowledged fact that not much could be done to manage the former category of 
prominent factors catapults us to concentrate more on the latter ones as to how best we 
can overcome them.  Sooner or later, this ha s to be done in recogni tion of the axiomatic 
fact that environmental resources play pivot al role not only in pr oviding livelihoods but 
also in securing life supportin g ecological services to all forms of life – human, animal 
and plant.  But, the sooner done is better because environmental damages beyond a 
certain degree, become irreparable and irreversible.   
2. It, therefore, becomes imperative for al l of us to gear and galvanize all the 
resources at our disposal to minimize if not  altogether eliminate the possibilities of 
collateral damage done to the environment, ecology, forests and wildlife. 
3.  Environment is universal, ubiquitous and all pervasiv e comprising of entities – 
natural or manmade, external to oneself and their interrelationships, which provide value 
now or perhaps in the future to mankind.  Mana ging such a vast and wi der rather infinite 
spectrum of challenges, is undoubtedly a daun ting task entrusted to  the Ministry of 
Environment & Forests as a nodal agency in the administrative setup of the Govt. of 
India.  The ministry, since its inception on 4
th January, 1985 has been, through thick and 
thins of overriding and pres sing priorities, sometimes c onflicting and contradictory 
engaged in trying to strike a fine bala nce by planning, promoting, coordinating and 
overseeing environmental, ecological forestry and wildlife programmes and policies.  The 
main activities of the Ministry involve prot ection of the environment; conservation and 
survey of existing forests, wildlife, aqua tic bodies, water resources and eco-systems 
including biodiversity and ot her resources particularly in eco-sensitive zones for 
identification of new species of flora and fauna; afforestation and regeneration of 
degraded areas; prevention and control of pollution (air, water, noise, industrial); 
management of hazardous substances; mitigation and adaptation to climate change 
through adoption of cleaner technologies; pr omotion of sustainable development and 
better environmental governance; ensuring welfare of animals; capacity building; training 
and research in classical and molecular taxonomy; etc.  Apart from these national 
activities, the Ministry is also engaged in promoting in ternational cooperation through 
regional, bilateral and multilateral initiatives in the arena of environment and ecology.  
Issues relating to regional bodies like Economic and Social  Council for Asia & Pacific 
(ESCAP) and South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC) and 
multilateral bodies such as the Commission on Sustainable Development (CSD); Global 
Environment Facility (GEF) have been entruste d to the Ministry.  Besides, the Ministry 
also serves as the nodal agency for the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), 
South Asia Cooperation Environment Programme  (SACEP) and Intern ational Centre for 
Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMD) , as well as, for follow up on the United 
Nations Conference on Environment and Development (UNCED).  
4. Institutional Setup
 
4.1 The Institutional setup of the Minist ry includes a number of Directorates, 
Divisions, Regional Offices, Subordinate Offi ces, Boards, Autonomous Institutions and 
one Public Sector Undertaking, the details of which are as follows:- 

 
(a) Regional Offices: -  The Ministry has six Regional Offices covering 
various Zones of the country.  The No rth Zone Regional Office is located 
at Chandigarh; the Central Zone at Lucknow; the Northeastern Zone at 
Shillong and Bhubaneswar; the South Zone at Bengaluru; the Eastern 
plateau or upper East at Ranchi and the West Zone at Bhopal.   
(b) Subordinate Offices: -
  
(i) Botanical Survey of India, Kolkata;  
(ii) Zoological Survey of India, Kolkata;  
(iii) National Museum of Natural History, New Delhi;  
(iv) Indira Gandhi National Forest Academy, Dehradun;  
(v) Directorate of Forest Education, Dehradun;  
(vi) Forest Survey of India Dehradun;

7. Monitorable Targets of XI Five Year Plan 
7.1  As per the Mid-term Appraisal Do cument of the Planning Commission, the 
following 4 monitorable socioeconomic target s in the Environment and Forests Sector 
had been emphasised in the XI Five Year Plan period: 
 To increase forest and tree cover by 5 percentage points; 
 To attain WHO standards of air quality in all major cities by 2011-12; 
 To treat all urban waste water by 2011-12 in order to clean river waters; and 
 To increase energy efficiency by 20 per cent by 2016-17. 
 7.2  When the Committee enquired from the Ministry about the achievements in 
respect of the above targets,  the Ministry did not come out with specific and pointed 
reply.  Going through the replies, it is very  difficult to make out precisely the physical 
achievements.  In reply to the targets of in creasing forest and tree cover by 5 percentage 
points, the Ministry replied that in order to achieve the target of 5 per cent, an additional 
16.5 million hectares forest and tree cover ha d to be obtained by 2012.  But the tree 
planting during the Plan period was around 1.52 million hectare per year which if 
multiplied by 5, gives a figure of 7.6 million hectares during the Plan period, thus 
showing an overall shortage of plantation in  8.9 million hectares.  The Ministry further 
stated that given the constraints of land a nd financial resources, th e achievement of the 
target was ambitious.  With regard to the target of treating all urban waste water by 2011-
12 in order to clean river waters, the Ministry  stated that the primary responsibility of 
treating sewage was with the Municipalities.  The Ministry further added that maintaining 
cleanliness of rivers required minimum river water and it was the Ministry of Water 
Resources, which was the nodal Ministry to ensu re adequate water flow in rivers.  The 
Ministry thus had limited role to play in achie vement of this target.  On the target of 
attaining World Health Organisation standards of Air Quality in all major cities by 2011-
12, the Ministry had a very peculiar reply to offer.  The Ministry felt that the notified 
National Ambient Air Quality Standards in  India, based mostly on United States 
Environmental Protection Agency health Criteria (USEPA) documents and not WHO 
Guidelines would provide a more realistic and appropriate goal fo r achieving better air 
quality in India. Responding to  the monitorable target of en hancing energy efficiency by 
20 per cent points by 2016-17, the Mi nistry tossed the ball in th e court of the Ministry of 
Power stating that action on enhancement of energy efficiency and lowering energy 
intensity was the responsibility  of Ministry of Power.  The Committee feels that if the 
Ministry has to handle the socioeconomic mo nitorable targets given to it in such a 
casual and cavalier manner, the very purpo se of devising and deciding a target 
becomes meaningless.  The Ministry should  have, while or before fixing the target, 
thought as to whether the targets pertained to it or not.  But once the targets were 
set, the Ministry must have  made sincere and serious effo rts to meet them in close 
coordination and cooperation with the ot her concerned Ministries.  The Committee 
takes a very serious view on the way and the manner in which the targets given to 
the Ministry had been handled.  The Commi ttee feels that if the Ministry was not 
serious in trying to seriously pursue the ta rgets set, they must not have accepted 
these monitorable targets at all.  The Committee hopes that monitorable 
socioeconomic targets set for the XII Five Year Plan would not meet the same fate 
as the targets of the XI Five Year Pl an and therefore, recommends, that the 
Ministry should seriously and vigorously pursue the targets and goals set for the XII 
Five Year Plan so as to ensure that concre te achievements in re spect of each target 
are made.   

 
8.  Budgetary allocation of the Ministry of Environment & Forests in the XI and 
XII Five Year Plan 
8.1 The Ministry was provided an outlay of Rs. 10,000.00 Crores in the XI Five Year 
Plan (2007-12), out of which Environmen t & Ecology accounted for Rs. 3786.01 Crores 
and Forestry & Wildlife Rs. 6213.99 Crores.  Sector-wise distri bution was Rs. 1246.01 
Crores for Environment; Rs. 2540.00 Crores fo r National River Conservation Directorate 
(NRCD); Rs. 2943.99 Crores for Forests & Wildlife; Rs. 3150.00 Crores for National 
Afforestation & Eco-Development Board (NAEB) and Rs. 120.00 Crores for Animal 
Welfare.  However, by the end of the Plan period, the actual outlay, based on year-wise 
allocation remained at Rs. 9231.00 Crores with  sectoral share of Rs. 1913.34 Crores; Rs. 
2760.75 Crores; Rs. 2611.44 Crores; Rs. 1826.47 Crores and Rs. 119.00 Crores for 
Environment; NRCD; Forests & Wildlife; NA EB & Animal Welfare respectively.  
Environment & Ecology thus finally account ed for Rs. 4674.09 Crores and Forestry & 
Wildlife Rs. 4556.91 Crores.  While Environment & Ecology got Rs. 888.08 Crores 
more, Forestry & Wildlife got Rs. 1657.08 Cror es less than the init ial earmarking of 
Budgetary allocation.  Ther e was, however, a reduction of Rs. 769.54 Crores in the 
original outlay for the XI Five Year Plan which got restricted to Rs. 9231.00 Crores as 
against Rs. 10000.00 Crores.  On a comparative analysis of the original/ initial vis-à-
vis actual Sector-wise outlay, it is found that while National Afforestation and Eco-
Development Board which consists of the key programme of National Afforestation 
was the worst sufferer, Forests & Wildlife was the second worst sufferer in terms of 
reduction in allocation.  As against an initial amount of Rs. 3150.00 Crores and Rs. 
2943.99 Crores, earmarked under these Sectors, the final outlay came down to Rs. 
1826.47 Crores and Rs. 2943.99 Crores, showing a reduction of Rs. 1323.53 and Rs. 
332.55 Crores respectively.   
8.2  The Ministry was able to utili ze the amount of Rs. 8470.46 Crores, Rs. 3899.67 
Crores under Environment & Ecology and Rs. 4570.79 Crores under Forestry & Wildlife, 
thus, leaving an amount of Rs. 1529.54 Crores unutilized in comparison to the original 
allocation of Rs. 10000.00 Crores and Rs. 769.54 Crores in comparison to the final 
allocated outlay of Rs. 9231.00 Cores.  The Mini stry has informed that the utilisation 
ratio for the first 4 years of the XI Plan remained in the range of around 99 per cent but in 
the last year of the Plan pe riod, i.e., the year 2011-12, the utilisation ratio came down to 
79 per cent.  The lower expend iture/utilisation has been stated to be mainly due to 
reduction in Ministry’s Plan outlay at RE  Stage by Rs. 230.00 Crores in 2009-10 and Rs. 
298.00 Crore in 2011-12.  The other reasons fo r sizeable shortfall in the 2011-12 were 
attributed mainly to the general administra tive and procedural r easons like delays in 
receipts of proposals, lack of adequate proposals, non/late  submission of utilisation 
certificates, revalidation of unspe nt balances, completion of wo rks, etc.  Further reasons 
given included implementing agencies in ma ny schemes, being the State Govts./ Various 
Departments, whose performance depended on timely release of matching Grants, time 
lag in release of funds by th e Ministry and actual availa bility of funds to such 
implementing agencies, etc.  Th e overall utilisation percentage of the allocated resources 
worked out to 91.76 per cent for the XI Plan.

9.4  The Committee enquired from the Mini stry whether the XII Five Year Plan 
allocation was in consonance with the obser vation made by the Pl anning Commission in 
its Mid-term Appraisal of the XI Five Year Pl an Document that an allocation of at least 5 
per cent of the Annual Central Plan Outlay for the Environment and Forestry Sectors 
separately needed to be ensured preferably by the XII Five Year Plan.  The Ministry of 
Environment & Forests stated that neither th e overall XII Five Year Plan allocation nor 
the Annual allocation of the Ministry were in  accordance with the above observations of 
the Planning Commission, despit e the fact that the Minist ry had been consistently 
highlighting the lowering of its relative prio rity in Plan outlay allocations over the 
various Five Year Plans to the Planning Commission, despite growing importance of 
environmental, ecological and forestry issu es over these years.  The Ministry also 
submitted a chart showing percentage share of Environment and Forests Sector in Central 
Plans which is given at Annexure-I.  
9.5  This shows that while the share of th e Ministry in the Central Sector Plan 
allocations was 0.83 per cent in the VII Five Y ear Plan, it came down to 0.48 per cent in 
the VIII Five Year Plan.  After registering some increase over the next two Five Year 
Plans, i.e., IX and X,  the percentage share came down sharpl y to 0.43 per cent in the XI 
Five Year Plan as compared to the 0.67 per cen t in the X Plan and in  the XII Five Year 
Plan, it has further come down to 0.41 per ce nt.  Over the last 4 Annual Plans, the 
declining trend continued unabated.  While in the year 2010-11, the share of Environment 
& Forests Sector in the Annual Central Outlays was to the exte nt of 0.42 per cent, it had 
consistently come down to  0.39 per cent in 2011-12, 0.37 pe r cent in 2012- 13 and this 
year, it has further gone down to 0.36 per cent.   

 
9.6  The Committee expresses its deep anguish  over the declining pe rcentage of share 
for the Ministry of Environment & Forests in the overall Central Plan outlay in the 
successive Five Year Plans/ Annual Pl ans despite increasing importance of 
environmental issues.  The Committee takes a ve ry serious note of the fact that while in 
the VII Five Year Plan, the percentage of share was 0.83 per cent, it has gone down by 
more than 50 per cent to 0.41 per cent in th e XII Five Year Plan.  The Committee is of 
the considered view that Planning Commi ssion must not consider Budgetary Support 
made to Environment & Forests as non-produc tive, non-priority and hence avoidable.  
The Planning Commission needs to understand  and realize that the damage done to 
environment, disturbance made to the ecologi cal balance can’t be easily repaired and 
restored.  It, therefore, becomes expedient that the very process of degradation and 
degeneration of environmenta l resources be contained and minimized to the possible 
extent through preventive and curative measures  before it is too late and it is possible 
inter-alia by mounting environmental surveillance and reinforcing monitoring mechanism 
– the task assigned to Ministry of Environm ent & Forests.  For doing all these sufficient 
monetary support is undoubtedly required.  The Committee, ther efore, recommends 
that the Planning Commission must act on its own observation of allocating 5 per 
cent of the Annual Central Sector Outlay to Environment and Forestry Sectors in 
right earnest.  The Committee also recomme nds that Ministry of Environment & 
Forests must not only forcefully and vigorously take up this matter with the 
Planning Commission but also apprise it of the details of response gathered from the 
Planning Commission in this regard.  The Committee also recommends that the 
Planning Commission must ensure full a llocation of the approved outlay during the 
XII Plan period and should not resort to an y cut at RE Stage in any of the Annual 
Plans unless Ministry itself is not in a positi on to utilise the full allocation.  In any 
case, full requirements of the Ministry of  Environment and Forests must be met.  
The Ministry must, at the same  time, make all out efforts to make full utilisation of 
allocated budgetary outlay so as not to  provide any alibi to the Planning 
Commission for reduction at RE Stage.

10.6  The Committee feels that this phenome non of underutilization of allocated outlay 
is a very serious matter towards which the Ministry needs to focus its attention in a more 
pragmatic and professional manner and in itiate concrete measures.  Merely, 
reemphasizing and reiterating that the Minist ry has already in place a robust and sound 
monitoring mechanism would not do any good pa rticularly in view of the fact that 
underutilization of allocated budgetary res ources has turned out to be a recurring 
phenomenon.  It becomes all the more impera tive, because underutili zation of allocated 
resources provides the Planning Commission and th e Ministry of Finance with an alibi to 
make less allocation in the next year and also allows them to use it as a tool to reduce the 
approved BE outlay at the RE Stage.  The Mini ster of Finance has made it amply clear in 
his budget speech.  The Ministry can justif y its demand for additional resources only 
when it is able to first utilise th e entire resources allocated to it.  The Committee, 
therefore, strongly recommends that the Mi nistry of Environment & Forests must 
make sincere, serious and potent efforts by way of meticulous  planning, timely 
implementation and stricter monitoring of  schemes/projects and should not come 
out with the same lame and routine excuses for underutilization year after year.   
10.7  The Committee also notes that the Ministry has not been getting annual 
allocations as per the ratio of outlay approved for the XII Five Year Plan.  If the total 
approved outlay of Rs. 17874.00 Crores for th e entire XII Plan period be evenly 
distributed among the 5 Annual Plans, the average allocation comes to approximately Rs. 
3547.80 Crores per Annual Plan.  The Committee finds that for 2012-13, the first year of 
the Plan period, the plan allocation at BE level was less by Rs. 1144.80 Crores and if it is 
seen in the perspective of the RE alloca tion, this gap furthe r widens to Rs. 1747.80 
Crores which is almost the half of the a nnual allocation during the XII Plan period.  The 
Committee taking a serious view in this ma tter, feels that by doi ng this, Planning 
Commission is making a mockery of a pproved outlay for the XII Plan period.  The 
Committee therefore, recommends that the Planning Commission must desist from 
such practices and allocate budgetary resources in the Annual Plans in proportion it 
is due to the Ministry or else the very pur pose of Five Year Plan allocations gets 
defeated and falsified.
