its people.  The Committee recommends that  the Planning Commission should not  
further reduce Plan allocation of the De partment on any pretext so that its 
important programmes do not suffer for want of funds. 

7. PHYSICAL ACHIEVEMENTS OF THE DEPARTMENT IN 2012-13 
7.1 Following were the main achievements of the Department in 2012-13:-  
i) During the first year of the XII Pl an, three operationa l flights of PSLV 
have been successfully conducted i. e. operational flights of PSLV C19 
carrying RISAT-1 sate llite (on April 26, 20 12), PSLV C21 carrying 
French Remote Sensing Satellite- SP OT-6 and Japanese microsatellite – 
PROITERES - on commercial basi s (on September 9, 2012), PSLV C20 
carrying Indo-French joint mission SARAL along with 6 micro/nano 
satellites (on February 25, 2013). 
ii) The acceptance test of Indigenous Cr yogenic Upper stage for the next 
developmental flight of GSLV (G SLV-D5) has been completed. Stage 
preparation, integration & testing activ ities of the stages of the launch 
vehicle are progressing well. The la unch of GSLV-D5 is scheduled for 
May-June, 2013 which will carry GSAT-14 communication satellite with 
12 transponders            (6 Ku and 6 Ext-C) and a Ka band beacon.   
iii) Significant progress has been made towards the development of GSLV 
Mk III, capable of placing 4 Ton clas s of communication satellite in Geo-
Transfer orbit.  Preparations to un dertake the first experimental mission 
(X- Mission) of GSLV-Mk III using th e flight units of two S200 solid 
strap-on motors and L110 liquid core  stage along with a passive C25 
cryogenic stage is progressing well. The Experimental X- Mission, during 
2013 is slated for launch in 2013. 
iv) Considerable progress has been made towards development of Semi-
Cryogenic Engine. The design of the e ngine has been successfully carried 
out. Work towards, establishment of speci alised test facilities and material 
development has also been initiated.   
v) R & D activities on ad vanced launch vehicle technologies including Air 
breathing propulsion and Reus able Launch vehicles ar e progressing well.  
As a first step towards realising a Tw o Stage To Orbit (TSTO), a series of 
technology demonstration missions ha ve been conceived.  For this 
purpose, a winged Reusable Launch Vehicle Technology Demonstrator 
(RLV-TD) has been configured.  Rea lisation of flight hardware for the 
RLV-TD mission is also underway.  The first technology demonstrator 
mission of Reusable Launch Vehicle is slated for the year 2013-14. 
vi) The Department has developed Geo St ationary Satellite Launch Vehicle 
(GSLV) to lift its co mmunication satellites weighing two tonnes and 
above to a distance of 36,000 km from  earth. After a mixed bag of seven 
launches since 2001, four of them failure s, ISRO is perfecting this rocket 
and also coming out with a four-tonne version, the GSLV Mk III.  
7.2 The Committee takes note of the achiev ements of the Department in 2012-13. 
The Department  has not only successfully  launched its state-of- the-art technology 
satellites such as Indian Radar Imaging Satellite (RISAT-1), Indian Communication 
Satellite (GSAT-10), etc. but has also launche d satellites for foreign customers viz.,  
France (Sport-6),  Japan (PROITERS) , Canada (SAPHIRE) and the United 
Kingdom (STRaND). The Department has also  entered into successful international 
collaborations such as Saral and Megha-Tro piques with France which is already an 
established power in space technology.  These achievements show that the credibility 
and reliability of Indian Space programme  is now firmly and well established 

internationally. The Committee congratula tes the Department for taking Indian 
Space programme to such glorious heights.    
 7.3 The Committee hopes that the Department would not only continue to 
maintain the same level of performance but endeavour to perform better and better 
in the remaining years of XII Five Year Plan so that  our space programme in its all 
dimensions achieves a position  that is second to none in the world.

Department.  
8.3 In the financial year 2010-11, the tota l B.E. allocation including Plan and Non-
Plan was  .5778.04 Crores, which got reduced to 4880.04 Crores at the R.E. Stage and 
the actual expenditure incurred was only Rs. 4482.23 crores i.e. less by Rs. 397.81 crores.  
Similarly, the total B.E. outlay of  6626.04 Crores for the financial year 2011-12 was 
reduced to 4432.04 Crores at the R.E. Stage, while  the actual utilisation was only  
3784.27 Crores i.e.  648 Crores less than the RE allocation.   
8.4   The Committee finds that some of the reasons for underutilisation in 2010-11 
and 2011-12 are common and mostly of admini strative nature viz. non approval/delay in 
approval of Manned Mission Initiative; phasi ng out expenditure on Semi-Cryogenic tests 
facilities based on procurement status; phasing  out payments on procurement, etc. In 
2011-12, one of the reasons given is non-releas e or less release of grants-in-aid to 
autonomous bodies due to availa bility of un-utilised funds.  All this suggests that the 
projections for budgetary allocation by the Department are not based on realistic 
assessments of actual requirements.  
8.5 The Committee takes strong exception to  such a casual approach adopted by 
the Department in earmarking of funds  which results in precious and scarce 
resource remaining unutilised. Budgetary resou rces are very scarce and it is the 
duty of the Department to make optimum uti lisation of funds allocated, both 
qualitatively and quantitatively. Underu tilisation of allocated funds for 
consecutively three years does paint a dismal picture of the capability of the 
Department to properly plan, monitor and execute its spending.    
8.6 The Committee finds that th e total budgetary allocation in 2012-13 both Plan and 
Non Plan of  . 6715.04 crores made available to the Department at the B.E. stage was 
reduced to  4880.00 Crores at R.E. stage out of which,  4439.19 Crores i.e. 91 per 
cent of RE allocation was utilised by the Department till 28.2.2013. 

8.7 The Committee finds that the BE 2012-13 al location made to the Department 
was reduced at the RE Stage due to poor spendability of the Department, besides for 
meeting the ceilings communicated by th e Ministry of Finance. The Committee 
expresses its concern over the poor fina ncial performance of the Department 
reflected by non utilisation of  . 1835.04 crores during the year 2012-13, out of 
which the major share belonged to Plan a llocations to the tune of . 1815.01 crores.  
The Committee feels that this is not a health y trend especially if seen in the context 
of the claim of the Department of h aving a very sound and robust monitoring 
mechanism.  The Committee is not at all am used by the figure of 91% utilisation of 
R.E. allocation in 2012-13 as given by th e Department.  The Committee, therefore, 
reiterates that the Department should ma ke sincere and serious efforts to fully 
utilise allocated resources in the year 2013-14. 
8.8 The Committee is constrained to observe that the Department appears to 
have a strong, monitoring mechanism only on paper as it has failed to produce 
satisfactory and desired target of ensuring  full utilisation of allocated resources.  
The Committee, therefore, recommends th at the Department should further 
strengthen its monitoring mechanism and make it more robust to ensure full and 
effective utilisation of allocated funds.

10. MAJOR PROGRAMMES AND SCHEMES 
 The programmes/projects of the Departme nt of Space can be classified into 
following broad categories:- 
I Space Technology; 
II  Space Applications;  
III Space Sciences; 
IV INSAT operational; and  
V  Direction and Administ ration/other programmes. 
 The details of the pr ojects/programmes, A nnual Plan allocations vis-à-vis their 
utilisation, etc. are discussed in the succeeding  paragraphs:- 
I   SPACE TECHNOLOGY   
Space Technology consists of two components viz. Launch Vehicle Technology 
and Satellite Technology.  
11.    LAUNCH VEHICLE TECHNOLOGY 
11.1 The main focus of the Space Transporta tion Systems during XII plan period will 
be towards achieving self-sufficiency in la unching satellites, deve loping launch vehicles 
for enhanced payload capability, adopting ap propriate outsourcing strategies for assuring 
production of launch vehicles, stepping up of infrastructure  for launch vehicles and 
developing advanced technologies for the fu ture. Towards that end, enhancement of 
production limits of PSLV Vehicle systems with vigorous indus try participation, 
completion of qualification of indigenous Cryogenic Upper Stage (CUS), proving GSLV 
with indigenous cryogenic stage, as a reliable  workhorse launch vehicle,  completion of 
development and qualification of C25 Engine & Stage, completion of one experimental 
and one developmental flight of GSLV Mk III with 4.0 T GTO capability, progress on 
the development of Semi cryogenic engine w ith the establishment of test facilities, 
augmentation of spaceport infrastructure to meet the launch vehicle requirements shall be 
pursued. During the XII Plan period, 17 PSL V missions, 6 GSLV MK-II missions and 2 
GSLV MK-III missions (including one e xperimental mission) are aimed for 
accomplishment.   
11.2 GEOSTATIONARY SATELLITE LA UNCH VEHICLE (GSLV) 
11.2.1 GSLV programme is intended to de sign and develop an operational launch 
vehicle capable of placing 2 - 5 Ton and a bove capacity communicatio n satellites into 
Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit (GTO). The fi rst flight of GSLV took place from SDSC-
SHAR on April 18, 2001 by la unching 1540 kg GSAT-1. It was followed by six more 
launches , GSLV-D2 on May 8, 2003 (GSAT- 2  1825 kg), GSLV-F01 on September 20, 
2004 (EDUSAT 1950 kg), GSLV-F02 on July  10, 2006, GSLV-F04 on September 2, 
2007 (INSAT-4CR   2130 kg), GSLV-D3 on April 15, 2010 and GSLV-F06 on 
December 25, 2010.  GSLV-MK III Developmen t programme was approved in April 
2002 with total approved cost of .2498 Crores.  The cumulative expenditure up to 
March, 2012 has been  2304.44 Crores which is about 92 per cent of the total approved 
cost.     
11.2.2 The DoS was inquired by the Committ ee about the progress made in the 
development and operationalisation of the thir d stage, indigenously built liquid-fuelled 
Cryogenic Engine in the light of  the fact that in itially ISRO had planned a GSLV-MKIII 
launch with an indigenous upper Cryogeni c Engine during 2012 but later on it was 
rescheduled to 2013.  Explaini ng the reasons for extending th e deadline, the Department 
informed that time schedule was deferred due to incorporation and implementation of all 

recommendations of Failure Analysis Committ ees set up after failure of GSLV-F06 and 
GSLV-D3 IN 2010 in the indigenous cryogenic stage for the next flight of GSLV.  
11.2.3 Informing about progress made in launc h of GSLV Mark-III, the Department 
submitted that major qualification tests such as  lower shroud structural qualification test, 
Acoustic test in wind tunnel, Steering engine Actuator test, Flight acceptance tests of 
Main engine & Steering engines and flight acceptance test of Fuel Booster Turbo Pump 
(FBTP) & Oxidiser Booster Turbo Pump (O BTP) were  successfully completed. The 
integration of the indigenous cryogenic stage identified for the next launch of GSLV is in 
advanced stage at the LPSC facilities, Mahendragiri near Nagercoil in Tamil Nadu. 
11.2.4 The Department further informed that during the deliberations on the 
development of indigenous cryogenic stage,  it was assessed that demonstration of 
vacuum ignition of cryogenic engine on gr ound as well as in vacuum condition would 
provide sufficient confidence for the next flight. The ground test of the cryogenic engine 
under vacuum conditions was planned in March 2013. In view of these technical reasons, 
the next launch of GSLV (GSLV D5) with  indigenous cryo stage was rescheduled to 
sometime in 2013.   
11.2.5 In view of the good progress of the programme, the Planning Commission has 
also adequately funded the programme of GSLV MK-III development as the amount 
allocated for the same has been almost doubled from .72.09 Crores at B.E. 2012-13 to 
.139.53 Crores i.e. an increase of  .67.44 Crores this year.   The Committee is happy 
to note that the Planning Co mmission has provided adequate  funds for the development 
of GSLV MK-III and hope that Department w ould be able to successfully develop it in 
this year. 
11.2.6 The Committee understands that the ad vancement of Indian Space Mission 
depends mainly on the upgradation of Spa ce transportation vehicles for launching 
Satellites having a payload capacity of 4-5 tonnes for applicat ion in Manned Space 
Mission/Mars Orbiter Mission and Cha ndrayaan-2. Keeping this in view, the 
Committee feels that all out e fforts should be made by the Department to upgrade 
the performance of the GSLV technology and make it perfectly reliable and full 
proof.   
11.2.7 The Committee, therefore, recommends  that Department should endeavour 
to achieve the above goal as early as possi ble.  The Committee would also like the 
DoS to ensure successful test ing of vacuum ignition of cryogenic engine on ground 
as well as in vacuum condition with i ndigenous cryo stage, which was earlier 
scheduled for March, 2013, at the earliest an d positively by the end of the current 
Fiscal. The Committee further recommends that the enhanced allocation of 139.53 
Crores for the project in 2013-14 must be fully utilized by the Department.  
11.3 SPACE CAPSULE RECOVERY EXPERIMENT (SRE) 
11.3.1 Space Capsule Recovery Experiment-II (SRE-II) Project is being implemented 
with the primary objective of realising a fully recoverable capsule. It shall also provide a 
platform to conduct micro-gravity experiment s.  SRE capsule has four major hardware, 
namely, Aero Thermo-structure (ATS), Sp acecraft platform, deceleration and floatation 
system and payloads.   
11.3.2 SRE-II project was approved after the su ccessful launch of SRE-I in January 2007 
with an approved cost of . 42.00 Crores. The cumulative expenditure was 39.83 
Crores till March 31, 2012 which was about 95 per cent of the approved cost.  
11.3.3 The Committee inquired from the Depa rtment about the revised target of 
launching SRE-II and factors that led to th e revision of the target. The Department 

affirmed that the target of launching SRE -II had been revised as the optimum usage of 
Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle’ s (PSLV) payload capability a nd a suitable co-passenger 
for SRE-II was to be identified. The  indi genous Carbon-Carbon flight model Nose cap 
for the SRE-II was under progress and was expected to be realised by the end of 2013. As 
per the Department's version, SRE-II would be flown onboard PSLV by 2014.  
11.3.4 Coming to the budgetary allocation, the Committee finds that while an amount of 
. 4.40 Crores was allocated for this project  at B.E. 2011-12, it was reduced to . 2.20 
crores at the R.E. and only .  1.73 crores could be actually spent.   At B.E. 2012-13, 
SRE-II was allocated . 2.20 Crores which wa s reduced to .1.00 Crore at R.E. stage. 
In, 2013-14, however, the programme has been  allocated a meagre amount of . 0.50 
Crores.  The Committee is given to understand th at this is because of delay in launching 
of another companion satellite scheduled to be launched through PSLV with a payload of 
1200-1300 kgs, while SRE just weighs 650 kgs. The Secretary mentioned that SRE-II 
mission, in all likelihood, will be accomplished by 2014. He, further, remarked that the 
launch of SRE-II would be juxtaposed with the launch of CARTOSAT-II.  
11.3.5 The Committee expresses its concern over the tardy progress of SRE-II 
project. Even after utilising 95 per cent,  (. 39.83 Crores) of the total approved 
outlay (Rs. 42 crores) of the SRE-II ti ll March 31, 2012, the SRE-II programme has 
not yet taken off. The Committee, however,  hopes that the two problems plaguing 
the programme, namely delayed identification of suitable co-passenger for optimal 
usage of PSLV payload capability  and th e indigenous Carbon-Carbon flight model 
Nose cap for SRE-II would be addressed at the earliest and the scheduled launching 
of SRE-II in 2014 will be adhered to. 
11.4 MANNED MISSION/HUMAN SPACE FLIGHT PROGRAMME 
11.4.1 The objective of Human Spaceflight Programme is to undertake a human 
spaceflight mission to Low Earth Orbit (LEO) carrying a crew of two and return them 
safely to a predefined destination on earth.  The Committee desired to know the reasons 
behind fluctuations in allocation to manne d Mission Initiatives/Human Space Flight 
Programme, which had been the flagship programme of the Department.  The programme 
was allocated . 150.00 crores at B.E. level in 2010-11 but the actual expenditure 
incurred was only . 19.26 crores. Rs. 98.81 Crores was allocate d at B.E. 2011-12 but 
drastically reduced to . 13.77 Crores at R.E. stage and the actual expenditure in 2011-12 
was merely . 11.17 crores. Similarly, in 2 012-13, the B.E. allocation of 60.46 Crores 
was reduced to . 14.00 Crores at the R.E. stage, out of which only an amount of . 6.14 
crores was actually utilized  till January, 2013.  .27.00 Crores has been allocated to this 
programme in 2013-14.  
11.4.2 The Department informed the Committee that the budget allocated for manned 
Mission initiatives/Human Space Flight Progr amme has two components- One approved 
by the Government but still in its Pre-pr oject phase of deve lopment of critical 
technologies, but other one was  yet to be approved by the Government i.e. Phase-I 
towards design development, flight testing of crew module, PS4 augmented service 
module and development of crew escape sy stem.  Explaining the reason behind lower 
allocation at RE stage, the Department apprised that as Phase-I of the Programme was not 
yet approved, the RE provision had been reduced limiting the expenditure only to Pre-
project phase.  The provision of . 27.00 Crores in B.E. 2013-14 is limited to pre-project 
phase of development of critical technologi es for Human Space Flight Programme. The 
allocations made under manned mission initiative are as per the targets envisaged for the 
year 2013-14.   

11.4.3 The Committee also inquired from the De partment about the proposals of sending 
a Human Space Mission to Moon and whether ISRO had adequate infrastructure and 
required capabilities for accomplishing th is challenging mission. Responding to the 
queries the Department elucidated that as a part of pre-project act ivities; a few critical 
technologies needed for Human Spaceflight Programme had been taken up.  Significant 
progress had been made in a few critical  technological areas su ch as Crew Module 
development, Environment Control & Life  Support System (ECLSS), Space suit and 
various similar areas which were undertaken during pre-project activities phase. The first 
development model of cabin lighting system was realised and tested as well.  The 
Department further emphasised that, ISRO had the capability to carry on with the Human 
Space Flight Programme, however, the infrastruc ture required for this programme has to 
be built up and the process of acquiring infrastructure will  only be embarked on after 
obtaining approval of the project from the Government. 
11.4.4 The Committee is happy to know that the Department has the requisite 
potential and required capabilities to conduct the manned mission and has made 
significant progress in some critical tec hnologies like crew module development, 
environmental control and life support system , space suite, etc. which  have been 
taken up as pre-project activities.  The Committee knows that this is a very sensitive 
and delicate mission and hence the Departme nt needs to tread very cautiously and 
carefully in this mission.  The Committe e further recommends that as considerable 
progress has been made towards this missi on, the Department should expeditiously 
obtain Government approval for the phase-I project of design development and new 
module testing, etc.    
12.     SATELLITE TECHNOLOGY 
12.1 RADAR IMAGING SATELLITE - RISAT- 1A    
12.1.1 RISAT-1, the first state- of- the art remo te sensing Satellite to provide data to 
Indian user community, was successfully launched on 26 April, 2012.  It was the first 
microwave Radar Imaging Satellite built by ISRO. 
12.1.2 RISAT- 1A Programme of the Department  aims to build a follow-on mission to 
RISAT-1 with C-band multi-polarised Synthe tic Aperture Radar having capability of 
imaging under all weather conditions.  Th e target for launch of RISAT-1A with 
indigenous PSLV rocket is scheduled fo r 2017-18.  In 2012-13, RISAT-1A was not 
allocated any amount; however, an allocation of . 1.00 Crore has been made to this 
programme in 2013-14. 
12.1.3 The Committee is aware that RISAT, an op tical satellite that relies on sunlight to 
illuminate the ground below has certain advantag es over Radar Satellite. It could prove 
useful in studying glaciers in  the Himalayas, figuring out the amount of snow melting in 
summers, establishing ways to monitor crops techniques, etc. RISAT-1's radar data is 
likely to find many applications, including in geology, terrain mapping and forestry and 
oceanography.   
12.1.4 While the Committee is happy to note the successful launch of India's first 
indigenous Radar satellite, RISAT-1 in April,  2012, it finds that there is hardly any 
progress as far as development of RISAT- 1A is concerned.  Given that Radar 
satellite technology is tremendously be neficial not only for flood mapping, 
agriculture but also, for glacial st udies, the Committee recommends that 
Department take up in right earnest expe ditious building of RISAT-IA well before 
its targeted launch in 2017-18. The Committe e, also recommends that adequate 

funds be made available for this Mission so that funds crunch does not adversely 
impact the expeditious completion of the Mission. 
12.2 SATELLITE BASED NAVIGATION  
12.2.1 Satellite based Navigation service is an  emerging satellite based system with 
commercial and applications. Establishmen t of an independent Indian Regional 
Navigation Satellite System (IRNSS) over In dian region with a constellation of 7 
satellites was planned to be realised during the XII Five Year Plan. Considerable progress 
has been achieved in realising the various  subsystems of these satellites and the 
constellation shall be completed during th e XII Plan. Implementation of the final 
operational phase for satellite based augmen tation system (SBAS) GAGAN (GPS Aided 
Geo Augmented Navigation) over the Indian Airs pace is also an important target for XII 
Plan.  Formulation of Indian Satellite Naviga tion Policy to facilitate growth of Satellite 
based navigation application will also be  pursued.  Work towards augmentation of 
IRNSS system with 4 additional satellites shall also be initiated during the XII Plan. 
12.3     INDIAN REGIONAL NAVIGATIONAL SATELLITE SYSTEM (IRNSS) 
12.3.1 In response to a query by the Committee regarding the progress made by the 
Department in developing the IRNSS and te ntative schedule for launching  the first 
satellite of IRNSS constellation, i. e.,  IRNSS-R-1A  along with roadmap for 
operationalising full constellation, the Depa rtment informed that out of the seven 
satellites, three satellites are to be put in Geo stationary Orbit (GEO) and four satellites in 
Geo Synchronous Orbit (GSO) to provide two kinds of services, a Standard Positioning 
Service (SPS) for common civilian users an d a Restricted Service (RS) for special 
authorised users in L5 and S bands. The gr ound system consists of IRNSS Navigation 
Centre (INC) and IRNSS Satellite Contro l Facility (IRSCF) and the associated 
Navigational software development.  
12.3.2 The Department apprised the Committee th at the final integration and testing of 
the first IRNSS spacecraft (IRNSS-R1A) have b een completed and it is proposed to be 
launched in June 2013. After evaluating the performance of the first satellite, the 
subsequent satellites would be launched at regular intervals. IS RO has also drawn a 
roadmap for realisation of the IRNSS constellation by the end of 2015.  
12.3.3 In reply to a query as to what extent  launch of seven sa tellites of the IRNSS 
constellation would help reduc ing India's dependence on GPS System and in location 
identification for launching precision weapons, the Department informed that the IRNSS 
being independent satellite navigation system, the receivers capable of utilising the 
signals of IRNSS can provide the position so lution even in the absence of GPS (Global 
Positioning system) with position accuracy equi valent to that of the position solution 
provided by the use of GPS si gnals. All GPS applications in position determination and 
the location identification for launching precision weapons will be supported by IRNSS. 
12.3.4 The Committee feels that the Indian Regional Navigation Satellite System 
(IRNSS) has very useful application and th erefore, all out efforts must be made to 
see that it becomes operational at the earliest and any case within the stipulated time 
so that the nation is able to reap it s benefits.  The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Department should pursue this programme with all 
seriousness and sincerity so that there is no time and cost overrun and its benefits 
start accruing to the nation as soon as possible.     
12.4 GPS AIDED GEO- AUGUMENTED NAVIGATION SYSTEM (GAGAN) 
12.4.1 The Committee desired to know about the progress made so far with regard to  
GPS aided Geo-Augmented Navigation Syst em (GAGAN) and bene fits that would 

accrue  from it. The Department informed that final Operation Phase known as GAGAN-
FOP was in progress while GAGAN Final System Acceptance Test (FSAT) was 
successfully completed on July 16-17, 2012. After the recent launch of GAGAN Payload 
on-board GSAT-10 and subsequent integration with ground system, two satellites GSAT-
8 and GSAT-10 Signal in Space are available ove r Indian Sub-continent. All the sectors 
where GPS standalone system works woul d get benefited by the GAGAN system. The 
GAGAN system though primarily intended for pr oviding precision navigation service for 
civil aviation, would in additi on, provide enormous applicati ons in the field of location 
based services, intelligent transportation syst em (Air, Sea, and Land), survey involving 
positioning and timing applications. 
12.4.2 The Committee feels that with the operationalisation of GAGAN, Indian 
space programme would reach a phase when India can become a major hub of air 
navigation through operation of air services  from India. This achievement is more 
significant at a time when superior space based navigation is in greater demand. 
India can reap its advantage being placed at the axis of routes connecting Europe 
with Southeast Asia.  Further, by having an  indigenous Satellite, based on Regional 
GPS Augmentation System India can gain bo th in terms of market and strategic 
importance. The Committee, therefore, re commends that GAGAN should be made 
operational as soon as possible so that its benefits could become available to the 
country and its people at the earliest. 
III SPACE APPLICATIONS 
12.5 National Remote Sensing Centre  
12.5.1 National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC), Hyderabad is responsible for satellite 
data acquisition and processing,  data dissemination, aerial remote sensing and decision 
support for disaster management.  Under 'National Remote Sensing Centre' B.E. 
allocation of 273.52 Crores in 2012-13 has been reduced to  214.87 Crores at R.E. stage 
i.e., a reduction of  58.65 Crores. The B.E. 2013-14 allocations has been further 
reduced to 199.00 Crores.  
12.5.2 When the Committee desired to know the reasons for such a substantial reduction 
in allocation, the Department informed that  the B.E. 2012-13 prov isions for National 
Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC) of  273.52 Crores also included an allocation of 50.00 
Crores towards the construction activities for new campus at Regional Remote Sensing 
Centre (West), Jodhpur. However, due to  extensive planning efforts involved in 
designing a new campus, the amount could not be  utilised.  Hence, allocation to NRSC 
was reduced to  214.87 Crores at RE stage. B.E. allocation in 2013-14 to NRSC has 
been kept at 199.00 Crores as the major fundi ng requirements towards the establishment 
of Antarctica Ground Station for Earth Observ ation Satellites have been met during the 
financial year 2012-13.  
12.5.3 The Committee expresses its serious displeasure over the fact that the 
Department earmarked an amount of Rs. 50.00 crores in the year 2012-13 for 
constructing a campus, design of which is  yet to be finalised.  This resulted in 
avoidable non utilisation of the allocated outlay which could have been gainfully 
utilised in some other sche mes/projects. Secondly, non-co mpletion of the campus 
hampers the functioning of the Regional  Remote Sensing Centre, Jodhpur.  The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that such incidents of underutilisation purely on 
administrative grounds should be strict ly avoided and the construction of the 
proposed campus must be expedited.   

12.5.4 Providing the details of the progress made in the field of  remote sensing in India 
vis-à-vis other developed count ries, it has been informed that Indian Remote Sensing 
programme marked the completion of its 25 years on March 17, 2013. In the last 25 years 
Indian Remote sensing programme has made tremendous progress and has become a role 
model among comity of space fairing nations in  operational utilisation of remote sensing 
data for various applications of importan ce to the nation. In fact, India has made 
significant progress in the fiel d of remote sensing in comp arison to other developed 
countries. Remote sensing data from Indian sa tellites is made available to the global 
community through six active International Gr ound Stations (IGS) in Algeria, China, 
Germany and Myanmar and through re-seller network from 20 countries.   
12.5.5 The Committee congratulates the Department on completion of 25 years of 
its Remote Sensing Programme.  It is a matter of pride that this programme has 
become a role model among comity of nations pursuing space programme 
particularly in operational utilisation  of remote sensing data for various 
applications of greater importance to th e nation. The Committee is confident that 
the Department would continue to excel in the field of Remote Sensing applications. 
IV SPACE SCIENCES 
12.6 ASTROSAT I & II 
12.6.1 The ASTROSAT programme of the Depart ment is aimed at design, development, 
fabrication and launch of an astronomical observa tory of cosmic studies.  It is envisaged 
to be a national observatory for astronomical  observations by resear chers in India.  
ASTROSAT I & II was al located an amount of  10.00 crores at B.E. 2011-12 out of 
which the actual utilisation was only. 6.49 Crores.  The B.E. allocation in 2012-13 was 
reduced to Rs. 6 Crores which at R.E. Stage was further reduced to  2.55 Crores.  The 
allocation has been kept at .5.00 Crores for BE 2013-14. 
12.6.2 "ASTROSAT, a multi-wavelength space bor ne satellite was scheduled to be 
launched during 2009-10".  However, for r easons best known to the Department, the 
project was deferred.  As per the programmatic  physical target set by the Department for 
2012-13, ASTROSAT was scheduled to be la unched and operationalised through PSLV-
C22. Providing details regarding the progress of the project, the Department stated that 
assembly, integration and testing of vari ous sub-systems are progressing well.  
Development of flight models of payloa ds is nearing completion.  Based on the 
developmental status, the launch of ASTROSAT has been slated for 2014-15. 
12.6.3 In response to a query raised by the Co mmittee regarding the postponement of the 
target for launch of ASTROSAT, the Depart ment stated that si nce ASTROSAT has a 
scientific Mission that involved complex research in Space sciences, it was bound to take 
time. Another reason cited by the Department, for such inordinate delay was involvement 
of fellow scientists from countries across th e world. The Secretary informed that work 
was now progressing well with instrumentation part ready and reiterated that by 2014-15, 
the Department would be able to achieve the target.  The Committee, however, finds that 
integration of the instruments is yet to be done and is expected to be ready for launch by 
2014. 
12.6.4 The Committee understands that ASTROSAT is a complex scientific satellite 
in nature but notes that the even after almost ten years, this project is yet to be given 
a concrete shape. The Committ ee is of the opinion that Department should set its 
targets realistically and only after due co nsideration of complexities involved for 
repeated failure to meet targets lowers it s credibility in the ey es of public.  The 

Committee recommends that the Department  must make a sincere endeavour to 
launch the satellite as per the revised time  schedule i.e. 2014-15. 
12.7 INDIAN LUNAR MISSION -  CHANDRAYAAN-2 
12.7.1 Chandrayaan-2, a joint Space Mission with ISRO and Russian Federal Space 
Agency (ROSCOSMOS), Originally approved by Government in September, 2008 at a 
cost of . 425 crores excluding cost of GSLV and Lander, is an important step in India's 
Planetary exploration.   
12.7.2 Inter-Agency Agreement on cooperation for the joint mission was signed on 
November 12, 2007, between the two agencies. In February 2010, an amendment to the 
earlier agreement was agreed upon, wherein wh ile ISRO had the responsibility for the 
Rover Module, orbiter and the launch by GSLV. ROSCOSMOS was responsible for 
Moon  Lander module.  
12.7.3 Consequent to the failure  of the Russia-led inter-planetary mission, Phobos-Grunt, 
a sample return mission to Phobos (one of the moons of Mars), ROSCOSMOS decided to 
increase the reliability of their planetary mi ssions, for which increase in the mass of the 
Moon Lander by 250 kg. was required.  In May 2012, ROSCOSMOS suggested two 
options. First, a demonstration mission onboard  SOYUZ-2 launcher in the year 2015 and 
secondly a full scale science mission on-board SOYUZ-2 in 2017. ROSCOSMOS 
proposed that ISRO may provide  Indian Rover for launch sc heduled in 2015 or in 2017, 
also indicating that the 2015 opportunity i.e. Chandrayaan-2 involved mass limitation for 
Rover and higher risk.  
12.7.4 Based on the above inputs from Russian side and subsequent discussions held 
with them it was felt that the Mission called for a major programmatic realignment.   As 
such, an integrated programmatic review on Chandrayaan-2, chaired by Prof U.R. Rao 
carried out a critical assessment of India’s capability to desi gn and deploy a landing craft 
in a short time frame and a proposal was moot ed on the future direction of Chandrayaan-
2 Mission, concluding inter-alia that India could realise the Lander module too. 
12.7.5 With regard to progress made in th e Mission, the Committee has been informed 
that ISRO has shown its capability for Moon orbiter through CHANDRAYAAN-I and 
development of Rover Module as also a few scientific instruments to be flown on the 
orbiter and Rover had made good progress.  So me level of experimental studies for the 
Moon Lander had also been undertaken and the launch of Chandrayaan-2 by GSLV was 
planned by 2014. 
12.7.6 The Department has further informed th at due to programmatic re-adjustment, 
there could, however, be a te mporal shift in launching of  Chandrayaan-2 mission. Since 
the final configuration of the payloads is  under revision, the allo cation under the Indian 
Lunar Mission-Chandrayaan-1 & 2 has been decreased from  82.50 crores to . 56.01 
crores at R.E. stage 2012-13. This year the programme has been allocated . 78.00 crores 
at B.E. level.  
12.7.7 The Committee, in view of the subsequent developments that have taken 
place with regard to the in ter-planetary mission of Ch andrayaan-II, is of the 
opinion that ISRO should go ahead with the Mission with full confidence in its 
capabilities to achieve the mission successfu lly.  The process of indigenisation may 
take some time but it will make Indian Lunar programme, i.e., Chandrayaan -2 self-
sufficient.  India’s successf ul attempt to indigenously build cryo-technology was an 
outcome of technology denial regime wh ich proved a blessing in disguise.  The 
Committee is confident that this particular incident would give fillip to the efforts 

and resolve of the Department to work ha rder in order to overcome the challenge 
with added vigour and energy.  
12.7.8 The Committee, further, suggests that the Department should galvanise all 
the resources at its disposal and intensify it s efforts to ensure that the lunar orbiter, 
rover and Lander are developed at the ea rliest. The Committee would also like to 
caution the Department to take all nece ssary measure to make the Chandrayaan-2 
Mission a grand success learning lesso ns from Chandrayaan-1. The Committee 
further recommends that Planning Commissio n and the Ministry of Finance should 
extend all necessary financial/ budgetary support for the Mission. 
12.8 MARS ORBITER MISSION  
12.8.1 Mars Orbiter Mission is ISRO's first interplanetary mission with a spacecraft 
designed to orbit Mars in  an elliptical orbit.  India’s first mission to  Mars is proposed to 
be launched using Polar Sate llite Launch Vehicle in XL configuration (PSLV-XL) from 
Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota in October-November 2013. The mission has 
been designated as PSLV-C25.  
12.8.2 As per information provided by the Depart ment all the four stages of the PSLV-
C25 including the strap-ons and their respective sub-systems were under various stages of 
preparation. The integr ation of the launch vehi cle was planned to commence in the first 
week of August 2013. The Space craft, Mars Orb iter, is undergoing integration and 
spacecraft level tests. It is expected to take 300 days to reach the planet Mars, after which 
it will be commanded to get inserted in the Martian orbit. This will be an orbiting mission 
around Mars. 
12.8.3 As far as budgetary allocation is con cerned, under the Mars Orbiter Mission, 
although the B.E. and R.E. allo cation in 2012-13 was kept at  125.00 Crores, the actual 
utilisation as on January, 2013 amounted to . 10.87 crores only. However, during this 
financial year, the budgetary a llocation has been increased by 42.50 Crores and has 
reached 167.50 Crores. When the Committee enqui red whether the amount allocated 
was sufficient enough to run the programme, the Department informed that the budgetary 
provision was sufficient enough to meet the pr ogrammatic requirements of Mars Orbiter 
Mission.  The Department further informed that Mars Orbiter Mission being the first 
Indian space mission to Mars, was driven primarily by technological objectives which 
included design and development of a Mars Orbiter with the capability to perform earth 
orbit manoeuvres. The scientific objectives of the mission included exploration of 
Martian surface features and study of constituen ts of Martian atmosphere using specific 
scientific instruments.  
12.8.4 The Committee notes that Mars Orbi ter Mission has several scientific 
advantages. Mars has good potential for space industrialisation and the Department 
should pursue this Mission with all earnestness and sincerity to make it successful so 
that India is able to achieve all the desired objectives from the Mission.  
12.8.5  The Committee takes note of the fact that the main objective of the Mars 
Orbiter Mission is to demonstrate India’s technological capacity to reach Martian 
orbit which would pave the way for futu re scientific exploratory Missions. The 
Committee understands that sending satel lite to Mars, involving a journey of 
millions and millions of miles and a journe y time of about 320 days, is not an easy 
task.  The Committee has further been inform ed that for such a long space journey, 
higher propulsion efficiency of the rocket is extremely essential and it is to be 
ensured that spacecraft survives the moveme nt for such long days and remains on 
the right path towards Mars. This essentia lly involves monitoring of the spacecraft 

by sending commands from the space statio n that should not be delinked at any 
stage during the journey as delinking may lead to the mission failure.  Moreover, for 
success of the mission, the Department have to ensure that all the components of the 
spacecraft continue to work efficiently th roughout the life of the mission. Keeping 
all this in view, the Committee would expect DoS to be extremely careful in planning 
and execution of  the Mission so that  th e huge sum of money involved in the project 
does not get wasted.  
12.8.6 The Committee would furth er like the Department to ensure that the Mars 
Orbiter Mission progresses as per schedule,  departing on time from the orbit of 
earth in November, 2013.  The Committee is  also hopeful that the Mars Orbiter 
would enter in the orbit of Mars by September, 2014, as per schedule taking 
advantage of earth's proximity to Mars at that point of time. 
13. SPACE PROGRAMME AND INDUSTRY PARTICIPATION 
13.1 When the Committee asked whether the De partment had any plans to set up a 
National Committee to work out modalities of hiving off producti on of Communication 
satellites and PSLV to the i ndustry and also if a  roadmap had been drawn by the 
Department to launch a satellite in collaborati on with private companies, the Department 
apprised that ISRO was making focused effort s to enhance the participation of Indian 
Space Industry in the production of Communi cation satellites, PSLV and related sub-
systems. Currently, about 500 industries pa rticipate in space pr ogrammes by supplying 
components, small structures for launch vehicl es, satellites and ro cket propellants. In 
addition to that, industries were  also involved in supply of some of the fully assembled 
liquid stages for launch vehicles.  Operation of complex facilities like solid propellant 
plant at Satish Dhawan Space Centre was also done by private industry. 
13.2 It was also informed that the feasibil ity studies aimed to evolve a model for 
increased participation of industry in the I ndian space programme had been initiated in 
the DoS. A National Committee was also bein g proposed to be set up to assess the 
modalities and to evolve the policy framew ork required for this, while ensuring 
inclusiveness and transparency. 
13.3 The Committee is of the view that sharing the burden of producing launch 
vehicles and satellites by pr ivate sector would help ISRO shed some of its financial 
burden, which will help release funds for ot her research-oriented activities of the 
Department.  
13.4 Additionally, large scale involvement of private sector would boost Indian 
space programme and help generate employ ment as well.  The Committee feels that 
this is a step taken in the right direction and DoS should continue to make concerted 
efforts in this direction . The Committee, accordin gly, recommends that the 
Department should make concerted efforts to encourage greater participation of 
private sector in its activities.  
14. CONTRIBUTION TO THE SOCIETY  
14.1 The Committee is aware that DoS has developed valuable spin-off technologies 
which are proving to be beneficial for the society in general and rural, far flung and 
backward areas of the country in particular.  Some of the noteworthy societal applications 
benefiting the Indian Society are given below:  
 INSAT operational system has facilitated telecommunications, TV 
broadcast, providing access to TV fo r 850 million Indians. INSAT has also 
played an important role in the country’s social development with exclusive 
channels for vocational training and distant development education.   

 ISRO has successfully demonstrated the capability of application of 
satellite technology in  the health sect or through tale-medicine programme. 
Tele-medicine review supported through INSAT-3A and GSAT-12 satellites, 
has established networks to take supe r-specialist medical services to the 
remote and rural population. Tele-medicin e facilitates medi cal consultations 
between specialist doctors in the cities and local doctors at Rural/Primary 
Health Centers in the villages, there by strengthening the healthcare related 
service/training in the rural areas.   
 Tele-education enables informal e ducation, strengthens teaching 
mechanisms, and facilitates interactive training and skill development 
processes at the Panchayat/ village community levels, directly.   
 INSAT system has helped in impr oving the meteorological services, 
cyclone monitoring and issuing warn ing on impending cyclones through 
disaster warning receivers installed along the east and west coasts of the 
country.  
 Indian Remote Sensing satellites ha ve been the workhorse for several 
applications - encompassing the various sectors such as agriculture, land and 
water resources, forestry, environment, natural disasters, urban planning and 
infrastructure development, rural deve lopment, and forecasting of potential 
fishing zones. 
 The value-added, high-resolution sate llite images provide community-
centric, geo-referenced spatial information relevant to management of natural 
resources - like land use/ land cover,  terrain morphology, surface water and 
groundwater, soil characteristics, environment and infrastructure.   
 Satellite communications and Earth observation segments together provide 
support to disaster management at communities level - like stockpiling 
emergency communication equipments, vulnerability and risk related 
information, early warning and extreme weather information dissemination 
mechanisms. 
 With well-knit institutional arrangement s to integrate space applications 
emanating from INSAT and IRS systems towards societal development, ISRO 
has positioned itself to provide some of  the valuable services of direct 
relevance at the grassroots.  
14.2 The Committee commends the Department  for making very good use of its 
spin off technologies for soci ally useful purposes such as tele-medicine, tele-education 
networks, Village Resource Centres, Fo restry mapping, assisting  disaster 
management efforts, locating natural resour ces as also keeping a check on insurgent 
activities in the country, etc. 
14.3 The Committee, however, feels that a lo t more needs to be done by DoS  to 
fully realise the vision of Dr. Sarabhai "to play a meaningful role nationally and in 
Comity of nations, we must be second to none in the application of advanced 
technologies to the real problems of ma n and society".  The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the DoS should make con certed efforts to try to live up-to the 
expectations of the society, the people and provide them with greater facilities and 
benefits.   

 
 
15. CONCLUDING REMARKS  
15.1 Keeping in view the outstanding work that the Department of Space has 
undertaken, the kind of professionalism an d competence it has exhibited and the 
kind of core and critical programmes it ha s envisaged for future, the Committee is 
confident that the Department would contin ue to bring glory to the country by its 
achievements. 
15.2 The Committee is of the view that, in an age when cost benefit analysis has 
become an integral part of public spendin g, the Department of Space, must set an 
example for others to emulate by providing high returns in the form of concrete 
benefits to the country and its people on  every rupee invested in its programme.  
The Committee is confident that the Department  has the capabilities to do so and it 
will not betray the trust reposed by the Committee in its capabilities.

REPORT 
 
The Earth behaves as a si ngle, interlinked and self-regulati ng system, its components,                     
viz. atmosphere, oceans, cryosphere, geosphere and biosphere, function as a single system with 
complex interactions.  The scientific understa nding of the earth system helps to improve 
prediction of climate, weather and natural hazards as well as afford sustainable use of 
resources. Recognising the importance of st rong inter-relation of processes among various 
components of the earth, in 2006 the Ministry of Earth Sciences was established to develop and 
improve capability to forecast, weather, climat e and hazard related phenomena for societal, 
economic and environmental benefits. The Ea rth System Science Organisation (ESSO) was 
also established in the year October, 2007, to monitor and give  a overall policy direction to the 
Ministry.  The agenda for the earth system science in the country includes providing new 
perspectives on earth systems, better unders tanding of earth processes and applying this 
knowledge for sustainability of the Earth and developing services for the societal benefits.  
2. In view of the importance of  the fact that India has a va st coastline, stretching some 
7,500 kms and its Exclusive Economic Zone(EEZ) of about 2.02 million sq. km., the Ministry 
of Earth Sciences brought all the agencies of the meteorological and ocean development 
activities under one umbrella. The Ministry of Earth Sciences is mandated to provide the nation 
with the best possible services in forecas ting monsoons and other weather and climate 
parameters, ocean states, earthquakes, tsun amis, and other earth phenomena through well 
integrated programmes. The Ministry also de als with science and t echnology for exploration 

and exploitation of ocean resources (living and  non-living) and plays a nodal role for 
Antarctic/Arctic and Seismological research in an integrated manner. 
3. OBJECTIVES AND FUNCTIONS OF THE MINISTRY 
The Ministry of Earth Sciences has the following objectives and functions: 
 To improve weather forecast and provide advisory for agriculture, aviation, shipping, 
sports including the Extended Long Range Seasonal Monsoon forecast, 
 To  provide a wide range of ocean information advisories including fishery information, 
  To improve the understanding of Polar Science and its implications for climate change, 
 To develop technology for harnessing marine resources, 
 To conduct surveys for assessing non-living resources, 
 To assess coastal marine productivity and Marine Ecosystems, 
 To improve understanding of Climate Change Science, 
 To provide early warning of natural hazards viz. cyclone, tsunami, sea level rise, and 
 To promote basic research including Capacity building in the Earth System Science. 
4.  ORGANISATIONAL STRU CTURE OF THE MINISTRY 
4.1 The Earth Commission
, Ministry of Earth Sciences works in Mission Mode 
basis and is responsible for formulating pol icies, overseeing implementation of policies 
and programmes in mission mode and ensuring th e necessary interdisciplinary integration. 
The ‘Earth System Science Organisation(ES SO)’, under the Ministry has four major 
branches of earth sciences viz.(i) Ocean Sc ience & Technology Services, (ii) Atmospheric 
and Climate Science Services,  (iii) Geoscience  and  Technology  and  (iv)  Polar Science 
and Cyrosphere. The ESSO implements its policies through th e following eight 
institutions: 
 India Meteorological Department (IMD),  
 National Centre for Medium Range Weather Forecasting (NCMRWF),  
 Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology (IITM),  
 National Centre for Antarctic and Ocean Research (NCAOR),  
 National Institute of Ocean Technology (NIOT),  
 Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS),  
 Centre for Marine Living Resources (CMLRE), and  
 Integrated Coastal & Marine Area Management (ICMAM).   
      Each centre of MoES  has a we ll defined mandate  to conduct cutting-edge 
research in  a specific area of Earth System Science. 
5. FINANCIAL AND ADMINISTRATIVE POWE RS FOR THE EARTH        
     COMMISSION   
5.1 The Ministry, during the examination of  the Demands for Grants(2012-13) had 
apprised the Committee that the Earth Commission presently lacks financial and 
administrative powers and a draft Cabinet Note on conferring of said powers to the Earth 
Commission had been circulat ed to all the concerned Ministries/agencies and their 
comments were being obtained. The Committee in its 226 th and 236 th Reports had 
reiterated that the comments from the con cerned Ministries/agencies should be expedited 
and recommended that the administrative and financial powers be granted without any 
further delay to the Earth Commission.  
5.2 The Ministry informed the Committee th at the comments on the said issue has 
already been received from the Planni ng Commission, Departments of Expenditure, 
Economic Affairs, Personnel & Training, Space and Atomic Energy and have been 
suitably incorporated in the draft note.  However, the Cabinet Secretariat while giving its 

comments has insisted that inter-ministerial co nsultations cannot be dispensed with in the 
instant case and therefore the draft note has now  being circulated to the Departments of 
Ministry of Science & Technol ogy viz. Departments of Scie ntific & Industrial Research 
(CSIR), Biotechnology, and also to the Defence Research & Development Organisation 
(DRDO) for their comments. 
5.3 The Committee feels that undue del ay in devolution of appropriate 
financial and administrative powers to th e Earth Commission, which is responsible 
for formulating, overseeing and implementing the policies and programmes of the 
Ministry, hampers the overall functioning of the Ministry. The Committee, therefore, 
reiterates its recommendation made in its 226
th Report that immediate steps be taken 
to provide financial and administrative pow ers to the Earth Commission to enable it 
to effectively carry out its assigned role.  
6.  The detailed budget allocation of the Mini stry of Earth Sciences, for the year 
2013-14 was considered by the Department-re lated Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Science & Technology, Environment & Forests in its meeting held on the 2nd April, 2013. 
7.  MECHANISM TO MONITOR AND REVIEW ONGOING SCHEMES 
7.1  At the Ministry level, the ESSO Council setup by the Ministry, reviews the 
implementation of its programmes on a half year ly basis. At institute levels, particularly 
for the autonomous bodies of the Ministry, th e programmes are monito red periodically by 
the Research Advisory Committee of the centres. The Governing Council, Financial 
Committee of the respective centres provide di rection from both technical and financial 
angles. At the programme level, the schemes are monitored by Steering Committee 
constituted by the Ministry with experts dr awn from relevant fields.  Besides, the 
programmes of the Ministry are being monitored by Planning Commission, and the 
Cabinet Secretariat through its Result Framework Document (RFD) on an annual basis.  
7.2 The Committee was also informed that the performance of various schemes is 
being assessed periodica lly since 2009–2010, by th e Ad Hoc Task Group under the 
direction of High Powered Committee, constituted by the Cabinet Secretariat, as a part of 
RFD. The Ministry also informed that it has obtained RFD scor es of 95.07% and 97.15% 
for the years 2010–11 and 2011–12, respectively. The RFD score for the year 2012-13 is 
awaited.                    
7.3 The Committee notes with happiness th at the Ministry has been able to 
obtain high RFD scores, in the years 2010- 11 and 2011-12, which is indicative of the 
fact that the monitoring and review mech anism adopted by the Ministry has been 
successful in timely implementation of programmes. The Committee hopes that the 
Ministry would maintain the same level of  performance of its various schemes and 
even aim to secure a better RFD score, in the current fiscal.  
8. THE XIITH FIVE YEAR PLAN  
8.1 The Committee was informed that while an amount of Rs.7004.00crores was 
provided to it in the XIth  Plan, the plan outlay has been increas ed to Rs. 9506.00 crores 
during the XIIth Plan period. Further, the Minist ry also informed that  after reorienting its 
76 projects into 14 major programmes during the first year of the XIIth Plan, the Ministry 
has been able to effectively monitor and flawlessly implement the programmes in a more 
coordinated way towards achieving its targets.  
The major thrust areas of the XIIth Plan and its progress/achievements are as follows: 
 Monsoon Mission : The monsoon mission, was initiate d with the ultimate aim to 
improve the monsoon prediction over the country on all time scales. The necessary models 
for improving monsoon forecast had been inst alled and the first experimental seasonal 

monsoon prediction was carried out during 2012 and necessary improvements in the 
models had been carried out. 
 Exploration of Deep Sea Minerals: Seven cruises were conducted in Indian Ocean to 
identify potential areas and analysis of the collected samples, was under progress. 
 Augmentation of High Computing System : Technical and financial evaluation for a 
High Computing system were underway. 
 Cloud Physics Lab :  Necessary permission had been obtained for construction of a 
cloud physics laboratory at Mahabaleshwar(Maharashtra). 
 Seismological Research : Deep bore holes investigati ons in Koyna–Warna region of 
Maharastra has been launched to address majo r issues pertaining to the occurrence of 
earthquakes and their mechanism by drilling  deep boreholes of 6-7 km depth, in a 
continental earthquake zone, to  study physical and chemical  changes before, during and

art facilities was also being established.

 3rd Indian Permanent Station in Antarctica  - India successfully commenced 
operations at Bharati, third new permanent station at Antarctica from March, 2012 and 
scientific studies in the field of geosci ences, glaciology, atmosphere, paleoclimate and 
polar biology were being carried out.  
8.2 The Committee notes that the Mini stry has been provided an increased 
Budgetary support of Rs.9506.00crores durin g the XIIth Plan, which is Rs 2502.00 
crores more than the amount of Rs.7004.00cro res provided during XIth Plan Period. 
It also notes that during the XIIth Plan, the Ministry has been successful in 
monitoring and implementing its program mes in a more coordinated way towards 
achieving its targets, after the reorienta tion of its 76 proj ects into 14 major 
programmes. The Committee also hopes that with judicious planning and execution, 
the Ministry would be able to utilize the in creased allocation for the XIIth Plan in a

9. BUDGETARY ALLOCATION FOR THE YEAR 2013-14 
9.1 As regards the Budgetary allocation, the Committee was informed that the 
Ministry has been given a Plan allocation of  Rs. 1281.00 crores, against the Ministry’s 
demand for a Plan allocation of Rs. 2424.63 crores for the B.E. 2013-14.  The Committee 
also noted that in the year 2012-2013, the total B.E. outlay was Rs.1668.00 crores, which 
was substantially reduced to Rs 1195.00 cror es at R.E. stage and enquired about the 
reasons for the reduction of funds  allocated.  In repl y, the Ministry info rmed that it had 
achieved only an utilization of 40% of th e Budgetary outlay by September, 2012, and the 
Planning Commission had resorted to a drastic reduction in the outlay at RE stage of 2012-
13 citing funds crunch as the reason for the redu ction.  The Ministry further informed that, 
due to the drastic reduction at RE stage, seve ral new activities planned for implementation 
during the XIIth Five year Plan have been deferred for the time being. The Committee also 

noted that there has been no increase in  the Plan allocation during BE 2013-14 as 
compared to BE 2012-13, with the Plan allo cation stagnating at Rs. 1281.00 crores. In 
reply to a query, the Committee was info rmed that in the years 2009-10, 2010-11 and 
2011-12, the percentage utilization at B.E. stag e as compared to the Actual Expenditure 
had been 89.05%, 84.13% and 74.86% respectively. 
9.2 The Committee notes with co ncern the gross underutilization of funds by 
the Ministry over the years 2009-10 to 2011-12, which is evident from the decreasing 
trend of percentage utilization of allocated funds at B.E. stage, i.e. from 89.05% in 
2009-10 to 74.85% in 2011-12. It also notes that in the year 2012-2013, the B.E. outlay 
of Rs.1668.00 crores was cut down to Rs 1195.00 crores at R.E. stage, due to resource 
crunch and the fact that the percentage ut ilization of B.E. 2012-13 was only 40% till 
September, 2012, which again points towards the underutilization of funds. The 
Committee takes a strong view of the gross und erutilization of funds and feels lack of 
proper monitoring of projects on the part of  the Ministry is the principal reason for 
underutilization of funds. The Committee, th erefore, recommends that the Ministry 
should only seek funds to th e extent it can utilise and sh ould meticulously monitor its 
spending from B.E. stage itself, so that  huge underutilisation of funds could be 
avoided.  The Committee further recommends that plan outlay for the year 2013-14 
should be adequately enhanced to offset reduction of plan allocation made at RE 
stage in the year 2012-13 so that the total pl an outlay of the Department for the XIIth  
Five Year Plan does not get reduced and the Department is able to achieve all of its 
plan objectives for the XIIth  Five Year Plan.  
MAJOR PROGRAMMES OF THE MINISTRY

‘Atmospheric Observation Systems Network’ had been allocated  Rs. 206.00 crores in B.E.

allocated in the B.E. 2013-14. When the Committee enquired into the reasons for the 
fluctuation, the Ministry stated that the drastic reduction in the budget at RE 2012-13 stage

fiscal. Due to this reduction, several new ac tivities planned/envisaged for implementation 
during 12
th Five Year Plan have been deferred fo r the time being. The Ministry further  
justified the allocation of Rs. 200.00 crores in B.E 2013-14, which was made to clear the

Meteorological Department (IMD) Phase-II’ was also envisaged un der this budgetary 
head.

II’ programme, it proposes to further augment the meteorological observational systems 
and forecasting tools to improve the weather forecasting services. It also envisages to 
develop weather & climate monitoring and fo recast services over the Himalayan region

10.4 In reply to a query, the Ministry stated  that significant increase in the success 
rate of meteorological obser vations had been exibited af ter the reorientation of the

network and services, satellite related meteorological products , block level agro-
meteorological services, meteor ological services at airports were being implemented

is of prime importance, specially in view  of the climatic changes which had taken 
place over the recent past a nd the fact that agriculture in the country primarily

capabilities of the Department have incr eased significantly. The Committee while 
complementing the Department on this achievement and taking note that the 
Department has initiated modernization of IMD Phase-II programme with a view to 
further improve the weather forecasting services, would like the Department to

10.6 The Committee, keeping in view the large extent to which the Himalayas 
affect the weather and monsoon pattern in the country and the need for developing 
deeper understanding of Himalayan meteor ology to obtain better accuracy in 
weather forecasting, welcomes the programme ‘Integrated Himalayan Meteorology

th Five Year Plan, a major

meteorological services have brought a substantial economic benefit of Rs 50,000

th Five Year Plan, concerted effort s would be made to achieve the

Weather and Climate', which were not included under this head earlier. All these programs 
have been approved during 2012-13 and the funds  have been allocated accordingly in this 
fiscal. 
MOONSOON MISSION 
11.3 The Ministry informed the Commit tee that the monsoon mission was a multi-
institutional and inter-agency research programme, for impr oving monsoon forecasts over 
India on all time scales i.e. from Short ra nge to seasonal. The M onsoon Mission with a 
budget of Rs.400.00 crores is to be implemented during the 12 th five year plan (2012-17).  
Under the monsoon mission, a dynamical pred iction system for predicting the monsoon 
weather and climate on all time scales was being implemented and was expected to 
improve prediction skills. A major highlight of the mission was the participation of 
research and academic institutions from India and abroad in collaborative research work to 
improve the monsoon forecasts. Under the monsoon mission, a coupled climate model, 
was implemented at the Indian Institute of  Tropical Meteorology (IITM) for extended 
range (up to one month) for seasonal monsoon forecasts. Another coupled model of United 
Kingdom Meteorological office was implemented at the National Centre for Medium 
Range Weather Forecasting (NCMRWF) for shor t range forecasting up to two-weeks. In 
this mission 16 projects (8 from India a nd 8 from abroad) are approved for funding under 
this mission.  
11.4 The Committee notes that the Mini stry had engaged the services and  
participation of research and academic in stitutions from India and abroad in 
collaborative research to improve the monsoo n forecasts. Further, 16 projects, eight 
from within the country and eight from ab road are being funded under this Mission 
for improving prediction skills.  The Co mmittee recommends that the Department 
take all necessary measures so that the pr ogramme achieves its objective of improved 
capabilities for more accurate monsoon predictions.  
11.5 Regarding the percentage of accuracy of the Monsoon predictions, the Ministry 
provided the following details of the forecast and actual rainfall of All-India monsoon 
during the period, 2008-2012, in terms of the ‘Long Period Average’(LPA), which is a 
measure of the average rainfall, over a period of time:  
Year Forecast (%of LPA) Actual (% of LPA)
2008 100 98 
2009 93 78 
2010 102 102 
2011 95 101 
2012 96 92 
            As may be seen from the seasonal forecasts, the monsoon rainfall during the last 5 
years were found to be reasonably accurate, except for the year 2009, when the actual 
percentage was 78 against  a forecast percentage of 93. 

11.6 In reply to another query regarding the efforts made by the Ministry to improve 
the weather and climate prediction services and bring them at par with the highest 
international standards of accuracy, the Ministry  informed that at present, the operational 
seasonal monsoon forecasts, in the country we re prepared using advanced statistical 
models, which have some limitations. The alternative method to prepare seasonal forecasts 
was the use of dynamical models, based on co upled ocean-atmosphere models, in which 
the dynamics and physics of both the oceans a nd atmosphere were explicitly forecast, 
using high performance super computers. Howeve r, at present, the skill of the dynamical 
models in the country was not meeting the re quirements of true inte rnational standards. 
The monsoon mission launched by the Ministry therefore aims to improve the skill of these 
dynamical models further and more accurate monsoon forecasts were expected. Ministry 
further stated that to improve weather pred iction, it was necessary to improve atmospheric 
and oceanic observations. Therefore, the Mi nistry was making efforts to improve and 
expand the existing observational networks and generate increased satellite derived data 
for assimilating into weather prediction models.  
 11.7    The Ministry also informed that  Weather and climate predictions depend on 
observations/data  regarding initial weather conditions and to account for uncertainty in 
initial conditions (due to inadequate observa tions) ensemble forecasts were required in 
which different forecasts are generated by changing the initial conditions. At present due to 
limitations of computing resources, no ensemb le forecasts were being generated. The 
Ministry, therefore, proposes to prepare en semble forecasts once th e computing facility 
improved. The Ministry also informed that  for generation of operational weather and 
climate forecasts and for carrying out res earch on improved models, there was a high 
demand for high performance computers. At pr esent, the weather forecasting institutions 
working under the Ministry had computers of a computi ng capacity of around 100 Tera 
(10
12) Flop. However, for working on improved weather models, for the planned modeling 
activity, high performance computing (HPC) facility with 2.5 Peta (10 15) Flop was 
required. The Ministry was therefore planning to acquire the HPC with capacity around 2.5 
Peta Flop during the next couple of years. 
11.8     The Committee notes with satisfac tion that the ‘Long Period Average’(LPA) 
percentage of accuracy attained in rainfall forecasting was almost equal to the actual 
rainfall occurred in the country, every year from 2008 to 2012, barring the year 2009, 
when the actual rainfall was 78% against the forecast percentage of 93.  The 
Committee, however, observes that for generation of accurate operational weather 
and climate forecasts, more research on improved models was required, for which 
application of high performance computers with a computing facility of 2.5 Peta 
Flops was required.  The Committee, therefore,  feels that there is a genuine need for 
the Ministry to acquire the High Performa nce Computers with around 2.5 Peta Flop 
and high performance computing facility was essential for improving its forecasts 
capabilities and therefore recommends that ad equate funds for it should be made 
available to the Ministry at the earliest.   
12. CLOUD MICROPHYSICS  AND AIRBORNE PLATFORMS 
12.1 The Committee has been given to understa nd by the Ministry that the efficiency 
with which clouds produce rain at the surface varies greatly from one place to another. The 
Committee, accordingly, would like to apprecia te the statement of the Ministry that the 
understanding of these processe s regarding interaction  of  cloud with aeros ols was very 
essential for rain enhancement purpose.  In this  context,  Ministry's  effort to develop a 
programme  "Cloud Aerosols Interaction a nd Precipitation enhancem ent" (CAIPEEX) is 

welcomed by the Committee as there is a need  for simultaneous measurements of aerosols 
and cloud micro physics for studying aerosols  interactions which can be done only by 
airborne platforms by procurin g aircraft for atmospheric re search.  The Committee was 
informed by the Ministry last year that act ion had been initiated to develop cloud physics 
lab at Mahabaleshwar to investigate precipitation process, classify clouds and estimate rain 
rate.  The Committee is also happy to note th at a mobile X-band, D oppler Weather Radar 
has been installed and commissioned near the Mahabaleshwar lab.  In this connection, it 
may be mentioned that in reply to an ear lier recommendation of the Committee, in its 236 th 
Action Taken Report,it has been mentioned by the Ministry that construction of the 
Mahabaleshwar lab will commence after the e xpiry of the monsoon season in October, 
2012 and the same is expected to be completed by June, 2013.  The Committee feels that 
as June, 2013 is approaching, the Ministry sh ould make all out effort to complete the 
construction of the said lab as per schedul e so that better understanding of processes 
regarding interaction of clouds with a erosols is achieved and used for rain 
enhancement purposes.   
12.2 The Committee also observed that the ‘Air borne Platform’ was allocated at B.E. 
stage of  2012-13, an amount of Rs. 50.00 crores  , which was later reduced to a nominal 
level of Rs. 0.50 crores at the R.E stage. Ho wever, in the current fiscal of 2013-14, it has 
been increased substantially to Rs. 30.00 crores  at B.E. stage. When the Committee asked 
for the reason behind the drastic reduction at R. E. stage in the year  2012-13, the Ministry 
informed that in order to achieve the objectiv es of the Airborne Platforms, the Indian 
Institute of Tropical Meteorology (IITM), co nsulted various departments and submitted a 
Detailed Project Report(DPR) in November, 2013. The EFC document was prepared on the 
basis of DPR, which lead to delay in completion of formalities for the approval of DPR and 
accordingly, the fund of Rs. 50.00 crores under th is head could not be utilized during the 
year 2012-13. The Ministry further stated that the EFC of the Ministry, has now 
recommended Rs 240.00 crores for acquisition of Airborne Platforms. Keeping this in view 
a token  sum of Rs 30.00 crores had been kept in the budget of the current fiscal for the 
said purpose.   
12.3 The Committee notes that in view of th e crucial role of airborne platforms 
in  cloud micro physics and aerosols int eractions studies, the Committee in its 226
th 
report        (Para 11.20)  has strongly recommended for a adequate budgetary support 
for such studies.  The Committee notes that due to the procedural bottlenecks, 
Ministry could not utilise funds allocated for it during 2012-13 and even in the budget 
of 2013-14 only a token provision has been made.  The Committee recommends that 
the Ministry should seriously pursue acquisi tion of Airborne Pl atforms so that its 
studies aimed at better unders tanding of processes regardi ng interaction of clouds 
with aerosols and using it for rain e nhancement purposes are completed as per
