15. SEISMOLOGICAL RESEARCH PROGRAMME 
15.1 The Ministry intimated that the prim ary objective of Seis mological Research 
Programme was to have comprehensive mult i- parametric geophysical observations in 
seismically active areas of the country which include the following: 
 Deep crustal studies across the Indian continental margin and the interior,  
 Andaman subduction zone, and  
 Active faults of India.   
      The Budgetary allocation for th e said programme at B.E. 2013-14 was Rs.80.00 
crores  as compared to Rs 55.00 crores in B.E. 2012-13. 
15.2 In this context, the Committee in its 226
th Report had recommended as 
follows: 
 “The Committee also notes that pres ently, various aspects of seismology 
related research are being carried out in a fragmented way by several 
research, academic and State and Central Government institutions in the 
country. In view of the extreme killer and destructive potential of earthquake 
as a natural phenomenon, the Committee fully endorses the proposal of the 
Ministry to set up a sepa rate research institute of the nature of ‘National 
Centre of Seismology’ which is ex clusively devoted to study of the 
mechanics of earthquakes, geo-tectonic  movements and all other aspects of 
earthquake so as to avoid/minimise the loses of life and property, a field 
which is yet to by mastered by the human mind.” 
15.3 In reply to action taken on said reco mmendation of the Committee, the Ministry 
stated that issues relating to  the preparation, circulation of  EFC documents, finalization of 
site/land/construction of building and the moda lities for the construction of  the National 
Centre for Seismology (NCS) to conduct focuse d research in the area of seismology, was 
under consideration. The Ministry further informed in the meeting of the Committee  held 
on  2
nd April, 2013, that the required land for esta blishment of NCS had been earmarked at 
Ayanagar Complex  (Gurgaon, Haryana) and is expected to be completed in a period of 
about three years after the approval of the EFC. 
15.4 Committee expresses displeasure at the slow pace with which procedural 
formalities are being completed and even after lapse of more than one year, EFC 
approval for the project has not yet been taken.  The Committee recommends that all 
procedural formalities including approval of EFC should be completed without any 
further loss of time and NCS set up within three years from now.  
15.5 The President in his address to th e Parliament on the 21.02.2013, has announced 
that the Government would set up a dedicat ed Seismological Research Laboratory and 
launch a first-of-its-kind research programme in earthquake prone Koyna-Warna region of 
Maharashtra to study ‘precursor changes’.  
 15.6       During the meeti ng of the Committee held on 2 nd April, 2014, the Ministry in 
reply to a query stated that the entire process of earthquake was not yet well understood, as 
the earthquake occurs 10 to 15 kms deep insi de the earth and neither was there any  
process to measure it nor was any process to observe it.  Since earthquake is a regular 
occurrence in the Koyna-Warna region (Mah arashtra), the Ministry intimated the 
Committee that it is going to put a bore-hole th ere and collect seismological data during 
the earthquakes. A location specific Bore-H ole Geophysics lab would also be setup at 

Karad (Maharastra) to measure through bore-hole s, the properties of rocks before, during 
and after an earthquake. All these activities would be coordinated under the NCS.  
15.7      The Committee welcomes the initiative of  the Ministry to establish a location 
specific Bore-Hole Geophysics lab at Karad(Maharastra) in the Koyna-Warna region 
to measure through bore-holes, the propert ies of rocks before, during and after an 
earthquake. The Committee feels that such a la boratory would help in providing 
knowledge and much needed data about the  earthquake processes, for aiding 
scientific investigations leading to better understanding about the mechanisms of 
faulting, physics of earthquakes and also developing models for better earthquake 
forecast in future and recommends that Mini stry should ensure that the laboratory 
start functioning within three years i.e. simu ltaneously or before the National Centre 
of Seismology is set up.   
16. OCEAN SURVEY AND MINE RAL RESOURCES PROGRAMME 
16.1 The Ministry informed that this prog ramme was primarily aimed at conducting 
surveys for harnessing the marine non-living re sources in a sustaina ble way available in 
the Indian EEZ and deep sea region of the Indian Ocean which includes gas hydrates, poly 
metallic nodules, hydrothermal sulphide minerals etc. All ongoing projects of the Ministry 
and the new initiatives of the XIIth Plan ha ve been integrated into this programme. 
Besides, continuing the ongoing projects, the major emphasis would be on the research 
activities relating to the Hydrothermal Su lphides containing valuable noble metals 
available along the mid oceanic regions of the Indian Ocean. 
16.2         The Committee noted that ‘Ocean Survey and Mineral Resources’ was allocated         
Rs.70.00 crores at B.E. 2013-14, in comparison to the R.E. 2012-13 allocation of                     
Rs. 50.00crores. The Ministry explained that the increase of Rs. 20.00 crores in allocation 
of funds during 2013-14 over the R.E. 2012-13, was primarily to meet the expenditure 
relating to the programme on Hydrothermal Sulphides which was launched in 2012-13. 
The project had been recommended for im plementation in-principle by the Inter-
Ministerial Group, as a follow-up action of th e decision by the Committee of Secretaries 
(CoS). The Ministry further explained that it  was a major national initiative which focuses 
on the study of seafloor hydrothermal system s at mid-ocean ridges with emphasis on the 
survey and exploration for hydrothermal sul phide deposits on the Central Indian Ridge 
(CIR) in the Indian Ocean. The discovery of su ch systems in the deep oceanic realm along 
the mid-ocean ridges had kindled a lot of interest primarily on account of the high 
concentration of base metals viz. Copper & Zinc and also many noble metals viz. Gold, 
Silver, Platinum & Palladium in them. Apar t from their economic potential, sea-floor 
hydrothermal vents were among the most pr oductive ecosystems on Earth and also contain 
dense biologic communities, as Sulfide from hydrothermal fluids pr ovides the energy to 
drive these productive systems. National Centre for Antarctic and Ocean Research 
(NCAOR), Goa, an autonomous body under the Ministry had been entrusted with the 
responsibility for implementa tion of the programme in its entirety on behalf of the 
Ministry.   
16.3            Similarly, the Polymetalli c Nodules, are nodules cont aining Manganese, Iron, 
Nickel, Copper, Cobalt, Lead, etc. occurring at  a depth of 4 to 5 Km in the deep oceans 
lying on the sea bed. India presently has 75,000 sq  km area in the Central Indian Ocean 
Basin(CIOB) for developmental activities targeted at harnessing of these metals. As 
regards the Gas Hydrates the Ministry inform ed that they are naturally occurring solid 
compounds containing natural gas, mainly Meth ane and water and are important as they 
are considered to be source of clean fuel. A detailed seismic survey has been undertaken in 

the Andamans, Kerala-Konkan basin & the Kris hna-Godaveri Basin an d the results were 
being analysed. 
16.4     The Committee notes that the Ministry proposes to undertake survey and 
exploration in the deep oceanic realm along the mid-ocean ridges in the Indian ocean 
for hydro thermal sulphide  deposits havi ng high concentration of base and noble 
metals apart from continuing  its Po lymetallic Nodules and Gas Hydrates 
Programmes from the funds allocated und er Ocean Survey and Mineral Resources 
Programme.  The Committee understands that so far as its Polymetallic Nodules 
Programme is concerned, it is still at exploration stage, while for Gas Hydrates 
Programme, technology is yet being augmente d for exploration purposes.  Therefore, 
the dream of commercial exploitation of these minerals or gas hydrates is still a 
distant dream.  The Committee recommends that the Ministry pursue with greater 
vigour its Mineral Resources Programme and make an endeavor to produce concrete  
results  from this programme in next few years.   
17.         ENVIRONMENT MONITORING AND RESEARCH 
17.1 In reply to a query as to whether any Environment Monitoring and Research 
Programme was being designed by the Ministry to check the pollution in seas/oceans and 
whether any mitigation measures have been carri ed out, the Ministry informed that it had 
been implementing a programme to carry out Environment Monitoring  of water quality 
from pollution point of view and was checkin g pollution in seas at  20 locations along 
coastal states and Union Territories. The Minist ry further stated that  the pollution data so 
collected was provided to the Central Pollu tion Control Board(CPCB) and State Pollution 
Control Boards (SPCBs) for their use for designing pollution mitigation measures, etc.   
The Committee was also informed that anothe r area of concern regarding coastal pollution 
was the Harmful Algal Blooms (HAB), a type of toxic algal species, within India’s EEZ.  
17.2 HARMFUL  ALGAL BLOOMS 
           The oceans are the homes of 2000  micro-scopic algal species which constitute 
the base  of the marine food web and the bene ficial algae intrinsically facilitate food web 
processes as they channel car bon or energy into marine food web.   There were, however, 
a few dozen of algal species whose blooms are associated with serious  adverse impacts on 
environment.  The Ministry mentioned in response  to a query of the Committee  that 
recent studies indicate harmful Algal Blooms were increasing both in terms of frequency 
and extent for which pollution, particularly  marine pollution  was the major contributing 
factor. They have further mentioned that  HABs secrete toxic substances which was 
released  through food chain which causes death among humans and apart from this, 
HABs also cause adverse changes in bio-geoc hemical cycles altering eco-systems having 
cascading effects on marine biota. The Ministry  have mentioned  that for the past ten 
years, the Ministry was monitoring the adve rse effects of HABs in the Indian EEZ with 
particular reference to blooms dynamics and de veloping predictive  capabilities  of the 
occurrence of  such bloom.    
17.3 The Committee is aware of the fact th at rising HABs along the Indian coast  had 
led to serious eutrophication thereby killin g a big section of fish population.  The 
Committee had also observed that HABs blooming was more  prevalent along the west 
coast of the country  than on the east coast.   The Committee is, therefore of the opinion 
that  entire scenario  requires a deep study   particularly regard ing the  regular bloom 
occurrences and  shell fish poisoning  from algal toxin causing human fatalities along the 
Indian coast.  The Committee, therefor e, recommends that Ministry may take up a 

programme, in collaboration with other Mi nistries and national and international 
institutes or bodies, as may be necessary to address this issue.  
18. The Committee notes that the Ministry through its various 
schemes/programmes provides a vast rang e of societal benefits such as 
meteorological, agromet services etc., be sides being responsible for exploring & 
exploiting the marine resources and co nducting polar research. The Committee after 
examining the various aspects of the Demands for Grants (2013-14) of the Ministry of 
Earth Sciences, is of the view that Mini stry should prudently utilize funds made 
available to it, having due regard to reco mmendations contained in the report and 
efficiently implement its various schemes and programmes in the year 2013-14.

INTRODUCTION 
At the time, India gained independence in 1947, one of the most challenging tasks 
before the newly independent nation was to  bring out of abject poverty a very large 
proportion of its people and to achieve a reasonable  standard of living for them.  Our 
visionary leaders of that era clearly visu alized the role of Science & Technology in 
meeting this formidable challenge and accordingly from the beginning made sincere 
efforts to develop necessary infrastructure  and environment for growth of science & 
technology in the country.  Promotion of scie nce & technology was r ecognized as one of 
the national priorities with the aim to make  full use of science & technology in achieving 
faster growth and development of the count ry. Scientific Policy Resolution of 1958 and 
the Technology Policy statement of 1983 have  guided the growth & development of 
Science & Technology in the country.  

2. The Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) and its constituent 
laboratories were established as country’s R&D centres in public sector, primarily for 
converting research to technologies having co mmercial potential.  Today, its 37 national 
laboratories, 39 outreach centre, 6 units and 3 innovation complexes are carrying out 
industrial research in divers e scientific areas. Some of these areas are affordable 
healthcare, water purification, dr ug discoveries and their clini cal trials, bio jet fuels, bio-
ethanol, protection of Indian  traditional medicinal knowledge, solar energy, improving 
the yield of crops, etc. 
3. Council of Scientific and Industrial Research estab lished in 1942, subsequently 
became one of the two autonomous organizati ons under Department of Scientific and 
Industrial Research which itself became one of  the three Departments of the Ministry of 
Science and Technology, established in 1985. 
4. The Department-related Parliament ary Standing Committee on Science & 
Technology, Environment and Forests consider ed the detailed Demand for Grants 2013-
14 of the Department of Scient ific and Industrial Research (D SIR) in its meeting held on 
3
rd April, 2013. 
5. DEPARTMENT OF SCIENTIFIC & INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH (DSIR)  
5.1 Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (DSIR), one of the Departments 
of the Ministry of Science and Technol ogy was established th rough a Presidential 
Notification dated January 4, 1985. Its mandate inter-alia includes promotion of 
industrial research for indigenous technology development, promotion, utilization and 
transfer. The subjects allocated to the Department are:  
i)  All matters concerning the Council of  Scientific and Industrial Research.  
ii)  All matters relating to National Research Development Corporation.  
iii)  All matters relating to Central Electronics Limited.  
iv)  Registration and Recognition of R&D Units.  
v)  Matters relating to UNCTAD and WIPO.  
vi)  National Register for Foreign Collaborations.  
vii) Matters relating to creation of pool for tempor ary placement of Indian 
Scientists and Technologists.  
5.2 The primary endeavour of Department of Scientific And Industrial Research 
(DSIR) is to encourage indus try to increase their share in  country’s R&D expenditure, 
support a larger cross section of small and medium industrial units to develop state-of-the 
art, globally competitive technologies of hi gh commercial potential, catalyze faster 
commercialization of lab-scale R&D, enhan ce the share of technol ogy intensive exports 
in overall exports, strengthen industria l consultancy and technology management 
capabilities and establish user friendly inform ation network to facilitate scientific and 
industrial research in  the country. Two autonomous orga nizations namely, Council for 
Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) and Consultancy Development Centre (CDC) 
and two public sector undertak ings namely National Research Development Corporation 
(NRDC) and Central Electronics Limited (C EL) are under its admi nistrative control. 
DSIR also provides institutional host facilities and assistance to Asian & Pacific Centre 
for Transfer of Technology (APCTT) as a focal point in the country. 
6. MECHANISM TO MONITOR AND RE VIEW THE ONGOING SCHEMES  
6.1. The Committee was informed that th e progress of all projects under the 
Department was monitored at various le vels. Ongoing programme s/projects were 
reviewed and monitored with the help of Technical Advisory Committees, Steering 
Committees and Project Review Committees. At the end of five year plans, the 

Department also conducts third party reviews.   At present, the Department was carrying 
out third party review for its Technopr eneur Promotion Programme (TePP) and 
Technology Development and Demonstrati on Programme (TDDP) being operated since 
11th plan period. The Department has further informed that Result Framework Document 
exercise had further helped in strengthe ning the monitoring mechanism of ongoing 
schemes.  
6.2 It was also informed that in CSIR, th e Cluster concept of participative planning 
and monitoring was evolved duri ng mid-term appraisal of 11
th Five year pl an and would 
be continued in 12 th Five Year Plan as well with grea ter rigor and focus. A detailed four 
tier monitoring mechanisms have been evolved by the Department regarding CSIR 
projects. The Department has mentioned that at Laboratory level, the respective research 
council monitor’s projects and then task force does it at the project level. At Cluster level, 
the Cluster Director monitors programmes,  and at Headquarters level, External 
Monitoring Committees review pr ogress. Finally DG, CSIR reviews the overall projects 
after it was cleared at the Headquarter’s le vel. The dynamic mode of project operation 
also ensures that programmes can be reposi tioned and reoriented to meet the desired 
objectives. Apart from this, compilation of  comprehensive knowledge base information 
on Clusters and project wise white papers for appropriate benchmarking were additional 
features for the 12
th Five Year Plan monitoring of projects.   
7. RESULT FRAMEWORK DOCUMENT (RFD) 
7.1 From the year 2009-10, Result Framework Document (RFD) has been introduced 
by the Cabinet Secretariat’s Performance Management Division wherein the project 
performance of all scientific  departments of the Government was evaluated by a third 
party, appointed by the Performance Management  Division of the Ca binet Secretariat. 
One of the most important features of RF D was that under it schemes, programmes and 
activities were defined in quantitative terms and the achievements of the projects were 
reviewed by the Adhoc Task Force consisting of former Secretaries of Government of 
India. In this context, the Committee was informed by the Department that under RFD, 
the Department has achieved high compos ite value scores of 95.84% in 2009-10 and 
again 95.97% in 2010-11.  
7.2 When it was enquired from the Department about their performance during the 
last financial year in term of RFD, the De partment informed that its score in RFD for 
2012-13 was expected to be around the same level as in 2011-12 which was 93.90%. It 
was stated that decline in RFD performance below 95% during 2011-12 was because of 
unsatisfactory performance of the Depa rtment in the mandatory indicator on 
“Independent Audit of implementation of Grievance Redressal mechanism (GRM)” fixed 
by Cabinet Secretariat, where the department  lost 2 marks. Further, achievements under 
certain targets were lower since they were not  fully within the control of the Department 
and required co-operation from external agencies.  
7.3 The Department assured that in order to  maintain RFD score above 95%, that it 
would evolve stricter mechanisms of monito ring the work progress in the department as 
well as solicit prompt co-operation of external agencies by maintaining contact with them 
on monthly basis or even at shorter intervals.    
7.4 The Committee notes decline in projec t performance of the Department on 
RFD score in two successive years viz 2011-12 and 2012-13.  The Committee, 
however, takes note of the fact that lower performance of CSIR partly resulted from 
non approval of the 12
th Five Year Plan schemes of DSIR.  The Committee hopes 
that the Department would make all out ef fort to improve its RFD score in 2013-14 

by more stricter monitoring of its programmes and by taking pro-active measures to 
get required cooperation from the concerned external agencies.  
8. ACHIEVEMENTS OF COUNCIL OF SCIENTIFIC AND INDUSTRIAL 
RESEARCH (CSIR) 
8.1 As per the information furnished by DSIR, some of its most significant 
achievements during 2012-13 are given below:  
8.2. CSIR’s World Ranking  
8.2.1 CSIR has been placed at 82
nd Rank as per SCIMAGO Institutions Ranking World 
Report 2012 and is the only Indian organi zation among the top 100 global institutions. 
CSIR holds the 17th Rank in Asia and is placed at the first position in the country.  
8.3. Publications & Awards  
8.3.1 CSIR published 4716 research papers duri ng 2011 with an average impact factor 
per paper as 2.568 in SCI journals of nationa l and international re pute contributing to 
9.43% of Indian R&D literature. Several rese arch papers were published in high impact 
factor journals like ‘Lancet’ (IF 38.278), ‘N ature’ (IF 36.28), ‘Science’ (IF 31.20), 
‘Chemical Society Reviews’ (IF 28.76) etc.   
8.4. CSIR Scientists in Frontiers of Science  
8.4.1 Some significant awards/ recognitions to  CSIR Scientists during 2012-13, are as 
follows:  
Fellowship/Award Number 
Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Awardees  2 
Fellows of Indian National Science Academy  9 
Fellows of Indian Academy of Engineers  3 
Fellows of Indian Academy of Sciences, Bengaluru  4 
Fellows of National Academy of Sciences, Allahabad  8 
Infosys Foundation Award  2 
INSA Medal for Young Scientist  5 
CSIR Young Scientists Award  10 
8.5 CSIR further informed that their scie ntists get recognitions  through awards by 
having membership of editorial boards of pr estigious international journals, etc.  The 
details are as under: 
Award/ Recognition Number 
International award/recognitions 27 
8.6 Value Generation through Intellectual Property 
 
8.6.1 CSIR has filed 258 patents abroad and 163 patents in India. It is maintaining a 
portfolio of 3250 patents abroad and 2350 pa tents in India.   The Committee was 
informed that the rate of commercialization of CSIR patents is above 9%, which is much 
higher than global average of 3-4% and the Committee is appreciative of it. 
8.6.2 While the Committee would not like to indu lge in outrightly contesting the claims 
of the most significant achievements narrated above by the Department, it would not tend 
to agree with/accept them at their face valu e either.  The Committee has its own reasons 
and reservations to differ. The Committee is of the view that the 82 nd global ranking of 
CSIR is not at all in consonance with the newly acquired economic and political clout of 
the country in the international community or its international stature in the fields of 
Space, Nuclear Technology, Information Techno logy, Biotechnologies etc. The fact that 
CSIR is the only organization in top 100 global organizations  should not be a matter of 
solace for it as it is the on ly organization in the country which has been working for over 
last 70 years with a mandate to develop stat e of the art globally competitive technologies 

of high commercial potential.  The global rank ing of CSIR is refl ective of its standing 
vis-à-vis other global organizations in the field and is an indicator of its overall 
performance.  Modern India with its 127 crore people, cannot pride itself with 82nd global 
ranking of its premier organization like CSIR.  Even worse is the Asian ranking where it 
stand at 17 th position.  It further goes altogether athwart th e national aspiration of 
emerging as a global superpower, as also the aspiration of positioning India among the 
top five global scientific powers by 2020 enunciated in the Sc ience, Technology & 
Innovation Policy, 2013. The Committee is of the view that in order to fulfill 
aspirations of modern India, CSIR should aim to become amongs t at least first 10 
global organization in its field and it sh ould strive hard to achieve that ranking 
within next 5 years, for that alone would gi ve it position of pride in the hearts of 
millions of our young men & women.  
8.6.3 As regards the credit for research papers having been published in high impact 
factor journals like Lancet, Nature, Scien ce, etc; the Committee has came across some 
conflicting and contradictory f acts which do not corroborate  the tall claims of the 
Department.  The Committee has been informed  that a sample chec k of top 14 research 
papers of the CSIR has revealed that these research papers are not related to any scientific

11. TRADITIONAL KNOWLEDGE DIGITAL LIBRARY (TKDL) 
11.1 The Department informed that TKDL wa s created to prevent misappropriation of 
traditional medicinal knowledge of India at In ternational Patent Offices. India has signed 
TKDL Access Agreements with countries li ke USA, Canada, UK, Australia, Japan and 

Germany. Negotiations are under way to conclude the Access Agreement with 
Intellectual Property Office of New Zealand. Under the agreem ent, examiners of patent 
office can utilize TKDL for search and exam ination purposes only and cannot reveal the 
contents of TKDL to any third party unless it  is necessary for the purposes of citation. 
TKDL Access Agreement is unique in nature and has in built safeguards on non-
disclosure to protect India’s interest against any possible misuse.  
11.2 Beginning  in July 2009, CSIR has id entified 5000 patent applications at 
International Patent Office’s which concer n Indian Systems of Medicine and TKDL 
evidences have been filed at pre-grant stag e under relevant provisions at these Patent 
Offices in more than 1073 cases till June  2012. Success has been achieved in 137 cases 
where the patent applications have either  been withdrawn/cancel led/declared dead/ 
terminated or have the claims amended by a pplicants or rejected by the Examiner(s) on 
the basis of TKDL submissions. Similar outco mes are expected in the remaining cases 
also.  
11.3 When the Committee desired to know the future plans of the Department, the 
Department mentioned that additional 1.0 La kh formulations from Ayurveda, Unani and 
Siddha are proposed to be included in TKDL. Providing access of CSIR-TKDL to 
publically funded R&D institutions  for promoting research in  the field is also under 
consideration. 
11.4 In order to prevent misappropriation of traditional medicinal knowledge of 
India at International Patent Offices, the TKDL initiative of the Department is a 
welcome step. The Committee notes that CS IR through TKDL has been able to 
prevent grant of patents in  137 cases of misappropriatio n of India’s traditional 
medicinal knowledge at International Pate nt Offices like-USPTO, EPO, CIPO etc 
and that though they have identified 5000  patent applications at International 
Patent Office’s which concern Indian Sy stems of Medicine and TKDL, evidences 
have been filed at pre-grant stage under rel evant provisions at these Patent Offices 
in more than 1073 cases till June 2012. The Committee, however, expresses its 
concern that out of 5000 identified cases,  the Department has, till June 2012, filed 
evidences only in 1073 cases.  The Committee feels that undue delay is not desirable 
in such sensitive cases and Department shou ld ensure that evidences etc are filed in 
all the cases expeditiously.  The Department must take pro-active  steps not only in 
zealously preserving and protecting our p recious traditional medicinal knowledge 
but also make best use of it in providing affordable health care to our people.

13.2 HIGHWALL MINING IN INDIA 
13.3 This is a new technology developed by the CSIR under ‘Physical and Engineering 
Sciences Cluster’. Under this technology, th e life of opencast mines can be extended 

without disturbing the surface dwellings, and maintaining economy and productivity. It is 
a remotely operated coal mining technol ogy closely related to underground mining 
methodology. The method comprises extraction of coal from a series of parallel entries 
driven in the coal seam from the face of  the Highwall. These entries are unmanned, 
unsupported and unventilated. Highwall Mining can  be successful only if a feasible 
design of extraction is made taking into consideration of complex geology and existence 
of multiple coal seams in Indian Coalfields, which is unique in many respects.  
13.4 According to CSIR the following mining sites had been considered for Highwall 
Mining operations i.e.  
(a) Ramagundem Opencast Project-II, M/s Singareni Collieries Company Ltd, 
(SCCL); 
(b) Medapalli OCP of M/s Singareni Collieries Company Ltd. (SCCL); 
(c) Quarry SEB and AB, West Bokaro of M/s Tata Steel Ltd. (TSL); and 
(d) Shardah Opencast Project of M/s South-Eastern Coalfields Ltd. (SECL).  
13.5 CSIR had designed the extraction methodology by Highwall Mining for above-
mentioned mines except for Shardah Opencast. The first Highwall Mining System started 
on 10th December 2010 at Opencast Project- II (OCP-II), Ramagundam Area-III (RG-III) 
of Singareni Collieries Company Ltd. (SCCL). At present, an approximate amount of 
10.5 lakhs tonnes of locked-up coal has been  extracted by Highwall Mining in India out 
of which M/s SCCL contributed about 4.5 Lakhs  and M/s SECL has produced nearly 6.0 
lakh tonne of coal.  
13.6 TERAFIL WATER FILTERS & NEERI-ZAR 
13.7 CSIR was successful in developing a nd disseminating low cost and effective 
systems for water purification for the benefit of society at large as detailed below:  
13.8. TERAFIL:  CSIR conducted 21 training/demons tration programs all over the 
country for field testing and popularization of  the TERAFIL filters appropriate for both 
domestic and community water supply. In th e recent past, about 4000 domestic Terafil 
water filters were sent to benefit flood a ffected victims of Bihar, West Bengal and 
Odisha. The technology had become very popular which was evident from 93 technology 
transfers for Terafil filtration media disc  and 80 technology transfers for community 
water filtration system design. It was estimated that about six lakhs of filters have already 
been produced by licensees.  
13.9 NEERI-ZAR:  This technology has been made availa ble free of cost for societal 
benefit. Its technical design de tails were being provided to th e interested agencies as and 
when sought.  CSIR installed 100 units in the flood affected remote areas of Baitu block 
in Barmer District in October 2006 and 250 units  were installed in Aila Cyclone affected 
area of Godkhali Ghat, South 24 Parganas, Basanti Block, Sonakhali of Sundarban 
district (West Bengal) in 2009 to treat pond wa ter contaminated with saline water. CSIR 
installed 20 units in tribal areas of Melghat in Amravati District of Maharashtra.  
13.10 The Committee feels that potential of  the above mentioned technologies 
developed by CSIR need to be fully expl oited to derive maximum benefits fron 
them.  The CSIR must convince Ministries of Coal & Mines etc on the utility of the 
Highwall Mining and for its adoption on  a large scale. Si milarly, it should 
collaborate with the Minist ries of Rural Development, Urban Development and the 
other related Ministries & State Governme nts for large scale adoption of water 
purification filters & technologies.  CSIR has informed that its water purification 
technologies have been successfully tested in flood affected areas. A number of states 
in the East and North East region part icularly Bihar and Assam and Southern 

States like Karnataka and Tamil Nadu are hit almost every year  by floods causing 
tremendous scarcity of drinking water and the technology developed by CSIR could 
be gainfully utilized in providing drinking  water in such flood hit states.  The 
Committee recommends that CSIR should de monstrate utility of its technology to 
such flood prone states so that country  could reap full benefi t of technologies 
developed by CSIR.  The Committee, furt her, recommends that CSIR must also 
find solutions to problems faced by people like drying of ponds and their revival in 
the state of Jharkhand so that benefit of research of CSIR is also available in solving 
the problems faced by people.

CSIR‐Tech Private Limited (CTPL) has been  established in P une on May 2, 2011. The

creation and transfer.  
20.4.2 The Committee desired to know the e fforts made by CTPL to commercialize 
CSIR technologies.  In response thereto, the Department has apprised that the relationship 
between CTPL and CSIR has not been finalize d yet. The effort for the same is on. Thus 
CTPL has not commercialized any technology so  far. CSIR-Tech faci litates technology 
transfer arrangements between commercial enterprises and research labs; enables 
scientists and labs to spin-off ventures a nd leverage private inve stments; and creates

20.6 INTERACTION BETWEEN  INDUSTRY AND CSIR 
20.6.1 As per the report published in ‘Battelle  R&D Magazine in December, 2012 issue’ 
for the year 2012, India’s R&D funding is as  low as 0.85% of country’s GDP in 
comparison to developed countries. In Ja pan, it is 3.48%, in USA 2.68% and in China 
1.60%. Combining all 34 countries of Europe , it is 1.88% of the combined GDP of 
Europe. In case of Asia, a gamut of 20 c ountries is having R&D funding of 1.77% of the 
combined GDP of those countries.  
20.6.2 The Committee desired to know the compar ative contribution made by the private 
sector vis-à-vis contribution made by the public sector for R &D programmes in India 
and the world.  In their reply, the Department  has stated that based on ‘Research and 
Development Expenditure: A concept Pape r published in Deloitte, July 2011, the 
contribution made by the privat e sector vis-à-vis public se ctor for R&D programmes for 
different countries is as under:

20.6.3 Even the Planning Commission’s 12
th Five Year Plan Approach Paper states that 
as the Indian economy and society grow and modernize, the Indian Science and 
Technology landscape also has to change to meet the magnitude of new demands being 
made.  The paper also stresses the need fo r creating a strong R &D system within the 
scientific sector.  According to it, at pres ent, R& D expenditure in the country is only 
0.9% of GDP, of which about 3/4 th is in the public sector and only 1/4 th in the private 
sector.  This R &D expenditure at 0.9% of  GDP is, however, not at all adequate to 
develop strong R & D base needed as principle driving force for economic growth.  
20.6.4 The Committee notes with concern that  India is lagging far behind other 
countries of the world in respect of R & D contribution made by the Private sector.  
In comparison to developed countries of the world, India’s R&D funding from non-
government sector is abysmally low.  Ev en in comparison to our neighboring 
country China, we lag far behind. The percentage contribution of private sector and 
public sector to R&D contribut ion in India & China is nearly in reverse order.  In 
China private sector contribution is near ly 70% of R&D expenditure while in India 
it is Government which makes 75 to 80% co ntribution.  The Committee feels that in 
order to enhance funding in R&D, the private R&D contribution needs to be 
augmented substantially.  The Committee in its 227 th report had recommended that 
private sector contribution to   R&D needs to be enhanced to 50% from 25% during 

the 12 th Plan period by offering incentive s, forming partnership etc.  The 
Department in their Action Taken Rep lies had assured the Committee that every 
effort would be made to bring industries on board. Even the Government has in 
their 12th Five Year Plan Approach Paper admitt ed that private sector contribution 
is not adequate to develop strong R &D .  The Committee feels that somewhere we 
have failed in our efforts to woo private sector and nothing commendable has been 
achieved in this direction even in th e second year of the plan period.  The 
Committee, therefore, feels that mere assura nce given by the Department to make 
every effort to bring Industries on board,  will not help unless it draws a concrete 
time bound action plan to ensure that pr ivate sector contribution to R&D gets 
enhanced to 50% from existing 25% by the end of 12
th Five Year Plan.  
20.7 New Millennium Indian Technology Leadership Initiative (NMITLI) 
20.7.1 The Department has informed that  New Millennium Indian Technology 
Leadership Initiative (NMITLI) is a landmar k Public Private Partnership R&D scheme 
aimed at delivering cutting edge technologies  to provide India a global leadership 
position in select niche areas. During XI Five Year Plan, NMITLI has provided a unique 
platform for performing R&D in public-private partnership (PPP) mode.  
20.7.2 So far, NMITLI has evolve d 75 largely networked proj ects in diverse areas viz. 
Agriculture & Plant Biotechnology, General Biotechnology, Bioinformatics, Drugs & 
Pharmaceuticals, Chemicals, Materials, Information and Communication Technology and 
Energy. These projects involve  100 industry partners & 300 R&D groups from different 
institutions.  
20.7.3 During the XII Plan period, NMITLI pr ogramme will continue with its main 
objective and develop innovation based technologies. The programme looks beyond 
today’s technology and thus seeks to build, cap ture and retain for India a leadership 
position by synergizing the best competen cies of publicly funded R&D institutions, 
academia and private industry. The strategy adop ted for NMITLI is to obtain an inverse 
risk investment profile, i.e., low investme nt in high-risk technology areas (with global 
leadership potential) with investments increasing as developments take place and the 
projects move up on the innovation curve with reduction in risks.  
20.7.4 The NMITLI programme was allocated Rs. 60 crores at B.E. 2012-13 which was 
reduced to Rs. 40.00 crores at R.E. 2012-13 an d Rs. 45.00 crores has b een kept at B.E. 
2013-14 for this programme.   
20.7.5 The Committee in its 227
th report had recommended the following: 
 “The Committee feels that in view of budgetary constraints, there is a need for the 
Department to devise innovative ways for funding these schemes.  Public Private 
Partnership (PPP) model, levy of appropriate user charges, funding from other 
beneficiaries, sharing of profits arising fr om commercial exploitation of patents funded 
under schemes, etc. are some of the known ways in which requisite funds for 
implementation of schemes can be generate d.  The Committee hopes that the Department 
would be able to devise innov ative ways of funding schemes & achieve the targets set for 
2012-13 under these schemes.  The Committee, however, feels that Government should, 
to the extent necessary, provide adequate funds for these schemes at RE stage, so that 
targets set for 2012-13 under these schemes get realised in toto”.  
20.7.6 The Department in their reply had stated the following: 
 “The Department is in the process of obtaining the necessary approvals for the 
schemes and shall be able to mobilise the necessary funding for the same”. 

20.7.7 The Department informed the Committee that CSIR was monitoring projects 
under NMITLI Scheme very rigorously through Steering Committee after every 3 months 
and through Monitoring Committee after ever y 6 months. These committees review and 
ensure that projects are implemented as per plan. Financial progress is monitored through 
Utilization Certificates obtained twice a year. Funds are rel eased based on the Utilization 
Certificates. CSIR will continue these step s in the year 2013-14 also. CSIR is also 
sensitizing about risk coverage in PPP mode of R&D. 
20.7.8 The Committee appreciates that New Millennium I ndian Technology 
Leadership Initiative (NMITLI) star ted by the Department in the 11
th Plan and 
recommends that programme should be pursued with great vigour in the 12 th Plan 
so that a large number of research projects are undertaken under PPP mode and 
private investment in R&D which, at present is around 20 to 25%, increase

Civil Society). CSIR labs are under proces s of finalizing the locations for several 
TECHVILs in consultation with concerned st ate agencies, local communities and other 
stakeholders. Further, CSIR along with AcSI R has identified domain expert scientists, 
students and academics for implementation of the CSIR-800 scheme. 
20.8.3 The Committee lauds the objective with which CSIR 800 scheme has been 
launched.  The fact that more budgetary allocation has been made for the scheme 
than those demanded by the Department shows the importance that Government 
attaches to this scheme.  The Committee hopes that the Department shall endeavour 
to achieve the objective of the scheme of augmenting the income and quality of lives 
of one million rural citizens across the country during the 12
th Five Year Plan.  The 
Committee also recommends that the Depa rtment should formulate more such 
schemes to augment the income of poor and quality of their lives. 
20.9 CSIR Scheme for Open Innovation  
20.9.1 The Committee desired to know the detail s of CSIR Scheme for Open Innovation, 
Initiative for Inclusive, Participative and Collaborative Research & Development. The 
Department informed that in order to ma ke healthcare affordable to the common man, 
Open Source Drug Discovery programme (O SDD) was initiated by the Department 
during the 11th Five Year Plan. It was, furt her believed that the current Intellectual 
Property based models of pharmaceutical innov ation do not address the diseases of the 
poor such as Tuberculosis. The OSDD progra mme has now emerged as a new platform 

for innovation in the domain of healthcare particularly for treating diseases like 
Tuberculosis, Malaria, etc.  
20.9.2 CSIR is consolidating and taking forw ard the gains of OSDD to the 12th Five 
Year Plan. OSDD started with TB as the target disease but during the 12
th Five Year Plan 
it proposes to expand its drug discovery activities  to Malaria and Leishmaniasis       
(Kala-Azar) and launch clinical trials of a TB drug. The affordable healthcare principle 
underlies all activities of OSDD and would c over (a) Open Source Drug Discovery; (b) 
Open Source Drug Development; (c) Open Source Drug Delivery; and (d) Open Source 
Disease Diagnostics. CSIR further informed the Committee that for the financial year 
2013-14, the Department has projected Rs. 109 cr ores out of which only Rs. 70 crore has 
been approved. 
20.9.3 The Committee desired to know the time fr ame within which it would target to 
complete its clinical trials for diseases like TB, Malaria, Kala-Azar etc.  The Department 
informed that they were in the process of f iling an application for permission to initiate

and Infectious Diseases, New Delhi, a hospita l under Ministry of Health. This provides a 
novel model where publicly funded institutes are contributing together to bring drugs for 
treatment of diseases of poor like TB.  
20.9.4 Further the Department has also stated that Drug discovery and development is a 
long and risky endeavour plagued with uncertainti es. It will not be appropriate to provide 
a completion date to clinical trials. CSIR may initiate a clinical trial for Malaria, if an

20.9.5 The Committee appreciates the novel objective of its Open Source Drug 
Discovery Plan i.e. to make healthcare affordable to the common man.  The 
Committee notes that the programme was initiated in 11
th Five Year Plan with TB 
as target disease and is being extended to 12 th Five Year Plan to cover Malaria and 
Leishmaniasis (Kala-Azar) and hopes that  programme would lead to affordable 
treatment of these diseases for common man.  The Committee recommends that the 
Department should provide high priority to such socially useful programmes so that 
objectives of these programmes are achieved as early as possible.  
20.10 National Civil Aircraft De velopment Programme (NCAD)  
20.10.1    The Department of Scientific and Indu strial Research is known for its research 
and innovative ideas. In its que st for expanding its research  activities in  the aviation 
sector on one hand and break th e shackles of dependence on import of civil aircrafts on 
the other, CSIR muster courage and initia ted an over ambitious venture termed as 
National Civil Aircraft Programme (NCAD).  NCAD will be a 90 seater civil aircraft to 
be built with state of the art techniques de veloped with CSIR-NAL collaboration. It is 
included in the 12
th Five Year Plan of CSIR as a New Scheme.  
20.10.2    For the current financial year (2013- 14), an allocation of Rs. 10 crore has been 
made, as against the projected demand of Rs. 178 crores. 
20.10.3   The Committee in its 227
th Report had recommended the following: 
“The Committee hopes that formal Government approval for the programme 
would be available soon and the programme woul d start in right earnes t at the earliest.  
The Committee is also of the view that this  programme is of great national importance 
and sufficient funds be made av ailable to this programme so that our own indigenous 90 
seater aircraft becomes a reality in a short time from now”.  

20.10.4   The Committee enquired about the pr ogress made under this programme since 
last year. While informing the Committee about  the progress made so far, CSIR stated 
about the constitution of two Committees i.e.  Committee for creating Joint Venture (JV)

of Indian business houses to develop an Expr ession of Interest (EO I) and a draft Cabinet

the programme, identify work modules and wo uld also provide inputs for developing a 
Cabinet Note for obtaining ‘in-principle’ a pproval. Based on the recommendations of the 
two Committees, the National Civil Aircraft  Development Programme  would be finally 
formulated.  
20.10.5       Further, CSIR-NAL has made an assessment of the programme by carrying 
out a Feasibility Study for the development of a 70-90 seat er National Civil Aircraft. The 
Feasibility Study Report included Market  Assessment, Configuration Definition, 
Development Strategy, Cost Estimates and th e Business Model. As per the Feasibility 
study, the total estimated cost of the project  is Rs 7555 crore out of which Rs 4355 crore 
is for design & development phase and Rs 3200 crore for series production phase of the 
aircraft. Both the phases would involve Joint Venture with private sector. 
20.10.6    The Committee is perturbed to obs erve that very little progress has been 
made with regard to this important programme. In order to develop capabilities for 
development of aircrafts with large passenger capacities, the Committee is of the 
view that the Department should complete this programme at the earliest so that 
new programme of development of more so phisticated aircrafts of even higher 
passenger capacities could be taken and India acquires capabilities to compete with 
established countries like USA and France in  this field.  The Committee accordingly 
recommends that the Department should se riously work for successful completion 
of the programme at the earliest.

20.12   PUBLIC SECTOR ENTERPRISES  
20.12.1   National Research Development Corporation (NRDC)   
20.12.2    National Research Development Co rporation (NRDC) was incorporated on 
31st December, 1953 as a Section 25 comp any under the Companies Act with an 
objective to promote, develop and commercia lize indigenous technologies. As per the 
objectives set out in its Me morandum and Articles of Asso ciation, NRDC was mandated 
to commercialize the technologies devel oped by all the resear ch laboratories and 
institutes of CSIR and other public funded re search institutes, un iversities including 
autonomous research institutions.  
20.12.3 The Committee enquired from the Depart ment about the efforts made by the 
NRDC to promote, develop and commercia lize indigenous technologies as per its 
mandate and the profit earned through that promotions/developments/commercialization 
of indigenous technologies.  The Department in their repl y has informed that National 
Research Development Corporation (NRDC) is engaged in obtaining assignment of 
technologies from various research institut ions and universities in the country for 
commercialization. During the last three years,  a total of 141 technologies and technical 
know-hows were assigned to the Corporati on by various R&D institutions across the 
country for commercialization. NRDC assists the technology developers i.e. research 
institutions / universities in  patenting their inventions, technologies and technical know-
hows, if they so desire. Out of the 141 t echnologies and technical know-hows assigned to 
NRDC during the last three years, 22 have been filed for patent protection by the research 
institutions / universities themselves. NR DC provided assistance for filing patent 
applications for 37 technologies and the rema ining were without patent protection. The 
total revenue generated by NRDC  in terms of lump-sum premium and royalty by way of 
licensing, marketing and commercialization of th e said technologies during the last three 
years is Rs.1968 lakhs.  
20.12.4   However, according to the Annual Report, for the year 2011-12, the 
Corporation incurred loss to the tune of Rs. 84.54 Lakhs (befor e tax) as compared to loss 
of Rs. 158.23 Lakhs in the previous year. The Committee notes with concern the poor 
performance of NRDC. The Committee feel s that the purpose for which an 
organization is created gets defeated if it fails to deliver.  The mandate of NRDC is 
to commercialize the technologies developed by the research laboratories and 
institutes of CSIR and other public funded research institutes, universities including 
autonomous research institutions. The p oor record of NRDC in obtaining patents 
for technologies & technical knowhow assigned to it, coupled with losses incurred by 
it, speaks volumes of its malfunctioning & lack of professionalism.  The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Department should introspect the causes of failure 

of NRDC and its poor performance and work  out a strategy to ensure that NRDC is 
in a position to fulfill the purpose for which it was established.

 REPORT 
The long history of Biotechnology had w itnessed productive use of biological 
processes to create useful goods for th e benefit of mankind. Rapid scientific 
developments in the past few decades have produced a knowledge base and set of tools 
and techniques that enable biological pro cesses to be better unders tood and controlled to 
an extent never possible before. During th e first half of the 20th century, knowledge 
from the scientific fields of Chemistry and Genetics, combined to provide a revolution in 
the field of life sciences. Advances in ge netic engineering since 1953 had led to the 
acceptance of the role of DNA, combined with its molecular structure, to bring about the 
development of new tools and techniques in genetic engineering, which in turn brought 
about huge advances in biotechnology. As of today biotechnology is applicable in 
diverse fields like healthcare, food, mining, plastics, agriculture and animal husbandry 
etc.   
1.1 With a view to give a new impetus to the development in the field of modern 
biology and biotechnology, as mentioned abov e, in the country, the Government of 
India, initially set up an  Independent Board in 1982, which became a full-fledged 
Department of Biotechnology under Minist ry of Science & Technology in 1986.  The 
Department of Biotechnology is today a ma jor national research and development 
agency and provides nearly two-third of the Research & Development support in the life 
science sector in the country. The Depa rtment endeavours to wards creating an 
institutional framework and human resour ces for nurturing scie nce and technology for 
advancement in their respective fields. To nur ture ever augmenting growth in the field 
of Biotechnology, the budgetary allocation of the Department has been increased from 
around Rs.23.00 crores in 1986-87 to over Rs . 1500.00 crores in 2013-14. The Indian 
biotech industry had expande d threefold during 2009-11 to record revenues of US $3 
billion and is expected to grow further in the coming years.  
2. MANDATE  OF THE DEPARTMENT 
2.1 The main mandate of the Depart ment of Biotechnology is as under:- 
 To evolve policies and integrated progr ammes in biotechnology and ensure their 
implementation and monitoring;  

 To identify specific programmes of Research and Development and 
manufacturing in biologicals and biot echnology and oversee the initiation and 
pursuit of related research and manufacturing activities;  
 To identify, set up and support Centres of Excellence for Research and 
Development in biotechnology and ensure pr oper dovetailing of their activities as 
per national priorities and objectives;  
 To act as a screening, advising and appr oving agent of the Government with 
regard to import and transfer of ne w technologies for the manufacture of 
biologicals, biotechnological products and their intermediates;  
 Evolve safety guidelines for biotec hnology Research and Development and 
manufacturing in India;  
 To act as the central agency for the impor t of genetically manipulated materials, 
culture, cells, specimens, tissues and biotech produc ts including DNA and RNA 
of any type or size and for promoting their production in the country;  
 Serve as the inter-ministerial and in teragency nodal point for all specific 
international bilateral and multilateral Research and Development collaborations 
and agreements in the area of biotec hnology and act as the nodal point for all 
technology transfers in the area of biotechnology;  
 Manufacture and ensure application of  recombinant, cell-based and DNA 
vaccines, diagnostics and other biotechnological products;  
 To evolve programmes for Human Res ource Development in the area of 
biotechnology;  
 Serve as an administrative and impl ementing Department of agencies, 
commissions, boards, etc. specifically formed by the Government for fulfilling the 
national objectives in biotechnology and also to serve as the nodal point for Bio-
informatics including training and cr eation of infrastr ucture, collection, 
dissemination and exchange of information relating to biotechnology; 
 Establishment of National Biotechnology Regulatory Authority;   
 To deal with matters relating to the following institutions:  
 International Centre for Genetic E ngineering and Biotechnology (ICGEB), 
New Delhi; 
 National Institute of Immunology (NII), New Delhi; 
 National Centre for Cell Sciences (NCCS), Pune; 
 Centre for DNA Fingerprinting & Diagnostics (CDFD), Hyderabad; 
 National Institute for Plant Genome Research (NIPGR), New Delhi; 
 National Brain Research Centre (NBRC), Manesar, Gurgaon; 
 Institute for Bioresource and Sustainable Development (IBSD), Imphal; 
 Institute of Life Sciences (ILS), Bhubneshwar; 
 Translational Research in Health Science and Technology Institute, 
Faridabad;  
 Rajiv Gandhi Centre for Biotechnology, Trivananthpuram; 
 UNESCO Regional Centre for Education, Training & Innovation in Biotechnology, 
Faridabad; 
 National Institute of Biomedical Genomics, Kolkata; 
 Institute for Stem Cell Science and Regenerative Medicine, Bangalore 
 National Agri-Food Biotechnology Institute and Bioprocessing Unit, Mohali, and 
 National Institute of Animal Biotechnology, Hyderabad. 

 Matters relating to: 
 Bharat Immunologicals and Biological s Corporation Limited (BIBCOL), 
Bulandshahar, Uttar Pradesh; and 
 Indian Vaccines Corporation Limited (IVCOL), Manesar, Gurgaon. 
2.2 The Department-related Parliament ary Standing committee on Science & 
Technology, Environment and Forests consider ed the detailed Demand for Grants (2013-
14) of the Department of Biotechnology (DBT) in its meeting held on 3rd April, 2013. 
3. MONITORING MECHANISM OF  THE DEPARTMENT AND THE 
RESULT FRAMEWORK  DOCUMENT (RFD)  
3.1 The Committee was informed that fo r monitoring of the schemes of the 
Department, 20 subject specific task forces c onsisting of about 250 experts have been set 
up, who  monitor  the progress of the projects on half-yearly or annua l basis, which also 
includes site visits. An elaborate monitoring m echanism also exists for all Public Private 
Partnerships schemes, which involves visits at the project implementation sites by Project 
Monitoring Committee (PMC) comprising of two area experts, one officer from the 
Department and a financial expert, every si x months to review the progress of the 
projects. Besides, project review were also being done by the Technical Steering 
Committee (TSC) every year and thus the annual financial re leases were made based on 
the successful completion of specified milestone s/targets. The Department added that to 
strengthen the system further, an online project registration and monitoring system 
namely “EPROMIS” had been started since 2011-2012, where all the documents were 
available for online scrutiny and review at all permitted levels.  
3.2 As regards the implementation of the Results Framework Document (RFD), the 
Department, informed that the targets, timelines and achievements as per the RFD format 
for the year 2011-2012 had been recently re viewed by the High Powered Committee 
(HPC) on Government Performance and based on the data submitted by the Department, 
it had approved a composite score of 89.72 for the year 2011-2012, as against 85.03 score 
worked out by the Department of Biotechnology . It also added that during the financial 
year 2010-2011, it had obtained the third rank amongst all the Ministries, as per the 
evaluation carried out by the Performan ce Management Division (PMD) of Cabinet 
Secretariat in terms of accomplishing agreed objectives of the year. 
3.3 The Committee appreciates the Department for putting in place an 
innovative online system i.e. “EPROMIS” since 2011-12 for the registration and 
monitoring of projects. The Committee is  also appreciative of the good results 
obtained by the Department in the RFD assessment for the years 2010-11 and 2011-
12, which suggests that various mechanisms put in place by the Department have 
worked effectively in these two years. The Committee hopes that the Department 
would aim and achieve even better RFD scores in future. 
4. 12TH  FIVE YEAR PLAN 
4.1 The Department informed the Committee that a total budgetary allocation                          
of Rs. 11,804.00 Crores had been made for the 12
th five year plan (2012-2017), against a 
proposed outlay of 18,000.00 Crores. The allocation for the 12 th Plan was 143.89% more 
than the allocation of Rs . 4,840.00 Crores made for 11 th Plan (2007-2012). The major 
thrust areas of the 12th Plan are as follows: 
(i) Expand available pool of research scholars a nd scientist at all le vels (Ph.D, Post 
Doctoral Fellows, young faculty) in biologi cal and interdisciplinary space by 3-5 
folds;   

(ii) Connecting and augmenting existing co mpetences across institutions and 
universities for bio-economy and social impact;  
(iii) Expanding, diversifying career paths with a linkage to high-end interdisciplinary 
sciences, innovation, translation and entrepreneurship;  
(iv) Strengthening regulatory science and infrastructure;  
(v) Expanding existing autonomous R&D institutions; 
(vi) Expansion and commissioning of bioclust ers at Faridabad, Mohali, Kalyani and 
Hyderabad and setting new clusters; 
(vii) Establish DBT grants-in-aid or partners hip research and translational centres 
through long term support in 5 best universities/institutions;  
(viii) Reorient “Grand Challenge Programme” Sche me of 11th Plan to address national 
priorities in various developmental s ectors through bottom-up approach and also 
encourage discovery led innovative ideas;   
(ix) Rejuvenate and establish new research resources, facilities and services;  
(x) Leverage international collaboration for partnerships in cu tting edge areas 
research, education and technology development, access, acquisition; 
(xi) Continued and Sustained support to publ ic private partnerships with new 
innovative funding schemes; 
(xii) Promoting discovery led innovation and strategic investments in priority sectors; 
(xiii) Promoting new generation biotech industries; 
(xiv) Technology acquisition, transfer and licensing for product development;   
(xv) Communication platform/system for creating awareness and public understanding 
of biotechnology with special reference to agriculture biotechnology;  
(xvi) Expediting legal framework and legislations; 
(xvii) Strengthening and consolidation of major 11th Plan initiatives;  
(xviii) Promote policy research and analysis in biotechnology;  
(xix) Reengineering the economic model for bi otechnology product/industry development; 
and  
(xx) Reforms in funding and project management.  
4.2 The Committee notes that there is a significant incre ase of 143.89% in 
allocation of this Department for the 12 th Plan over the allocation made for the 11 th 
Plan, though it substantially falls short of  the outlay of Rs. 18, 000 crores sought by 
the Department for the 12 th Plan period.  The Committee is happy to note that the 
Department during the Plan period inter-alia proposes promotion of new generation 
biotech industries and sustained support to public private partnership, which are 
amongst the thrust areas of  the Department for the 12 th Five Year Plan.  The 
Committee hopes that the Department through its concerted efforts would be able to 
promote public private partnership in a significant way and help establish  new 
generation biotech industries on a large scale which will not only generate 
employment but would also help country rea p in a big way the benefits  of new 
generation biotech industries.   
5. BUDGETARY ALLOCATION FOR THE YEAR 2013-14 
5.1 As regards the Budgetary Allocation, the Committee was informed that the total 
B.E outlay for the year 2013-14 is Rs. 1502.06 crores (with a Plan component of Rs. 
1485.00 crores). The Committee also notes that in the year 2012-13, the total allocation 
of Rs. 1500.39 crores (with a Plan component remaining the same at Rs.1485.00crores) at 
B.E. stage was reduced to Rs. 1315.72 crores at R.E. stage. Explaining the reasons for the 
underutilisation in the year 2012- 13, the Department stated that the Ministry of Finance 

reduced the allocation at R.E. stage by about Rs. 185.00 crores, even though the 
utilisation of the Department was around 55% of B.E. by the end of 2 nd quarter of 2012-
2013 i.e. 30th September, 2012. The Department as a result of the reduc tion of funds had 
to re-prioritize its programmes for 2013-2014.  
5.2 In  reply  to a  query as   regards the  percentage of utilization of funds as 
compared to he total Plan allocation over th e last three years, th e Department provided 
the following  information :

5.3 The Committee notes with concern the red uction of plan allocation of the 
Department at R.E. stage in the years 2011-12 and 2012-13 despite good utilization 
of allocated funds by the Department.  If this trend is not rev ersed immediately, at 
the end of the 12
th Five Year Plan, the Departme nt would end up having a plan 
outlay which will be much less than the approved plan outlay of the Department 
and this in turn would adversely impa ct achievement of targets set by the 
Department for the 12
th Five Year Plan.  The Committee is of the view of that 
growing international stature of India in th e field of biotechnology should not suffer 
a setback on account of fund crunch and accordingly, recommends that no 
reduction should be made in the approve d plan outlay of the Department and 
reduced plan allocation for the year 2012- 13 should be balanced  by the higher 
allocations at R.E. stage in the year 2013-14.   
6. RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT PROGRAMME 
6.1     As regards the Budgetary allo cations for the Research & Development 
programme, over the last three years, the Committee was informed of the following: 
          ( i n  R s .  C r o r e s )  
Year B.E.(Plan) R.E.(Plan) Actual

2011-12 Rs.418.90 Rs. 420.00 Rs. 432.95
