16. Referring to the work being done by the CSIR labs in the petro-chemicals sector,
the Secretary stated that the Indian Institute of Petroleum, Dehradun has developed not
only lab-based knowhow but also total basic engineering packages on its own or with firms
like Engineers India Ltd. The Institute is also providing technical services to the industry by
way of product evaluation, physical-chemical analysis, plant recommissioning, trouble-
shooting and catalyst regeneration. IIP has recently developed a single step process for
converting Cyclohexane into Adipic Acid which is used in the synthetic fibre industry. This
milestone has been achieved in collaboration with M4. Adarsh Chemicals and Fertilizers and
Lummus Crest of USA. As per the terms of the agreement, this would involve an exclusive
transfer for the first three years. Replying to a query from the Committee, the Secretary
stated that IIP has established good links with the petroleum industry, and out of the
resultant technology transfer, CSIR’s product value is somewhere near Rs. 1700 crores; Rs.
650 crores being from its own technology. The CSIR has been responsible for the setting up
of a Rs. 200 crore plant for aromatic extraction of benzene, which is one of the largest in
terms of product value, and is completely based on indigenous technology developed by IIP.

17. The Committee was told that though this did not fall strictly with the areas
presently under consideration of this Committee, CSIR was also engaged in R&D in the
energy sector. The Indian Institute of Chemical Technology, Hyderabad has studied the
combustion characteristics of certain varieties of Indian coal whose ash content various
between 20 to 40%. The Department has been trying hard to take the pilot plant based on
the ‘Integrated Gasification Combinede Cycle Power Generation (IGCC)’ to a
demonstration stage of 100 MW. This is a cleaner technology which would avoid fly ash
pollution and other benefits. The technology is ready but the Department has not been able
to make headway in progressing this despite taking up the matter at various levels. This
technology, no doubt, requires a very large investment, but when the future power needs are
taken into account it is clear that the technology developed can be of great value and should
be taken further by the Ministry of Power. The Department can provide all the inputs, but
others concerned will have to participate effectively in the implementation. On being
specifically asked as to what the response of the Ministry of Power was, the Secretary
clarified that his Department had a number of meetings with the Ministry of Power. The
Ministry has stated that this would be included in its annual plan, but somehow this was not
done. The Ministry of Power basically agrees that this is an important programme, but when
it comes to arranging investment, real problems are encountered. It was pointed out to the
Secretary of the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research that the Department
would have an additional argument that, in the event of this technology being adopted,
considerable amount will be saved which is presently spent on removing the fly ash. The
Secretary, however, expressed his helplessness in the matter, saying that the arguments of
his Department are not effective enough in getting the required allocations. The Committee
wanted to know as to how much money was needed to put this technology on the rails. The
reply was that a 100 megawatt plant was estimated to cost about Rs. 400 crores. The
Department was, however, ready to obtain a share of Rs. 80 crores from industry. Recently,

18. The Committee feels that these indigenous efforts which have great potential for
power generation in the circumstances obtaining in India need to be suitably encouraged and

19. The Secretary of the Department also informed the Committee that CSIR was
engaged in intensive R&D on chemistry-based aspects of materials such as polymers,
alternative building materials and sensor polymers. The focus is principally on composites
and engineering plastics and development of technologies for the use of engineering plastics.
In this context he cited Polyphenylene Sulfide (PPS), which has temperature and chemical
resistance, and is used for non-stick cookware. Work is in progress on water absorbing
polymers, engineering plastics and technologies for plastic blends, etc. which are used for
two-wheeler parts. Besides, there is work on polyurethane which is used for water-proofing.

20. The Committee wanted to know whether knowledge of the Indian systems of
medicine is being used in the development of drugs in CSIR and whether traditional
knowledge has been used to develop pesticides and dyes/colours from plant sources. It was
explained that the Central Drug Research Institute (CDRI) has a systematic programme to
evaluate Ayurvedic formulations from the viewpoint of isolating compounds of therapeutic
values. CDRI has extracted the active fraction, Gugulipid, from Gugal which is a gum of the
plant commiphora mukul; this has been found to reduce cholesterol levels. Similarly, CDRI
has isolated active principles Bacosides A & B a memory enhancer from the herb ‘Brahmi’
which has beén known to possess memory improvement properties. Several other examples
of how the CSIR labs are developing drugs from plants were cited. As regards the use of
traditional knowledge to develop pesticides and dyes, etc. from plant sources, the reply
given was that the active principles from plant sources such as Acorus calamus, Annona
squamosa known to possess insecticidal activities have been isolated and are undergoing field
trials. CSIR laboratories are also working on natural plants for development of food colours
and dyes. Laboratory scale work has been carried out on isolation of food colours from
Curcumin, Kamala seed and flowers, Annato seeds, etc.

21. In response to a pointed query as to what R&D programmes were in hand for the
development of drugs to combat malaria which has recently come back in some parts of
country with a vengeance, the Committee was informed that IICT has developed technology
for Mefloquine, the only drug effective in cases resistant to Primaquine. Besides, CDRI has
isolated Arteether, an effective drug for cerebral malaria from a plant Artemisia annua,


8

native to China, and introduced by Central Institute of Medicinal and Aromatic Plants
(CIMAP) in the country. Phase II clinical trials are over and now multicentric Phase III
trials ae to commence. CDRI is developing a new drug, designated as compound 8053,
which has been found to be an effective anti-relapse anti-malarial drug. The laboratory has
signed an agreement with a company for carrying out clinical trials and the drug is expected
to be marketed by 1997.

22. The Committee has noted that the CSIR laboratories engaged in R&D in the health
sector have established good capabilities for synthesising chemicals of value as drugs. These
capabilities need to be utilized fully through careful planning and management. As yet
achievements in discovering new molecules for drugs have been limited; this is very vital to
respond to the post GATT situation in which we will have to deal with product patents. It is
noteworthy that the CSIR laboratories have focussed attention on problems of tropical
diseases, common to Indian conditions. Their R&D efforts in this direction will have to be
sustained. The Committee feels that with the strong infrastructural base in the chemical sector
relating to drugs, already established, and by taking full advantage of the vast store-house of
traditional knowledge available in our indigenous systems of medicine as also the rich
biodiversity that the country is blessed with, through a sustained effort it should be possible to
make breakthrough in dealing with our major health problems as well as in becoming a force
to reckon with in this area internationally.

23. The Secretary of the Department was pointedly asked by the Committee as to what
measures CSIR was taking: to strengthen the area of transfer of technology, which appeared
to be weak; to ensure that the technology of aromatic extraction is utilised by industry which
appeared to be somewhat lukewarm to it; to improve its design and engineering capabilities;
and to publicise its capabilities and technologies more effectively in attracting potential
clients. The Secretary in his reply conceded that the CSIR’s technology
marketing efforts, including those relating to technology transfer, have been rather weak
steps are afoot to strengthen them. The Research Councils of the laboratories have eminent
industrialists as members; out of five external experts at least three are from industry. The
recommendations of the Mashelkar Committee which had been appointed to go into various
aspects of this problem have been accepted and are being implemented. There are Business
Development & Marketing Groups in each laboratory; they been given the flexibility to
engage consultants for business development; several other related reforms have also been
put in place. As regards adoption by industry, of technology for aromatic extraction it was
pointed out that the the technology developed by CSIR for extraction of aromatics (benzene
and toluene) from reformed naphtha has been commercialised by M/s Bharat Petroleum
Corporation Ltd. (BPCL), Bombay and Cochin Refineries Ltd., Cochin; production around
of Rs. 200 crores is taking place. It is the single largest output from a CSIR technology
which has already been offered to Haldia Petrochemicals, and to the petrochemical complex
coming up at Madras. CSIR is also mounting vigorous efforts to strengthen its design
capabilities; for this design engineering groups are being created/strengthened in its chemical
laboratories. Alliances with leading design engineering and consultancy firms are also being
formed by CSIR to offer its technologies jointly; for example, IIP with Engineers India Ltd.
(EIL) and Lumus of USA, NCL, with Adarsh Chemicals, etc. CSIR has also recently made
several efforts to create necessary awareness about its capabilities. A book on S&T
capabilities/facilities of its laboratories has been published, and another book on technical
opportunities has also been brought out recently and widely circulated. The book contains
techno-economic data on selected 100 technologies. Besides, every laboratory has brought
out publications on its expertise, facilities and programmes. The Secretary of the


Department was, however, candid in admitting that notwithstanding these efforts, much still
remains to be done to publicise the capabilities of CSIR.

24. The Committee wanted to know details about the acceptance of the drug
Centchroman; and also what was the progress in the area of development of drugs for
AIDS. The Committee was informed that Centchroman, which is being manufactured in the
country, is available under the brand names of ‘Saheli’ and ‘Centron’; it has been generally
preferred over other oral contraceptives as it is non-steroidal and free from side effects. The
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare is activley considering inclusion of this drug in its
family welfare programme. The Committee was further apprised that insofar as AIDS is
concerned, the technology for Azidothymidine (AZT), the FDA approved drug for AIDS,
has been developed by IICT and licensed to M/s CIPLA, Bombay, who are manufacturing
the drug and making it available to patients on a ‘no profit’ basis. IICT and CDRI are
working on the development of lead compounds from natural plant sources as potential anti-
AIDS drugs. IICT is also working in collaboration with M/s Abbott Labs of USA on HIV-
Protease.

25. A question was posed to the Secretary as to what mechanism has been evolved by
the CSIR laboratories to market their technologies. It was explained that since 1988,
following the recommendations of the Abid Hussain Committee, the CSIR laboratories have
been given the option to market their technologies directly or through the National Research
Development Corporation (NRDC). The chemical group of laboratories, however, due to
their close linkages and contacts with the users/clients prefer to market their services and

28. The Committee was also informed that IICT is the only organisation where there is

Elaborating on the area of drugs, Director IICT referred to the problems inherent in
the discoveries of new drugs, particularly in the context of the new GATT regime. Any new
drug discovered in the world has a life of 7 to 10 years, though the patent is valid for 20
years. Most of the molecules, however, drop out by the time they enter the market. In our
country, 4 years are normally taken to develop a new process. to discover a new drug better
than the existing one, which is not only highly science-based but is very expensive, is very
difficult. Unfortunately expertise available in the country in this regard is very limited. The
area of biology constitutes a weakness. he was, however, optimistic that in the next few
years, IICT will be in a position to come out with some molecules against cancer and HIV as

33. The Director, Central Electrochemical Research Institute, Karaikudi submitted before
the Committee that the main thrust of his Institute is to do pure and applied research on a
range of aspects of electrochemical science and technology. Over the years the Institute has

develop technology for import substitution and also to develop new technologies for strategic
materials. The most important thrust areas are: corrosion science and engineering; fuel cells;
all types of batteries primary and secondary, of low density and high current density and
deep discharge stable batteries including automobile and tank batteries.

34. There are nine Divisions for R&D work at Karaikudi. The areas covered are: metal
plating, both fine and coarse; electro-polishing; electro-machining; iron sensors and various
other types of sensors; solid and liquid electrode systems; fabrication and testing and
certification of equipment used in electrochemical science and technology.

35. The Committee was informed that the research component of the work in the lab is
apportioned as 25% basic and 75% applied; the Institute handles consultancy projects and
sponsored projects both from private industry as well from Government agencies. The
Institute provides technical services and executes grants-in-aid projects from Government
agencies. Over the years the Institute has been able to file about 600 patents and develop
more than 160 processes; out of these 110 processes have been successfully transferred to
industry both in the small scale and medium scale. As a result of this a fairly good amount is
receiyed as recurring royalties and lump sum premiums. The Institute has laid equal
emphasis on human resource development and upgradation of knowledge for which short
term and refresher courses are given particularly for those involved in this area of science
technology and industry. Over the last five years the major contributions of the Institute
have been in the area of perfecting the Supervisory Control and Monitoring and Data
Acquisition System for monitoring the corrosion in off-shore and on-shore structures, oil and

type of battery for use in the National Literacy Mission; the Institute has. perfected the

and selling it at subsidised price. The Institute’s work in the area of chromium metal plating,
development of sensors for monitoring pollution, and development of electrocarboxylation
and sulpha-oriented products has also been quite significant.


36. The Committee was told that for the last 10 years the policy of the Central
Electrochemical Research Institute (CECRI) has been to interact with strategic departments
like the Department of Atomic Energy, Defence Research and Development Organisation
(DRDO), and its laboratories like DMRL and the Department of Space and its scientific

37. Around 6.5% of the world’s production of chemicals is contributed by
electrochemicals; and India’s share of production of electrochemicals is valued at Rs. 2500
crores. In comparison with U.S.A., Japan and other developed countries where 20% of the
electrical energy produced is consumed by the electrochemical industry, only about 9% is

48. As regards the impact which the new GATT regime was going to have on the R&D
in science and technology in the country, the Director NCL pointed out, in a Note submitted
to the committee, that the Trade Related Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS) Agreement
was going to present the Indian S&T community with the biggest challenge, and it is in the
area of patents that the impact will be more discernible, for the reason that the norms and
standards of protection envisaged in the TRIPS Agreement are significantly different from
India’s own policies, laws and regulations. The impending change in the patent regime will
force the Indian industry as well as the R&D laboratories to move away from the well
trodden path of reverse engineering. The Indian Patents Act, 1970 provides virtually no
patent protection in the food pharmaceutical and chemical industry, whereas in terms of the
TRIPS Agteement a product patent will be required to be given in all fields of technology
without exception, and the duration of the patent has also to be at least 20 years. The
TRIPS Agreement even makes it obligatory to provide patents for engineered micro-
organisms and micro-biological processes to the exclusion of natural plant and animal
systems. The TRIPS regime poses a serious challenge to R&D institutions and the industry
in the country. R&D institutions which have so far focused on imitative research will have to
turn to innovative research. They will have to withstand the pressures of earning, and to
move away from short term revenue earning R&D programmes. R&D itself as a business,
with export potential, will emerge as a preferred strategy for both R&D Institutions and
technology-based Indian firms, provided they are able to deliver results of international
quality in time, and their costs are competitive. The area of durg research will also have to
undergo a sea change in strategy. With the acceptance of product patents, research on new
molecules will require different strategies and expensive and sophisticated infra-structure.
Since filing international patents and licensing them out will become an increasingly accepted
strategy, skills in patenting, filing reading and exploiting patents will be most crucial in the
years to come. Besides, scientific and industrial organisations such as CSIR will have to
formulate policies catering to diverse aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (IPRs). They
will be required to address themselves to the question of retaining the talent in their
institutions, because establishment of R&D centres by multinationals in the country would
attract the talented S&T people to join them due to very high remunerations and world class
facilities.

various States such as Gujarat, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and Orissa. The
speciality of this plant is that its dried seeds contain oil which is called liquid wax and is used for
leather finishing and important high value cosmetic applications. The market price for this oil is
around $ 30 per kilogram. Similarly, another technology for salvidora cultivation has been
developed. The salvidora again is an oil seed which grows in waste and saline lands. There are a
number of companies which are growing these plants. Both Jojoba and salvidora are now
being grown through tissue cultures. The emphais has all along been on developing clean
technologies. The Institute has been a pioneer in the field of iodisation of salt, technology for
production of iodised salt by the small scale industries is given by the Institute free of cost as per
Government’s regulations.

57. The Committee was told that the CSMCRI has been making concerted efforts in
developing technology for cultivation of marine algae which is used for agar agar production.
The emphasis is also to develop technology to produce marine algae for food purposes and
biomolecules. The Institute has a “Drugs from the Sea” programme funded by the Department
of Ocean Development, under which some 2-3 leads for different diseases such as cancer and
AIDS have been isolated from marine organism. This is a 14 laboratory coordinated
programme.


58. The Director emphasised that his Institute has been working primarily on a
commodity of low value but large volume. As a result of the training imparted by the
Institute to a large number of people, the quality of salt in the Runn of Kutch has gone up
so much so that the salt is now going for industrial use whereas earlier it was mainly
confined to edible sector. Through this the labour force has benefited, industry has benefited
and the market price of salt has gone up. The Institute has a number of strategies for the
post-liberalisation period. It wants to re-orient its activities and focus on economically viable
processes and emphasise commercialisation. Fully conscious of the challenges that the post
GATT regime poses, the Committee was told that the Institute would accord necessary
priority to research relevant for its future programmes. Modern methods, biotechnology and
other techniques would be employed to develop better species of Jojoba, Salvidora, etc. and
even better sea weed, which has great potential in terms of protein and could be used for
edible purposes. The Institute is also closely interacting with the Central Leather Research
Institute (CLRI) and National Environmental Engineering Research Institute (NEERI),
Nagpur etc. The Institute has developed a number of products which are patented in India;
in the coming years the Institute proposes to file patents abroad as well. Out of 42 processes
developed, 35 have been released and 300 licences for the processes have been awarded.
The Institute has 85 consultancy projects to its credit and the number of total patents filed is
284.

59. When asked about the involvement of some foreign companies in the manufacture
of salt, and the capabilities of indigenous industry in producing enough good quality salt, the
Director of the Institute replied that the standards of salt required by the industry have been
increasing all the time. The latest standards call for very low magnesium and calcium
content. The Institute has been working on this for quite some time and it has acquired a
technology with which this kind of salt could be produced.

60. As regards the point as to why indigenous salt is not as good as the American salt or
the Australian salt, it was explained that for improving the quality of indigenous salt the
Institute has a technology which has to be applied on a large scale. This aspect is engaging
the attention of the Institute. and some international companies are being consulted. The
Committee wanted to know as to why there was any need for collaboration with multi-
national companies in a sector like salt. It was stated that the Institute wanted to do it with
GHCL in one of its factories, and a demonstration was also given to them but finally they
compared this with the imported technology which was superior. The Director was candid
enough in admitting that the Institute does not yet have expertise in the country on
engineering aspects to compete with foreign technology, and hence they have to build up
necessary expertise by importing the technology.

61. The Committee feels that India has a vast coastline and there is enough potential for
production of both average as well as high purity salt. There does not appear to be any need
for entry of multinationals into an area like this. The Central Salt and Marine Chemicals
Research Institute, which has a clear mandate to bring about improvements both in terms of
quality as well as quantity in salt production in the country, should strengthen its R&D
appropriately and interact appropriately with other CSIR laboratories and engineering design
and consultancy organizations so that high purity salt is produced indigenously, requirements
of industry are met substantially and the need for import of salt or technology therefor, is

62. The Committee heard the Secretary, Department of Scientific and Industrial
Research again, who clarified some of the points which had emerged in the light of the

*scussions which the Committee had with the Directors of 5 CSIR laboratories working in


21

the chemical sector. Explaining a point as to why the cost of the drugs manufactured in
India is lower, he said that it is partly due to the reason that product patent is not being
observed, with the result that the expenses which are incurred in developing a new drug are
not there. High drug prices are a way for the large pharmaceutical companies abroad to
recover research costs as also to generate high profits. Besides, the laboratories in the
country are very good in finding new and innovative processes which, as compared to the
processes adopted in other countries, are often more efficient. Then there are the standard
aspects relating to lower costs of production in India. However, because of the product
patent coming in with the new TRIPS based regime, the scenario will change in the coming
years. As regards the results of trials to assess the potential use of centchroman as an anti
breast cancer drug, and against osteoporosis, the Secretary stated that one foreign company,
Zymo Genetics, is working on it along with the Central Drug Research Institute. If this
succeeds, this will be the only drug for osteoporosis and will have an enormous market.
There is an agreement that the royalties and other profits which will accrue on this account
will be shared with CSIR. Taking due notice of the concern expressed by the Committee
about the weakness of CSIR in the area of technology transfer and marketing mechanisms,
the Secretary submitted that not only the CSIR Headquarters but all its laboratories have
been treating this as their number one priority. as a result of which the linkages with
industries have grown and the confidence of the industry in CSIR technology, particularly in
the chemical sector, is very high today. Notwithstanding this, he, however, conceded that
CSIR’s total external cash flow from transfer of technology is still not as high as it should
be. To a question as to why the technology for mosquito repellant is still being imported and
indigenous industry, particularly CSIR, was not taking necessary steps even in such a small
sector, the Secretary replied that the mosquito repellant is an insecticide called allethrin and
the domestic demand for this is just 12 to 15 tonnes annually which is not sufficient for
setting up a commercially viable plant. Nevertheless, the IICT is coordinating with one of
the major producers of mosquito repellant for development of this technology on a
sponsorship basis and the possibility of the use of Azadrachtin derived from Neem is also
being explored.

63. Replying to a question from the Conimittee as to what were the specific industries
which were using catalyst technologies, the Secretary of the Department stated that M6
United Catalysts India Ltd. and M4 International Catalysts Ltd. are manufacturing and
supplying CSIR developed catalysts. Besides, a number of CSIR developed catalysts are
being used by the industry. In this context he referred to bimetallic reforming catalyst for
aromatics production—Indian Petrochemical Corporation Limited (I.P.C.L.); Octane
number improver for gasoline—Madras Refinery Ltd. (M.R.L.); zeolite catalysts for
isomerisation of xylenes—Indian Petrochemical Corporation Limited (I.P.C.L.); alkalisation
of Benzene (Hindustan Polymers); hydrodewaxing of heavy fraction of crude petroleum
(AKZO, Holland); iron-molybdate catalyst for Formaldehyde production (Cibatul), etc.

64. The Committee wanted to know the status of development of biopesticides and
biofertilisers in CSIR, to which it was pointed out that CSMCRI has carried out some
studies on the use of marine algae grown in Saurashtra and Coromandal coasts as
biofertilisers. Further work is in progress but still no standard technology is available to be
offered. ILCT has, however, done some work in the area of biopesticides . This is an area
that the Department of Biotechnology has been pursuing with various other national
institutions.

65. The Committee is very appreciative of the R&D work undertaken by the CSIR
laboratories in the area of chemicals. A great deal of this has involved reverse engineering,


import substitution and development of innovative process technologies for known products.
This had led to large volume production of many chemicals needed in various sectors of
national development. It is equally heartening that the R&D effort is constantly focussing on
environmentally clean technologies and on safer chemicals and process routes which is
essential. The Committee has, however, on the basis of its examination of the working of these
laboratories, found that there are weak spots which need immediate attention if the challenges
posed in the post-liberalisation era in the country and new TRIPS based regimes are to be
seriously met, and India has to emerge as a self reliant economic force on the global platform.
The Committee has been informed that CSIR has entered into agreements with quite a few
foreign companies, as part of its new strategies; but its own programmes relating to
innovative research and development of new technologies have to be considerably strengthened
before it becomes a serious international player. This calls for much more. integration and
coordination of work of the various CSIR laboratories as also with engineering design and
consultancy firms. The Committee is concerned that even though technologies in some
important areas of chemical industry have been developed by the CSIR laboratories yet the
response from the industry in taking these up has not been as positive as it should have been.
The Committee feels that this is not so much due to the lack of quality of these technologies
but is largely due to the lack of awareness in industry about the capabilities of CSIR and a
tendency to go in for proven production technologies from abroad. The Committee has noted
that CSIR has taken some initiative to publicise its technologies, but it appears that individual
laboratories are dealing with this largely on their own. Inter laboratory coordination within
CSIR and development of a proper mechanism for marketing and transferring technologies to
the industry is called for. The Secretary of the Department of Scientific and Industrial
Research has admitted that these aspects are seriously engaging the attention of CSIR; and
strategies are being devised to suitably strengthen these aspects. Linkages with industry are
being established, and in some of the laboratories transfer of technology is now a part of the
project right from its inception; the project itself is designed in consultation with the
concerned industry; fairly high representation is given to industry in the Research Advisory
Councils. The Committee, however, feels that there is need for a more dynamic perspective
planning to remedy the weaknesses in these vital areas. Coupled with this is the need for
CSIR to strengthen its capabilities in fundamental and basic research. The Committee feels
that this is not getting the necessary priority. The basic research capabilities have to be
broadly in the area of relevance to CSIR’s programmes. Universities and other academic
institutions too have to be involved in the gigantic task of developing a very strong base of
fundamental research in the country to cope with the emerging area of knowledge based high
technologies. CSIR has done a commendable job over the years in supporting such research in
the educational sector of India through its Extra Mural Programmes.

66. The Committee is concerned that the CSIR laboratories do not have a strong base in
respect of design and engineering capabilities. CSIR is no doubt seized of its handicaps in this
regard and efforts are under way to join hands with design organisations like Engineers India
Ltd. The Committee, feels that such. linkages have to be put urgently on a realistic and sound
basis so that the technology packages offered by CSIR are readily acceptable by industry.
Such linkages are no doubt, related to projects and technologies and some laboratories seem
to have established better linkages in this regard.

67. The Committee has found that many hazardous chemicals which pose a danger not
only to the health of the people but also to the environment still continue to be in use in our
country. The Committee recommends to the Government to examine this problem in its


entirety, particularly the implications arising from the use of toxic chemicals and of hazardous
industrial process routes, and ensure expeditious action for replacement of these chemicals
with less toxic and environment friendly chemicals and better processes.

68. On the basis of the evidence of the Directors of the 5 chemical laboratories of CSIR,
view has clearly emerged about the problems inherent in dealing with the scenario that is
unfolding with the operationalization of the new TRIPS regime. The Committee notes that
there exists a patenting unit in the CSIR; but the Committee clearly feels that its operations
are not of a scale as to match with the requirements of CSIR and on a national scale. CSIR
has plans to expand this unit, but the Committee feels that the area of patenting needs to be
looked at on an urgent basis with far greater strengthening than appears from current plans.
The emerging situation is serious and calls for determined efforts. The Committee
recommends that suitable steps be initiated by government in this area at the highest level and
services of experts and professionals be engaged. This will call for orientation of research
towards innovative research that can lead to patents, support for such research and for filing
patents nationally and internationally, strengthing patent search mechanism ability to deal
with patent violations awareness building relating to patents and patentability of research,
creating legal system capable of dealing with these new developments, and ensuring that
national interests are safeguarded in the many grey areas of emerging science and technology.

69. The Committee has noted that most of the CSIR laboratories engaged in the chemical
sector are quite old having been set up 30-40 years back; modernisation of these labs in a big
way is essential if they have to emerge as potential global players. Modernisation apart, for
which substantial funds are needed, the CSIR labs are not even in a position to manage their
regular operations with the help of existing allocations; substantial amounts are diverted from
plan to non-plan areas and what is left for plan purposes is greatly reduced. This is in spite of
the fact that they have been able to generate extra-budgetary resources. In such a situation it
would be unfair to expect them to compete effectively in the international arena. Government
has, therefore, to seriously examine the financial implications of their operations, iheir
viability and a way has to be found to ensure that they are effective instruments of not only
national development but also global competition. This will call for significant additional
funding by Government. It is equally important that the CSIR management evolve suitable
ways to make the CSIR labs operate on a self sustaining basis which is possible only if they
come out with technologies in which industry is interested and willing to pay for. If the
Government is not in a position to make immediately available all the funds required for a
meaningful modernization programme, then the Committee feels that the CSIR management
should identify core areas and projects which need immediate attention and the Government
should meet the full financial requirement of CSIR for these areas. This will result in
modernization in some way. CSIR should also appreciate that modernization has to be not
only in terms of facilities, infrastructure and equipment. It is necessary that the personnel are
also of the highest quality and imbued with a sense of elan and enthusiasm. This calls for
attention to human resource development and personnel policies appropriate to this need.

70. The post-GATT era places a lot of responsibility not only on the Government but also
on industry. With the advent of foreign companies into some significant sectors of industry in
our country, indigenous industry will have to compete with their technologies. For this
matching effort will have to be made by substantially increasing allocations for their own
R&D units, which are at present abysmally low. The country cannot indefinitely depend upon
import of foreign technologies; these in any case are, as submitted to the Committee, 10 to 15
years old and there is a general approach’ of foreign companies not to part with their latest


technologies. Therefore, in order to meet the requirements of the post—liberalisation period,
technologies will have to be evolved which would stand on a par with those of the foreign
companies. This calls for an integrated approach among all the scientific institutions and
laboratories engaged in R&D in different sectors and industry.

INTRODUCTION

Ernakulam in particular".

REPORT
The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science & Technology,
Environment & Forests has been undertaking study visits in various States/cities across the country
to assess their environmental status. As part of this exercise, the Committee undertook a study visit
inter-alia  to Kochi from 23rd to 26th November, 2015. During the visit, the Committee held
meetings at Kochi with NGOs/Civil Society Organisations/Experts as well as officials of
Government of Kerala and Union Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change to apprise
itself of the environmental issues of Kochi/Kerala.
2. At Kochi on 25th November, 2015, the Committee first heard the views of NGOs/Civil
Society Organisations/Experts on the environmental issues of Kerala in general and Kochi/Ernakulam
in particular. The Principal Secretary, Forest & Wildlife Department, Government of Kerala was
also present during the meeting. A list of NGOs/Civil Society Organisations/Experts and their
representatives who attended the meeting is at Annexure-I. A list of officers of Government of
Kerala and Union Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change who were present in the
meeting is at Annexure-II. Some NGOs/Civil Society Organisations/Expert also submitted written
memoranda.
3. Initiating the discussion with the NGOs/Civil Society Organisations, the Chairman of the
Committee urged the participants to give viable proposals which could be implemented straightway
without any major policy changes especially with regard to solid waste management, sewerage and
untreated water disposal to water bodies, regeneration of water resources, afforestation and
protection of mangroves on the banks of the wetlands in Kochi in particular and Kerala in general.
During the meeting, the members of the NGOs/Civil Society Organisations expressed their views
on a number of issues pertaining to the environmental issues of Kochi and Kerala. Later the
Committee held discussion with the officers of Government of Kerala and Union Ministry of
Environment, Forest and Climate Change on the subject.
4. Some of the views expressed by the NGOs/Civil Society Organisations/Experts are as
under:-
(i) The representative of All India River Protection Council drew attention to the air,
water and soil pollution in Kochi. He stated that the various water bodies in the state
were polluted, have become waste dumping places and nearing extinction but the
concerned authorities were not addressing the issue. He also stated that rainwater
harvesting should be made compulsory. He mentioned about lack of liquid waste
disposal facilities in Kerala. The liquid waste mixed with fresh water was a source
of mosquitoes and other bacterial diseases. He also stated that there was no proper
drainage system in Kochi and the existing system needed to be redesigned. He further
stated that the solid and liquid waste of the city finally went into V embanad Lake and
stressed the need for a decentralized solid waste disposal system. He further stated
that the only solid waste treatment plant at Bhramapura was not sufficient for the
city.

(ii) Shri K. Binu from Bazhoor, Kottayam District brought out the condition of mangrove
and stated that Kochi had lot of mangrove forests which have been totally destroyed
but nothing has been done.
(iii) The representa tive of Matsyafed brought out the problems regarding the
rehabilitation of coastal fishermen. He stated that the steady rise in sea levels and
the resultant ingress of the sea to the coastal land and swelling of water bodies
was causing irreparable damage to the livelihood opportunities of the fishermen. He
expressed concern on the fishermen and residents not being consulted by local
authorities to construct homes in coastal areas. He requested that the Central
Government should take steps for rehabilitation of the poor people in the coastal
area.
(iv) The representatives of Kerala Vrikhsa Prakrithi Samrakshana Samiti pointed out that
there has been severe destruction of trees for construction of metro rail corridor and
the wastes from of slaughter houses were being disposed into the water bodies. He
stated that the number of unauthorised slaughter houses in the city was very large.
(v) The representative of River Research Institute, Thrissur commented on the bad shape
of the 44 rivers in Kerala. She expressed her apprehensions on the illegal sand mining
and suggested sand holidays for 5 years, so that rivers get enough time to
accumulate sand. She suggested that catchment area treatment plants should be
established for increasing the capacity of irrigation. Ecological flow assessment and
Western Ghat Conservation should be given due importance. She also pointed out the
loss of fishes in riverine stretches and stated that tree plantation needs to be
supported.
(vi) The representative of Amicus Associates, Ernakulam referred to Supreme Court
judgment whereby river sand mining cannot be permitted below the summer water
level. He stated that illegal mining permits were being issued by the State Government
itself to the sand mafia.
(vii) The representative of Salim Ali Foundation emphasised the importance of conservation
of Western Ghats and was of the view that the word afforestation is a misnomer. He
said that it was impossible to calculate the loss of biodiversity and aesthetic value of
forest.
(viii) The representative of Kerala Tree Protection Council pointed out that the EIA
conducted by Delhi Metro Rail Corporation (DMRC) for metro rail project in Kochi
envisaged cutting of 443 trees and the project was sanctioned. However, later, the
implementing agency, Kochi Metro Rail Ltd. (KMRL) conducted another EIA and
cut 1400 trees. He also expressed the need for extending small area of
Mangalavanam bird sanctuary (3.7 hectare) by including the nearby area owned by
Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd., which they were not utilising. He also stated
that there was no ambient air quality monitoring equipment in the city. He also
dwelt upon violation of norms in issuance of sand mining orders and encroachment
in the rivers of the state.

3
(ix) Shri T.K. Suresh Kumar, a resident of Ambalappuzhha stated that the local residents of
Ambalapuzhha around Kapthithode are facing serious health problems like cancer due
to waste dumped from the adjacent fish and prawn processing plants/peeling sheds. He
requested for relocation of fish processing units.
(x) The representative of Topical Institute of Ecological Sciences pointed out that the
Vembanad Lake is heavily infested with the Eichhornia and Salvinia and action needs
to be taken to remove these weeds. He also demanded transparency in utilizing river
management funds.
(xi) Shri Sreedhar a resident of Kochi stressed the need for a wetland authority to preserve
the paddy fields and for wetland protection.
(xii) The representative of Port Watch Cochin stated that a huge quantity of sand had been
removed from the riverbed. He also stated that massive dredging had been carried out
in Cochin Harbors.
(xiii) Shri Vishunu Katha, Assistant Registrar, CUSAT, Kalamssary stated that waste
management in Kochi was a total failure and suggested for the waste segregation at
household levels apart from solid and liquid waste management. He also expressed his
views for promoting planting of medicinal trees, birth star trees and endangered trees
by subsidizing the cost involved.
(xiv) The representative of Lawyers Environment Awareness Forum, Kerala High Court
Advocates Association stated that the District Collector should be made the coordinator
to identify the ecologically sensitive areas.
(xv) Shri Premchand T.P., a resident of Kochi, pointed out the water logging, siltation and
deposition of dredging waste in Kochi.
5. The Committee thereafter heard the representatives of Government of Kerala and Union
Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change on the issues. While welcoming the officers
of the Central and State Government the Chairman stated that although Kochi can claim to be one
of the largest industrial hubs in Kerala, unscientific and environmental unfriendly disposal of solid
waste, ambient air quality reaching a critical level and high level of air pollution have led to Kochi
being the one of the India's top most environmentally problematic city. He also brought out the
issues of environmental degradation put forth before the Committee by the representatives of
NGOs/Civil Society Organisations and local people. He asked the officials to apprise the Committee
of the steps taken by different agencies to address these environmental issues.
6. The Principal Secretary, Forest and Wildlife Department, Government of Kerala, in his
presentation before the Committee gave an overview of state of forest and wildlife in Kerala. He
stated that Kerala had 14 districts and the density of the population was very high i.e. 859 per
sq/km, which was the highest in the country. The geographical area of the state is 38688 sq. km.
As per the Forest Survey of India the forest and tree cover of the state was 54.21% against the
national figures of 24.01%. The state maintained 28.42% of the forest area as Protected Area
which included 2 Tiger Reserves, 5 National Parks, 15 Sanctuaries and 1 Community Reserve. He
also pointed out that 410 sq. km. of forest land was diverted under forest (Conservation) Act,

4
1980. Some other points covered in this presentation were that many of the private forest (1696
sq km2) areas have been nationalised; land filling has been completely banned; the forest area is
increased based on the ecology; Kerala maintains 29% of total area as forest, which is higher than
any other state in south India; and boundary has been marked to separate the forest area.
7. Thereafter, the Committee identified following issues for interaction and makes observations/
recommendations thereon.
SOLID WASTE DISPOSAL/MANAGEMENT
8. The Chairman drew attention of the Principal Secretary, Government of Kerala to the pathetic
sight of waste dumping site at Kalamassary in Kochi. He also goaded the Principal Secretary to
give a definite time frame for deliberations on this issue and finding a solution therefor. The
Principal Secretary, while promising to take action in the matter, stated that there was only one
solid waste disposal unit at Bhramapuram, Kochi which was not able to take the load of whole city.
He also stated that it was difficult to process all the waste material, especially due to the rains and
humid conditions of Kochi which necessitated 6-8 months for drying. He also stated that they were
trying to find out another alternative site for a waste disposal plant. However, there was resistance
from the local people and the Government was not getting any land for the same.
9. The Committee is of the view that waste disposal management is integral part of any
city's planning. Not having adequate number of waste disposal plants does not reflect well
on the administration of Kochi. The Committee, therefore, recommends as under:-
(i) The waste dumping site in Kalamassery should be cleared within six months from
January, 2016. The plea of the State Government that Government was not
getting any land for the waste disposal plant is not tenable. The Committee
recommends that necessary action should be taken to identify a suitable site for
establishing a waste disposal plant, which could cater to the growing needs of
Kochi.
(ii) Open dumping sites are an eyesore and environmental hazard and can become a
health hazard too. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the State
Government should establish covered dumping sites which should be equipped
with incinerators.
(iii) Waste disposal plants should have modern methodologies for segregation and
scientific disposal of wastes.
(iv) Segregation of waste should become a part of waste disposal management. People
should be educated about the benefits of waste segregation and encouraged to
segregate the plastic and non-plastic waste at the household level itself. Requisite
mechanism for collection of such segregated waste should also be put in place.
REHABILITATION OF COASTAL FISHERMEN
10. The Committee drew the attention of the representative of State Government to the problem
of rehabilitation of coastal fishermen brought out by the representative of one of the organisations
appearing before the Committee. The Committee was informed by the Principal Secretary that the

5
State Government had spent a lot of money for their rehabilitation and they planned to construct
5000 flats for the fishermen for which budget allocation has already been made.
11. The Committee, while taking note of the Government's efforts, is of the view that
devising a strategy for rehabilitation of the fishermen is vital. Fishermen face a lot of
vagaries of nature on sea shore but often prefer to have their homes near the sea.
Therefore, the Committee recommends that the site for construction of their homes should
be carefully chosen so that they are away from high tide areas, floods etc. and their lives
are secured.
PROTECTION OF MANGROVE AREAS
12. The Committee drew attention of the State Government to the destruction of mangrove
forests, as brought out by some of the NGOs appearing before the Committee and sought
response. The Committee was informed by the Principal Secretary that Government of Kerala had
embarked on a mission in Konnore District in this regard. They had already taken over about 40
acres of mangroves forests and plan to expand this project in three more districts where mangrove
forests existed.
13. The Committee is of the view that mangroves act as buffers between the land and the
sea and are very important part of our biodiversity and their destruction in Kerala is a
matter of concern. The Committee, while taking note of the fact that Government of Kerala
has taken over 40 hectares of mangrove forests and intends to extend the project to other
three districts, feels that the Union Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
and State Government of Kerala should coordinate in this regard and take all necessary
steps to save and protect the mangrove areas from destruction, encroachment and garbage
dumping.
STATE OF RIVERS OF KERALA
14. The Committee was informed that all the 44 rivers originating from the Western Ghats and
its surrounding hills in Kerala are facing slow ecological death and losing their natural flow pattern
due to culminative impact of various interventions in the catchments and inside the river channel
including deforestation of the catchment areas, forest fragmentation, blocking the flows by dams,
encroachment and massive mining of hills.
15. The Committee is of the view that to preserve rivers Government should chalk out a
sustainable action plan. The Government should also consider declaring sand holidays in
identified rivers for a certain period to allow replenishment of sand and revival of the
ecological balance of the rivers. The restoration of river catchments should be taken up by
concerned authorities alongwith the NGOs etc. working towards forest protection. The
awarding of permits for sand mining from rivers in violation of Hon'ble Supreme Court
judgment also needs to be looked into seriously.
CONSERV ATION AND MANAGEMENT OF VEMBANAD LAKE
16. The Committee was informed that there were around one thousand five hundred to two
thousand boats in the lake to cater to the tourists and, all along the bank of the lake, residential

6
units had come up by reclaiming the part of the lakes. As per an estimate around 40% of the area
of the lake had been reclaimed due to increasing industrialisation and urbanisation. In the absence
of any proper sewage or drainage system, the sewerage from the residential units is drained into
the lake. It was also noticed that the colour of the lake water has turned into dark black and was
eutrophicated with sparse to dense infestation of water hyacinth and other submergent weeds. No
trace of aquatic life was noticeable.
17. Director, NIO informed that the problems of eutrofication and encroachment in the lake were
due to the deterioration of water quality caused by indiscriminate use of fertilizers and dumping
of agricultural and domestic waste. Growth of water weeds decreases water flow, block sunlight
from reaching aquatic plants and depletion of oxygen affecting the fishing community adversely.
18. The Committee had visited Vembanad Lake on 8th November, 2014 during its visit to Kochi
in November, 2014 and had reviewed the ecological health of the Lake.
19. The Committee expresses its serious concern over the pathetic condition of the lake
and the over-increasing eutrophication and pollution in the backwaters caused mainly due
to reckless reclamation, completely obstructing inflow of sea water into it and also due to
discharge of untreated sewerage into it. The Committee is of the view that the condition
of Vembanad Lake instead of improving during the period of one year since the last visit
of the Committee to Kochi, has deteriorated further.
20. The Committee feels that for ensuring the revival of the Kochi Backwaters, its
conservation and management, there is an urgent need to constitute an Independent
Vembanad Lake Development Authority with full powers on the lines of Chilika Lake
Development Authority in Orissa as the present arrangement lacked the requisite support
and coordination among different agencies. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
Ministry of Environment, Forests & Climate Change should devise an Action Plan to be
implemented within a definite time-frame in coordination with the State Administration /
State Pollution Control Board, to restore the health of the backwaters urgently. Following
steps need be taken within the time limit stated against each for restoration of the health
of the backwaters:-
(i) Mapping the residential structures along the lake by using technology like
satellite imagery etc. and placing the same in public domain, within six months.
Preventing further encroachments and reclamations by enforcing Coastal
Regulation Zone (CRZ) rules strictly;
(ii) Establishing treatment plants by the end of financial year 2015-16 for treating the
effluents/sewage falling into the lake;
(iii) Making regulations by March, 2016 for aqua tourism, especially house boats and
making them environment-friendly;
(iv) Establishing online pollution monitoring mechanism within nine months at the
strategic locations;
(v) Strict enforcement of environment / pollution norms and punishing the violators
severely with immediate effect.

7
(vi) Taking appropriate remedial measures with three months for aquatic weed
infestation.
Action taken in this regard within the prescribed time frame be notified to the Committee.
ISSUE OF ILLEGAL SLAUGHTER HOUSES
21. The Committee's attention was drawn to the issue of illegal slaughter houses and disposal of
slaughter house wastes into the water bodies. The Principal Secretary assured the Committee to
look into the issue of illegal slaughter houses and dumping of slaughter house waste in the water
bodies in Kochi.
22. The Committee recommends that the Government must take immediate necessary
action in the matter by either regularising or closing down such slaughter houses. It should
also be ensured within three months that wastes from such slaughter houses is disposed off
in a scientific and environment friendly manner at designated places.
23. During the meeting on 25th November, 2015 inter-alia  with the officers of the State
Government of Kerala, the Chairman of the Committee had sought a commitment to fix a time
schedule for an action plan from the Principal Secretary, Government of Kerala regarding the
problems related to waste disposal at Kochi. In response, the Secretariat of the Committee received
communication, dated 1st December, 2015 and 15th December, 2015 (Annexure-III & IV) from the
Additional Chief Secretary, Government of Kerala detailing the action plan for the scientific waste
management at Brahmapuram and Kalamasey in Kochi. It was assured that the action taken by the
local bodies will also be closely monitored.

Department related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science & Technology, Environment

There are-42 wards in Kalamassery Municipality and all average of 20 tons of waste is being
generated every day. Waste is being collected from .each households and commercial
establishments through Kudumbasree workers. The bio degradable waste thus collected is treated
at Brahmapuram plant for which the Municipality has entered into an agreement with Koohi
Corporation. On an average 4 tones of waste per day is being sent to the treatment plant. There

a shed at the cost of M/S Appolo Tyres. Waste removal work is interrupted due to the on going
Cochin 'Metro Construction Work and hence the waste is heaped at Kalamassery, which has led

In Kochi corporation, waste generated is segregated and collected from the source itself An

INTRODUCTION 
 
 
 I, the Chairman of the Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Science & Technology, Environment & Forests, having been authorised by the 
Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this Two Hundr ed Seventy-first 
Report on the Action Taken by the Department of Atomic Energy on the 
recommendations contained in Two Hundred Fifty-sixth Report of the Committee on 
Demands for Grants ( 2015-2016) of the Department of Atomic Energy , which was 
presented/lad in the both the Houses of Parliament on 5th May, 2015. 
 
2. There were Thirty one recommendations contained in the Two Hundred Fifty-
sixth Report of the Committee.  Action Taken Notes on the recommendations of the 
Committee were received from the Department on 3rd December, 2015. 
   
3. In the meeting held on 15th January, 2016, the Committee considered the draft 
Report and adopted the same. 
 
 
 
 
 
 ASHWANI KUMAR 
New Delhi: Chairman 
January 15, 2016 Committee on Science & Technology, Environment & Forests 
25 Pausha, 1937 Rajya Sabha 
 

REPORT 
   
 The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the 
Department of Atomic Energy on the recommendations contained in the 
Two Hundred and Fifty-sixth Report of the Department -related 
Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science & Technology, Environment 
& Forests on the Demands for Grants (201 5-16) of the Department of 
Atomic Energy, which was presented to both the Houses of Parliament on 5th 
May, 201 5. The Committee had in all made thirty one  
recommendations/observations in the report.  Action Taken Note on the 
report was received by the Committee on 3rd December, 201 5.  The 
Department has accepted all the recommendations of the Committee.  The 
Committee, on examination of Action Taken Notes, is satisfied wit h action 
taken by the Department in respect of recommendations/observations . 
However, the Committee would like the Department to take further action in 
respect of two recommendations as indicated in the Report  (Para Nos. 6.5 
and 7.7). 
 The Committee's reco mmendations, action taken thereon and 
comments of the Committee on the Action Taken by the Department of 
Atomic Energy are set out in the subsequent paragraphs:- 
FINANCIAL PROGRESS IN XII FIVE YEAR PLAN  
Recommendation (Para 6.5) 
 The Committee takes serio us view of the fact that in the first three 
years of current Plan nearly 27% of the allocation have been disbursed.  The 
major share i.e. 73% of the allocation has accumulated for the remaining two 
years.  It seems impossible to utilise 73% of the plan all ocation during the 
remaining two years.  The very purpose of long term planning in the form of 
Five Year Plan comes to a naught. While taking serious view of the fact that 
pro-rata allocations are not made annually, the Committee recommends that 
in the rem aining two years of the Plan period, allocations should be made 
and utilised on pro-rata basis to catch up the Plan targets. 
Action Taken by Government 
DAE accepts the recommendation of the Committee. The 
recommendation has been brought to the notice of Mi nistry of Finance. 
Action Plan is put in place for utilisation of the approved allocation. ID Note 
to the PMO seeking special consideration in the matter of re-appropriation of 
funds for Science & Technology Ministries have also been issued for 
consideration so that approved allocation need not be surrendered for want 
of approvals for the re-appropriation of funds among the Projects. 
Comments 
 The Committee takes note of the reply but would like the 
Department to pursue the matter with Ministry of Finance/P MO 
regularly. 

UTILISATION OF THE APPROVED OUTLAY: A TREND 
Recommendation (Para 7.7 & 7.8) 
 The Committee feels that the budgetary restriction imposed by the 
Ministry of Finance, as pointed by the DAE, was not the only reason for 
reduction in allocation at RE stage in 2012-13, 2013-14 and 2014-15, under-
utilisation of outlay by the Department might have also played a role in 
reduction at R.E. level.  
Action Taken by Government 
The Department accepts the observation of the honourable Committee 
that  the allocation has been under -utilised. The reasons for underutilisation 
has been discussed  and the action plan to overcome this has been chalked 
out in   the  review meeting conducted on 18.06.2015, by Secretary, DAE 
with the Heads of  Units/Aided Institutes/PSUs.  Further, it is submitted here 
that Plan review meetings have been conducted  by Secretary/Additional 
Secretary, DAE periodically. The Department could utilise about 58% of the 
budget under Plan head till October, 2015. 
Comments  
 The Committee takes note of the reply but would like the 
Department to constantly monitor the utilization of funds. 
Recommendation (Para 7.8) 
 The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department needs to 
improve its capability to utilise the allocated resources particularly i n the 
Plan Head through strict monitoring at regular intervals of the physical and 
financial performance of the projects and obviate the possibility of any 
reduction at Revised Estimate Stage. It is felt that considering the strategic 
importance of the institutions of the Department of Atomic Energy, financial 
cuts should be minimized and should not be insisted upon if strategic 
programmes were to be delayed as a result thereof.    
Action Taken by Government 
Department accepts the recommendations of the hon ourable 
Committee.  Action taken in this regard is given below : 
Apart  from  monitoring  at  Unit level/Department  level,  monitoring  
of  the  Plan projects  at micro level has been introduced. This has enabled 
29% of utilisation of the  Plan  expenditure  by  June, 2015  end. The  micro 
level monitoring is likely to  increase the capacity of utilisation of the 
allocation.  Further, it is submitted here that the Department has utilised 58% 
of the budget under Plan head till October, 2015. 
Comments 
 The Committee appreciates the monitoring at micro level besides 
at unit/Department level by the Committee and hopes that this will 
result in increased utilization of allocated resources. 
PROJECTED    DEMAND    AND    APPROVED   OUTLAY   FOR   
2015-16  

VIS-A-VIS 2014-15 
Recommendation (Para 9.8) 
 The Committee feels that reduction at B.E. to the tune of Rs. 6,506.00 
Crores against the projected outlay of Rs. 23,457.00 crore s and especially to 
the tune of Rs. 4109.00 crores under Plan Head against projected Plan BE of 
Rs. 10009.00 crore s in Demand no. 4 substantially. It has adversely 
impacted the Plan projects of the Department. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry of Finance should consider the proposal for 
increase in outlay at RE stage.  
Action Taken by Government 
Department accepts the recommendations of the honourable 
Committee and the recommendations  has  been  brought  to the  notice of  
the Ministry of  Finance for providing sufficient funds at RE 2015 -16 stage 
vide this Office DO No.3/2(4)/2014-Budget/6518 dated 26.05.2015. 
Comments 
 The Committee notes the reply and would like to be apprised of 
the progress  made in the matter. 
IMPACT OF CUT ON PROJECTS 
Recommendations (Para 9.15) 
 The Committee takes note of the fact that the Department had earlier 
also brought to the Committee’s notice a similar reduction of Rs. 957.22 
crores in the non-plan allocation under Demand No. 4, during the Demands 
for Grants for the year 2013 -14, and its adverse effect on the operational 
needs of the Heavy Wate r Plants, Nuclear Fuel Complex and BARC.  The 
Committee had accordingly recommended in its 239 th Report 
(recommendation no.11.2) for the enhancement of allocation.  The 
Department in its Action Taken Note had replied that "the recommendation 
of the Committ ee that the Department's Demand for funds should be 
adequately accommodated to obviate adverse effects on the critical or core 
activities due to shortage of funds" will be brought to the notice of the 
Ministry of Finance at Revised Estimate stage.  
Recommendation (Para 9.16) 
 The Committee expresses its serious concern over the matter that the 
issue has not been resolved yet and has come up again. There has been 
reduction of Rs. 2397.00 Crores in the outlay projected by the Department.  
Recommendation (Para 9.17) 
The Committee finds that despite the fact that the Department has 
been vigorously and forcefully taking up the issue of enhancement of 
allocation for the last three years but the Ministry of Finance had not been 
acceding to the request. In the proce ss, the strategic and crucial programmes 
of the Department are suffering. The Committee recommends that in the 
area of critical national importance, the Ministry of Finance should give 

maximum financial support for the programmes of the Department under the 
appropriate financing mechanism.  
Action Taken by Government 
The  Department  accepts the  concern  of  the  Committee  and  has 
taken up with Ministry   of   Finance   vide  this  Office  DO No.3/2(4)/2014-
Budget/6518  dated 26.05.2015. 
Department accep ts the recommendation of the honourable 
Committee and  the recommendation  has been brought to the  notice of  
Ministry of Finance for their kind consideration. 
Comments 
 The Committee notes the reply and would like to be apprised of 
the progress during Demands for Grants-2016-17. 
BHABHA ATOMIC RESEARCH CENTRE 
Recommendation (Para10.5) 
 The Committee takes note of the increased allocation to BARC, a 
prestigious Research & Development institution and hopes that a concrete 
action plan would be prepared to fully u tilise the allocated budgetary 
resources and important projects would be completed on time. 
Action Taken by Government 
Department accepts the observations of the honourable Committee. 
The action taken in this regard is given below : 
All out efforts are bei ng made to utilize the allocated budgetary resources 
and also to complete the important projects on time. Project review meetings 
are being held at micro level. With this, BARC could achieve utilization of 
funds for more than  99% of RE and FG for the years  2013-14 & 2014 -15.  
During the current financial year (2015 -16) also, as against, approved BE  
provision of Rs.1424.40 crore, the expenditure during first two months 
(April & May, 2015) was 26% of BE. The Monthly Expenditure Plan (MEP) 
targets have also be en met. Further, it is submitted here that BARC has 
utilised 50% of the budget till October, 2015. 
Comments 
 The Committee notes the fact that BARC had utilised 99% of 
Revised Estimate 2013 -14 and BE 2014 -15 allocation and could utilise 
50% of the budget t ill October 2015 and hopes that the BARC will 
continue utilizing its entire allocated budget. 
Recommendation (Para Nos.10.8 & 10.9) 
 The Committee notes the contribution of BARC in genetic mutation 
of crop plants using ionising radiation aimed at improved yields, resistant to 
diseases which have resulted in increased and improved production of 
several new crop varieties. Farmers have, thus, far benefitted from over 42 
new crop varieties produced by BARC.  
The Committee is however of the view that the Depart ment's research 
in nuclear agriculture has become more relevant than ever before in today’s 

context when agricultural yields are getting influenced and affected by 
climate change. Therefore, in order to meet challenges, the Department 
should intensify its efforts in developing high-yielding disease-resistant crop 
varieties. 
Action Taken by Government 
The Department accepts the view of the honourable Committee and in 
order  to  meet  the  challenges  in  agriculture,  the  Department  has 
undertaken through Bhabha Atomic Research Centre further R&D work for 
high yielding and disease resistant  pulses, oilseeds, wheat,  and  rice with 3 
more  Agricultural Universities (Raichur, Pantnagar, and Jabalpur) 
Comments 
 The Committee notes the reply.   
Recommendation (Para 10.11) 
 The Committee, while acknowledging the significance of Bhabha 
Atomic Research Centre (BARC) for popularising and marketing its socially 
beneficial technologies, recommends to the Department to chalk out a 
strategy to market its socially benef icial technologies such as Nisargruna 
Biogas Plant for handling biodegradable wastes; Sludge Hygienization 
Research Irradiation (SHRI) for treatment of municipal sewage, etc. 
including its technology on food preservation, nuclear medicine and 
healthcare, t hrough Technology Transfer & Collaboration Division so that 
base line of their users is increased.   
Action Taken by Government 
The recommendation of the Committee has been accepted by the 
Department and following socially beneficial activities are being progressed.   
1.  Nisagruna technology is being transferred to many techno -
entrepreneurs.  Presently, the number of this technology holders 
is more than 125. There are  about 190 Nisargruna plants 
installed at various locations in the country.   Many Municipal 
Corporations are now coming forward to install decentralized  
Nisargruna plants. BARC has signed MOUs with Municipal 
Corporations of  Chandigarh, Mumbai, Chennai, Rajkot and 
Tuticorin during this year to put up  such plants. State 
Governments of Maharashtra , Goa, Karnataka, Tamilnadu,  
Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh through their Urban Department 
or Pollution Control Boards are interacting with BARC to put 
up more plants for decentralized waste management. Ten plants 
were commissioned in the  year 2014-15. Eight plants would be 
commissioned under MOU with BARC  and other parties this 
year. This is also in line with Swatchh Bharat mission of  the 
Prime Minister.  Recently an MOU has been signed between 
BARC and Ahmedabad  Municipal Corporation to implement 
Dry Sludge Hy gienization Research  Irradiation facility for 

treatment of municipal sewage. Talks are on with   Nagpur and 
Bangalore Municipal Corporations, Punjab Pollution Control  
Board and it is proposed to approach other Municipal 
Corporations of India also to implement this technology.   
2.  Food preservation using irradiation is being popularised by 
making this technology easily accessible in various parts of the 
country. Some of these  plants are now working with full 
efficiency and licences are issued for  irradiating cereals, fruits 
and many agricultural products. These steps will  definitely help 
in increasing the number of users of such irradiated preserved  
12 food. Mangoes have been cleared for export and USA 
permitted to import  irradiated mangoes from our country.  In 
last 4 years, BARC have exported  about 1277 MT of irradiated 
mangoes to USA. Twelve irradiation plants have  been installed 
in public domain so far and 3 plants are functioning in 
Government  sector. 
3.  With regard to nuclear medicine and healthcare, a bout 25% of 
the patients  referred for nuclear medicine 
investigations/treatment are from the East and  North-East of 
India. In view of this, a proposal to set up a full -fledged 
Radiation Medicine Centre at the DAE -VECC Campus in 
Rajarhat, Kolkata, to  provide tertiary nuclear medicine support 
to East and North-East States has been initiated. The centre will 
support the Chittaranjan National Cancer  Institute at Rajarhat, 
Kolkata which is close to the proposed RMC -Kolkata.The 
VECC Medical Cyclotron is expected to be producing FDG by 
mid 2016.   A medical cyclotron will be set up in ACTREC 
Campus at Kharghar to augment the availability of low cost [F -
18] FDG for cancer and other (noncancer) patients. 
4.  During 2014-15, fourteen BARC technologies were transferred 
to 34 private  parties. MOU has been signed between 
Technology Transfer and Collaboration Division of BARC and 
CSIR-Tech, a private company, for  marketing BARC 
technologies. As per the MOU, CSIR -Tech shall promote  
BARC technologies amongst various industrie s and suggest 
suitable industries to BARC for possible technology transfer. 
Comments 
 The Committee while takes note of the reply.

KALPAKKAM

October, 2015  in   R&D  and  I&M   Sector.   An   additional   amount  of  
Rs.315   crore  is  
required   in  RE 2015-16 and the same has be en intimated to Ministry of  
Finance. 
Comments 
 The Committee while takes note of the reply.

 The Committee notes the help the Centre is providing to people of

treatment of Thyroid Cancer patients of the North -East region be further

Committee. In  this regard, the following are further submitted.   Regional

Institute is engaged in high dose lodine -131 Therapy of  Thyroid Cancer 
patients on regular basis and it is the only facility of its  kind in the State of

 The Committee takes note of the reply.

 The Committee, recommends that the Variable Energy Cyclotron

 The Committee takes note of the reply.  
MINERAL SECTOR 
URANIUM CORPORATION OF INDIA LTD. (UCIL) 
Recommendation (Para 13.7) 
 The Committee takes note of the fact that that Internal and Extra 
Budgetary Resources (IEBR) generated by UCIL have increased

Project, Meghalaya, the Committee finds that these projects are pending for 
want of environmental clearance. The Committee feels that the Department 
should pursue this matter with the Ministry of Environment, Forests & 
Climate Change vigorously to seek their early clearance.  

Action Taken by Government 
Department accepts the recommendations of the honourable 
Committee. The  matters related to above projects are being pursued at 
different levels in the Ministry of Environment and Forest (MoEF), New 
Delhi and with respective State  Governments.  Gogi uranium project in 
Karnataka After the successful Public Hearing (November 2010) a nd 
favourable recommendations of Expert Appraisal Committee (Mining) of

(December 2014) in terms of  Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) 
notification 2006 and UCIL was advised to  initiate the process of public 
hearing afresh. UCIL further enquired about the validity  of the baseline data

NABET accredited consultant (M/s MECON Ltd.) in October 2014 for

report. Prefeasibility  and Form -1 under EIA Notification  2006 are under
